root.title: Graph Cut-Coloring-Perfection Theory
root.top_down_role: Graph partition objectives and the interlocking optimization theory of coloring, cliques, stable sets, and vertex covers; general network-flow machinery, generic approximation theory, generic semidefinite optimization, and general graph-decomposition theory remain external dependencies.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point theorem for the standard fractional vertex-cover polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every graph \(G=(V,E)\), each vertex \(x\) of the fractional vertex-cover polytope \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:0\le x_v\le1\ (v\in V),\ x_u+x_v\ge1\ (\{u,v\}\in E)\}\) is half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme point of the fractional vertex-cover polytope has all coordinates in zero, one half, or one.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R^V:0\le x_v\le1\ \forall v\in V,\ x_u+x_v\ge1\ \forall\{u,v\}\in E\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable-Set, Clique, and Vertex-Cover Polytope Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull representations, complement and affine equivalences, and a conditional certificate-complexity failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \(P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_S:S\subseteq V\text{ is stable}\}\), \(P_{\mathrm{clique}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_C:C\subseteq V\text{ is a clique}\}\), and \(P_{\mathrm{vc}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf1_U:U\subseteq V\text{ is a vertex cover}\}\). Then \(P_{\mathrm{clique}}(G)=P_{\mathrm{stable}}(\bar G)\) and \(x\in P_{\mathrm{vc}}(G)\iff\mathbf1-x\in P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G)\). Moreover, if \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\), no system of valid inequalities with polynomial-time certificates of validity can have \(\mathbf1^\top x\leq\alpha(G)\) as a nonnegative linear combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These three polytopes are convex hulls of the corresponding incidence vectors. The clique polytope of a graph is the stable-set polytope of its complement, while complementing incidence vectors gives an affine correspondence between vertex covers and stable sets. If NP differs from co-NP, the stated polynomially certifiable inequality representation cannot derive the maximum-stable-set inequality by a nonnegative combination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{clique}}(G)=P_{\mathrm{stable}}(\bar G),\quad x\in P_{\mathrm{vc}}(G)\iff\mathbf1-x\in P_{\mathrm{stable}}(G),\quad \mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{coNP}\Rightarrow\text{the stated polynomially certifiable inequality system does not exist}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic clique, stable-set, cover, and coloring parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology and elementary identities for an undirected graph and its complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, a clique is a pairwise adjacent vertex set and $\omega(G)$ is its maximum size; a stable set is a pairwise nonadjacent vertex set and $\alpha(G)$ is its maximum size; a vertex cover meets every edge and $\tau(G)$ is its minimum size. A vertex coloring partitions $V$ into stable sets, with minimum size $\chi(G)$, while a clique cover partitions $V$ into cliques, with minimum size $\bar\chi(G)$. Moreover, $\alpha(G)=\omega(\bar G)$, $\bar\chi(G)=\chi(\bar G)$, $\omega(G)\leq\chi(G)$, $\alpha(G)\leq\bar\chi(G)$, and $\tau(G)=|V|-\alpha(G)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an undirected graph, define the clique, stable-set, vertex-cover, coloring, and clique-cover numbers by their respective maximum or minimum cardinalities. Stable sets correspond to cliques in the complement, clique covers correspond to colorings of the complement, every coloring has at least the clique number of colors, every clique cover has at least the stable-set number of cliques, and the vertex-cover number equals the number of vertices minus the stable-set number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)=\omega(\bar G),\quad \bar\chi(G)=\chi(\bar G),\quad \omega(G)\leq\chi(G),\quad \alpha(G)\leq\bar\chi(G),\quad \tau(G)=|V|-\alpha(G)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shannon Switching Game and its outcome classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the complete-information alternating arc-tagging game and the cut, short, and neutral classifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let distinct vertices of a graph $G$ be terminals. Players Short and Cut alternately tag previously untagged arcs. Short wins upon tagging every arc of some terminal-to-terminal path; Cut wins by preventing Short from obtaining such a path. The finite game has a winner. It is called a short game (respectively, cut game) if Short (respectively, Cut) can always win when moving second, and neutral if the player moving first can always win, whether playing Short or Cut. The terminals may equivalently be joined by a distinguished nonplayable arc $e$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two players alternately tag untagged arcs of a graph with two designated terminals. Short wins by acquiring an entire terminal path, while Cut wins by preventing this. Every finite instance ends with a winner. A short or cut game is one the corresponding player can win even when moving second; a neutral game is won by the first mover regardless of role. The terminals may be represented by a distinguished nonplayable arc.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph with two distinct designated terminal vertices.}
\text{Each move tags an arc not previously tagged by either player.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every instance has a winner and is classified as short, cut, or neutral according to the stated winning-player conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both players' winning conditions and the guaranteed outcome after all edges have been selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with \(|V|\geq2\). The cut player and short player alternately select previously unselected edges, with the cut player moving first. The cut player wins upon selecting every edge of some nontrivial cut, while the short player wins upon selecting every edge of some spanning tree. By the time every edge has been selected, at least one winning condition must hold: if the short player's edge set \(F\) is not connected on \(V\), a component of \((V,F)\) determines a nontrivial cut disjoint from \(F\), all of whose edges belong to the cut player.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a connected undirected graph with at least two vertices, the cut player and short player alternately claim unclaimed edges, starting with the cut player. The cut player wins by claiming an entire nontrivial cut, and the short player wins by claiming an entire spanning tree. Once all edges are claimed, one of these conditions necessarily holds.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
\text{the cut player moves first and each move selects one previously unselected edge}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{After all edges are selected, the short player owns a spanning tree or the cut player owns every edge of a nontrivial cut.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common Terminal-Separating Cut Packing Min-Max Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum packing of disjoint cuts simultaneously separating two terminal pairs in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite and let $s_1,t_1,s_2,t_2\in V$. The maximum number of pairwise disjoint cuts, each separating both $s_1$ from $t_1$ and $s_2$ from $t_2$, equals $\min\{\operatorname{dist}_G(s_1,t_1),\operatorname{dist}_G(s_2,t_2)\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, the maximum number of disjoint cuts simultaneously separating both terminal pairs is the smaller of the two terminal-pair distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|\mathcal C|:\mathcal C\text{ is a family of pairwise disjoint cuts, each separating both terminal pairs}\}=\min\{\operatorname{dist}_G(s_1,t_1),\operatorname{dist}_G(s_2,t_2)\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected networks with cut values determined by the arcs in each separating cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct nodes \(i,j\), an \([i,j]\)-cut is a bipartition \([S_{ij},\bar S_{ij}]\) that places \(i\) and \(j\) in different parts and whose cut arcs disconnect those parts. A minimum \([i,j]\)-cut \([S_{ij}^*,\bar S_{ij}^*]\) minimizes the prescribed arc-based cut value, denoted \(v[i,j]\). The all-pairs minimum-value cut problem is to determine \([S_{ij}^*,\bar S_{ij}^*]\) and \(v[i,j]\) for every unordered pair \(\{i,j\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An i–j cut separates i from j in an undirected network. A minimum i–j cut has the least value among such cuts. The all-pairs problem asks for a minimum cut and its value for every unordered node pair.
assumptions_latex: \text{Each cut has a value determined by its cut arcs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Determine }([S_{ij}^*,\bar S_{ij}^*],v[i,j])\text{ for every unordered pair }\{i,j\}\subseteq N.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), the directed two-terminal cut induced by \(S\) is \(\delta^+(S)\), and its capacity is \(c(\delta^+(S))\). The directed minimum-cut problem is
\[
\lambda_D(s,t)=\min_{S\subseteq V:\,s\in S,\,t\notin S}\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}c(a).
\]
Deleting \(\delta^+(S)\) destroys every directed path from \(s\) to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed two-terminal cut consists of all arcs leaving an s-containing set that excludes t; its value is their total capacity, minimized over all such sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), the undirected two-terminal cut induced by \(S\) is \(\delta(S)\), and its capacity is \(c(\delta(S))\). The undirected minimum-cut problem is
\[
\lambda_G(s,t)=\min_{S\subseteq V:\,s\in S,\,t\notin S}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}c(e).
\]
Deleting \(\delta(S)\) places \(s\) and \(t\) in different connected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected two-terminal cut contains the edges crossing an s-t vertex partition; the minimum cut has least total capacity among all such partitions.

children.title: Vertex-Capacitated Cut Models
children.top_down_role: Vertex-capacity regimes for terminal separation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, \(s,t\in V\) are distinct, and \(w:V\setminus\{s,t\}\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_w(s,t)=\min\{\sum_{v\in X}w(v):X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\},\ s,t\text{ disconnected in }G-X\}\).

notation.meaning: graph obtained by deleting vertices X and incident edges

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted internal-vertex deletion model with undeletable terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vertex-capacitated \(s\)-\(t\) cut is a set \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(s\) and \(t\) lie in different connected components of \(G-X\). Its cost is \(w(X)=\sum_{v\in X}w(v)\), and the optimization problem is
\[
\kappa_w(s,t)=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in X}w(v):X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\},\ s\not\leftrightsquigarrow t\text{ in }G-X\right\}.
\]
If no such set exists, the value is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex-capacitated cut deletes minimum-weight nonterminal vertices so that s and t become disconnected; terminals themselves cannot be deleted.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Capacitated Cut Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted nonterminal vertex-deletion model is standard and definition fits the leaf, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator is supplied. A source should also confirm the stated +infinity convention for infeasible instances.

children.title: Node-Splitting Network Constructions
children.top_down_role: Network representations used to encode vertex capacities.

assumptions_latex: A finite bound \(M>\sum_{v\ne s,t}w(v)\) represents infinite capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-capacity \(s^{\mathrm{out}}\)-\(t^{\mathrm{in}}\) cuts in the split network correspond cost-preservingly to directed vertex cuts in \(D\).

notation.meaning: large capacity exceeding every feasible vertex-cut cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard reduction of directed vertex cuts to directed edge cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace each \(v\in V\) by \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\) and \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\), add the internal arc \((v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\) of capacity \(w(v)\) for \(v\notin\{s,t\}\), and give terminal internal arcs capacity \(M\). Replace every \((u,v)\in A\) by \((u^{\mathrm{out}},v^{\mathrm{in}})\) of capacity \(M\). Then any cut of capacity less than \(M\) uses only internal arcs, and
\[
X=\{v:(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}})\text{ is cut}\}
\]
is a directed vertex cut of identical cost; conversely every such vertex cut induces this edge cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split every vertex into an input and output copy. Finite-capacity internal arcs encode vertex costs, while large-capacity arcs preserve the original adjacency.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Splitting Network Constructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the appropriate content kind, but the cost-preserving correspondence and the choice of split-network terminals require authoritative support. The source should explicitly validate the less-than-M qualification and the converse construction.

children.title: Node-Splitting Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Model features that preserve or obstruct the reduction.

assumptions_latex: The split network uses a bound \(M\) larger than the cost of every admissible vertex cut represented.
Each original traversal enters \(v^{\mathrm{in}}\), crosses its unique internal arc, and leaves \(v^{\mathrm{out}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without these conditions, minimum split-network edge cuts need not encode admissible vertex cuts or preserve their objective values.

notation.meaning: capacity used to forbid cutting structural or terminal arcs
total weight of a represented vertex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp modeling conditions for cost-preserving node splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cost-preserving correspondence fails if a structural arc can be cheaper than the represented vertex cuts: a minimum edge cut may then sever that arc instead of an internal vertex arc. It also fails if terminals are assigned finite removable capacities when the original model forbids terminal deletion. For undirected graphs, replacing an edge \(uv\) requires both directed arcs \((u^{\mathrm{out}},v^{\mathrm{in}})\) and \((v^{\mathrm{out}},u^{\mathrm{in}})\); omitting one changes reachability. Thus validity requires protected structural arcs, correctly protected terminals, and traversal through exactly one capacity arc per removable vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node splitting is valid only when structural arcs and protected terminals cannot be cheaply cut, and every original traversal crosses the appropriate vertex-capacity arc.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Splitting Validity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the terminal container, and the listed modeling hazards are plausible, but no source supports their asserted necessity or scope. The traversal condition should be stated specifically for removable internal vertices because source and sink traversals need not cross their terminal internal arcs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with weights \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
\(T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\subseteq V\) is a set of distinct terminals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}=\min\{\sum_{e\in F}c(e):F\subseteq E,\text{ no component of }G-F\text{ contains two terminals}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected edge multiway cut with all terminal pairs separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An edge multiway cut is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that every connected component of \(G-F\) contains at most one vertex of \(T\). Equivalently, for every distinct \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), vertices \(t_i\) and \(t_j\) are disconnected in \(G-F\). Its value is
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}=
\min_{F\subseteq E}\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c(e):|C\cap T|\le1\text{ for every component }C\text{ of }G-F\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge multiway cut removes minimum-weight edges so that no remaining connected component contains more than one terminal.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge Multiway Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is a precise definition of weighted undirected edge multiway cut and matches the leaf, but it has no cited authoritative source with a locator.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected, with distinct terminals \(T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\).
\(w:V\setminus T\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and terminals are not removable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{NMWC}}=\min\{\sum_{v\in X}w(v):X\subseteq V\setminus T,\text{ every component of }G-X\text{ contains at most one terminal}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected node multiway cut with undeletable terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A node-weighted multiway cut is a set \(X\subseteq V\setminus T\) such that each connected component of \(G-X\) contains at most one terminal. Its value is
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{NMWC}}=
\min_{X\subseteq V\setminus T}
\left\{\sum_{v\in X}w(v):|C\cap T|\le1\text{ for every component }C\text{ of }G-X\right\}.
\]
If two terminals are adjacent and terminal deletion is forbidden, no feasible vertex cut exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-weighted multiway cut deletes minimum-weight nonterminals until every remaining component contains at most one terminal.
knowledge_statements.title: Node-Weighted Multiway Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly models undeletable terminals and weighted nonterminal deletion, including the obstruction created by adjacent terminals. No authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected capacitated graph with terminals \(T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\).
For each \(i\), \(S_i\) is the source side of a minimum cut separating \(t_i\) from \(T\setminus\{t_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(F_j=\bigcup_{i\ne j}\delta(S_i)\) is a feasible multiway cut, and some \(j\) satisfies \(c(F_j)\le(2-2/k)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}\).

notation.meaning: minimum isolating region for terminal i
candidate formed by omitting one isolating cut

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical isolating-cut approximation scheme for undirected edge multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), compute a minimum cut \(\delta(S_i)\) with \(t_i\in S_i\) and \(S_i\cap(T\setminus\{t_i\})=\varnothing\). For every \(j\), form
\[
F_j=\bigcup_{i\ne j}\delta(S_i).
\]
Return a minimum-capacity member of \(\{F_1,\ldots,F_k\}\). Each \(F_j\) separates all terminals, and the returned set satisfies
\[
c(F_j)\le\left(2-\frac{2}{k}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute one minimum isolating cut per terminal, omit the most advantageous one, and return the cheapest resulting union; this gives the classical multiway-cut approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Isolating-Cut Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, but the exact feasibility and (2-2/k) approximation claims need an authoritative theorem-level citation. The hypotheses should explicitly require k at least 2, since the displayed factor divides by k and the intended multiway-cut setting has multiple terminals.

children.title: Simplex-Embedding Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Simplex-valued representations for multiway-cut relaxations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with capacities \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
\(T=\{t_1,\ldots,t_k\}\), and \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linear program is a relaxation of edge multiway cut, and every terminal-respecting integral labeling has objective equal to its cut capacity.

notation.meaning: simplex vector assigned to vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: CKR-type simplex relaxation for undirected edge multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assign each vertex \(v\in V\) a point \(x_v\in\Delta_k\) and fix \(x_{t_i}=e_i\) for every terminal. The simplex relaxation is
\[
\min\ \frac12\sum_{uv\in E}c(uv)\|x_u-x_v\|_1
\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_v\in\Delta_k\text{ for all }v\in V,\quad x_{t_i}=e_i.
\]
For an integral labeling \(x_v\in\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\), an edge contributes its capacity exactly when its endpoints receive different labels; hence the objective equals the induced multiway-cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embed vertices in the terminal simplex, fix terminals at distinct corners, and minimize weighted half-Manhattan edge lengths; integral embeddings exactly encode multiway cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Simplex-Embedding Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation appropriately describes the simplex LP and its integral-labeling interpretation, and the normalization is internally consistent. No authoritative source with a specific locator is provided for the CKR-type relaxation.

children.title: Geometric Rounding Families
children.top_down_role: Geometric partition mechanisms applied to simplex embeddings.

assumptions_latex: A feasible simplex embedding \((x_v)_{v\in V}\) satisfies \(x_v\in\Delta_k\) and \(x_{t_i}=e_i\).
The rounding rule assigns every vertex to exactly one terminal and fixes each terminal's assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output labeling induces a feasible edge multiway cut \(F=\{uv\in E:L(u)\ne L(v)\}\).

notation.meaning: random terminal labeling produced by rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic geometric rounding interface, independent of a particular threshold distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a feasible embedding \((x_v)_{v\in V}\). Sample the geometric parameters prescribed by a rounding distribution, use the resulting simplex regions to define a total labeling \(L:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and enforce \(L(t_i)=i\). Output
\[
F_L=\{uv\in E:L(u)\ne L(v)\}.
\]
Because distinct terminals receive distinct labels, \(F_L\) is a feasible multiway cut. Its expected capacity is
\[
\mathbb{E}[c(F_L)]=\sum_{uv\in E}c(uv)\Pr[L(u)\ne L(v)].
\]
A concrete rounding family is analyzed by bounding each separation probability in terms of \(\|x_u-x_v\|_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random geometric regions partition the simplex and label every vertex by a terminal. Edges whose endpoints receive different labels form a feasible multiway cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Rounding Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the leaf, and any terminal-respecting total labeling induces a feasible cut. However, the candidate does not specify an actual geometric rounding distribution or region construction, so it is only an abstract interface; no source identifies or supports the claimed rounding family.

children.title: Relaxation-to-Rounding Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance regimes governing losses between relaxed solutions and rounded cuts.

assumptions_latex: \(L(x)=\frac12\sum_{uv\in E}c(uv)\|x_u-x_v\|_1\) is the value of a feasible simplex embedding.
A rounding distribution satisfies \(\Pr[L(u)\ne L(v)]\le\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x_u-x_v\|_1\) for every edge \(uv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[c(F_L)]\le\alpha L(x)\), so the rounding approximation factor is at most \(\alpha\); conversely, an integrality-gap instance lower-bounds every LP-relative guarantee.

notation.meaning: edge multiway cut produced by rounding

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract relation among separation density, approximation ratio, and integrality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If every edge \(uv\in E\) obeys
\[
\Pr[L(u)\ne L(v)]\le\frac{\alpha}{2}\|x_u-x_v\|_1,
\]
then linearity of expectation gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[c(F_L)]\le\alpha L(x)\le\alpha\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}.
\]
For an instance \(I\), define its gap by \(g(I)=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{EMWC}}(I)/\operatorname{LP}(I)\). Any guarantee proved solely by comparing output cost with this relaxation must have factor at least \(\sup_I g(I)\); matching upper and lower values identify a tight regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge-separation bound of alpha times its LP length yields an alpha approximation. The relaxation's worst integral-to-fractional ratio limits any LP-relative analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-to-Rounding Gap Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation inequality is algebraically consistent, but no source supports the integrality-gap boundary claim. The symbol L is also used both for the objective L(x) and, through the prerequisite rounding record, for the random labeling L; these should be distinguished. A source must state the precise class of LP-relative guarantees to which the lower-bound assertion applies.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with weights \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\).
\(\mathcal{D}=\{(s_i,t_i):1\le i\le r\}\) is a collection of demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}=\min\{\sum_{e\in F}c(e):F\subseteq E,\ s_i\text{ and }t_i\text{ are disconnected in }G-F\text{ for every }i\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected edge multicut for an arbitrary collection of demand pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An undirected multicut is a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that, for every \((s_i,t_i)\in\mathcal{D}\), no path in \(G-F\) joins \(s_i\) to \(t_i\). Its value is
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MC}}=
\min_{F\subseteq E}
\left\{\sum_{e\in F}c(e):s_i\not\leftrightsquigarrow t_i\text{ in }G-F\text{ for all }i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\right\}.
\]
Pairs may share endpoints, and pairs not listed in \(\mathcal{D}\) need not be separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected multicut removes minimum-weight edges so that every specified demand pair becomes disconnected; pairs absent from the demand list may remain connected.
knowledge_statements.title: Undirected Multicut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record precisely defines weighted undirected edge multicut for a listed collection of demand pairs, and definition is the correct content kind. It lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines multicuts induced by vertex partitions, including ordinary cuts and 3-cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be an undirected graph and let $V(G)=X_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}\cdots\mathbin{\dot\cup}X_p$ be a partition into nonempty sets. The associated multicut is $\delta(X_1,\ldots,X_p):=\delta(X_1)\cup\cdots\cup\delta(X_p)$. A partition multicut with $p=3$ is a $3$-cut, and an ordinary cut is the case $p=2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partition multicut is the union of the edge boundaries of all nonempty blocks in a partition of the vertex set. Three blocks give a 3-cut, while two blocks give an ordinary cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(X_1,\ldots,X_p):=\bigcup_{i=1}^p\delta(X_i);\quad p=3\Rightarrow\text{$3$-cut},\quad p=2\Rightarrow\text{ordinary cut}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) has minimum capacity among all arc sets separating every ordered demand pair.

notation.meaning: Total capacity of an arc set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization definition for nonnegative-capacity directed graphs and ordered demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A directed multicut is an arc set \(F\subseteq A\) such that, for every \((s_i,t_i)\in\mathcal{D}\), the digraph \(D-F\) contains no directed path from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\). The directed multicut problem is
\[
\min\left\{c(F):F\subseteq A,\; t_i\text{ is unreachable from }s_i\text{ in }D-F\text{ for every }(s_i,t_i)\in\mathcal{D}\right\}.
\]
Demands are directional: separating \(s_i\) from \(t_i\) does not require separating \(t_i\) from \(s_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a minimum-capacity set of arcs so that no demand target remains reachable from its corresponding demand source.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Multicut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Directed Multicut container, but no inspectable source is supplied. A source-supported formulation should also state whether every ordered demand pair has distinct endpoints, since a demand (v,v) makes the stated path-separation condition infeasible under the usual length-zero-path convention.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected supply graph.
\(H=(T,D)\) is a demand graph with \(T\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restricting \(H\) restricts which terminal pairs must be separated and can define distinct multicut subclasses.

notation.meaning: Supply graph whose edges may be deleted.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demand graphs encode the terminal pairs constrained by an undirected multicut instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a supply graph \(G=(V,E)\) and demand graph \(H=(T,D)\), an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) is feasible precisely when
\[
\forall\,uv\in D,\qquad u\text{ and }v\text{ lie in distinct connected components of }G-F.
\]
A demand-graph restriction specifies a class \(\mathcal{H}\) and permits only instances with \(H\in\mathcal{H}\). Examples of mathematically distinct restrictions include matching demands, star demands, bounded-degree demands, and demands whose graph belongs to a prescribed minor-closed class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A demand graph specifies exactly which terminal pairs a feasible multicut must disconnect; structural restrictions on that graph define specialized problem classes.
knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Graph Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly encodes an undirected multicut through a demand graph and fits the terminal container. The asserted taxonomy of matching, star, bounded-degree, and minor-closed demand restrictions has no inspectable citation, so the record requires a source.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected bipartite graph and let \(\mathcal F=\{E[U]:U\subseteq V\text{ is a vertex cover and }E[U]\neq\varnothing\}\). Then the minimum cardinality of an edge set intersecting every member of \(\mathcal F\) equals the maximum cardinality of a pairwise disjoint subfamily of \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected bipartite graph, form the nonempty edge sets induced by its vertex covers. The minimum number of edges needed to meet every such set equals the maximum number of pairwise disjoint such sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\), let
\[
\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:|\{u,v\}\cap S|=1\}.
\]
The undirected global minimum-cut value is
\[
\lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c(\delta(S)).
\]
Any bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\) attaining this value is a global minimum cut. No source, sink, or terminal pair is prescribed; the optimization ranges over every nontrivial bipartition of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all nontrivial vertex bipartitions, an undirected global minimum cut minimizes the total capacity of edges crossing the bipartition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum edge cuts in vertex-transitive regular graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives edge connectivity and a structural dichotomy for all minimum edge cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a simple, connected, vertex-transitive, $r$-regular graph with $r\ge 3$. Then $G$ is $r$-edge-connected. Moreover, either every minimum edge cut of $G$ is the star of a vertex, or $G$ is obtained from a possibly nonsimple vertex- and edge-transitive $r$-regular graph $G_0$ by performing an $r$-clique insertion at every vertex of $G_0$. In the latter case, every minimum edge cut of $G$ is either the star of a vertex of $G$ or a minimum edge cut of $G_0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple connected vertex-transitive r-regular graph with r at least three has edge connectivity r. Every minimum edge cut is a vertex star unless the graph comes from inserting an r-clique at every vertex of a vertex- and edge-transitive r-regular base graph; in that case the other minimum cuts are inherited from the base graph.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is simple, connected, and vertex-transitive}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(G)=r\ \text{and either all minimum edge cuts are vertex stars, or }G\text{ has the stated clique-insertion representation and cut classification}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Undirected edge connectivity and minimum cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines edge connectivity both by disconnecting edge sets and by nontrivial cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), its edge-connectivity is \(\lambda(G):=\min\{|C|:C\subseteq E,\ G-C\text{ is disconnected}\}=\min_{\varnothing\ne U\ne V}|\delta(U)|\). A cut attaining this minimum is a minimum cut, and \(G\) is \(k\)-edge-connected when \(\lambda(G)\ge k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The edge connectivity of an undirected graph is the minimum number of edges whose deletion disconnects it, equivalently the minimum size of a nontrivial cut. A minimizing cut is a minimum cut, and the graph is k-edge-connected when this value is at least k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(G)=\min\{|C|:C\subseteq E,\ G-C\text{ disconnected}\}=\min_{\varnothing\ne U\ne V}|\delta(U)|,\qquad G\text{ is }k\text{-edge-connected}\iff\lambda(G)\ge k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V\), define
\[
\delta^+(S)=\{uv\in A:u\in S,\ v\notin S\},\qquad
\delta^-(S)=\delta^+(V\setminus S).
\]
Under the outgoing-cut convention, the directed global minimum-cut value is
\[
\lambda^+(D)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c(\delta^+(S)).
\]
A minimizing shore \(S\) is a directed global minimum cut. Replacing \(S\) by its complement generally changes the capacity, because \(c(\delta^+(S))\) need not equal \(c(\delta^-(S))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed global minimum cut minimizes outgoing arc capacity over all nonempty proper vertex shores; complementary shores need not have equal capacity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stage initialization, admissible operations, treatment rule, and construction of the certified minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Stage 1 initializes \(R=\{r_0\}\), sets \(x(r_0v)=g(r_0v)\) and all other arc values to zero, and assigns levels \(\Theta(r_0)=n\), \(\Theta(t_1)=0\), and \(\Theta(v)=1\) otherwise. For \(j\ge2\), move \(t_{j-1}\) to \(R=L_n\), remove it from \(U'\), saturate its arcs into \(U'\), set its arcs from \(U'\) to zero, select \(t_j\in L_j\), and lift every node of \(L_j\setminus\{t_j\}\) once. At a \(\Psi_x\)-positive node \(z\), push \(\alpha=\min\{g(zu)-x(zu),\Psi_x(z)\}\) on an increasable down-step arc \(zu\), or decrease \(x(uz)\) by \(\alpha=\min\{x(uz),\Psi_x(z)\}\) on a decreasable up-step arc \(uz\); if no push is possible and \(z\) is not alone on its level, lift \(z\). Repeatedly treat a highest-level nonsingular positive node outside \(t_j\). If none remains, return \(Z_j=U'\) when there is no positive node outside \(t_j\); otherwise, for a lowest-level singular positive node \(z'\) of level \(j'\), return \(Z_j=\{v:j\le\Theta(v)<j'\}\). In either case the returned \(Z_j\) satisfies the feasible-vector optimality criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each stage updates the root set, arc vector, and levels, then repeatedly pushes imbalance along admissible adjacent-level arcs or lifts blocked positive nodes. When no treatable positive node remains, it returns either all nonroot nodes or the level interval below the lowest singular positive node; the returned set satisfies the minimum-cut optimality certificate.
assumptions_latex: r_0,t_1,\ldots,t_n\text{ is the evolving node order}
\{R,x,\Theta\}\text{ satisfies the stated stage initialization and level properties}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t_j\in Z_j\subseteq U'\quad\text{and}\quad (x,Z_j)\text{ satisfies the optimality criteria for a }t_j\text{-minimizer}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level Properties of the Directed Minimum-Cut Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stage invariants for the root set, feasible vector, and level function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At stage \(j\), let \(R=R_j\), \(0\le x\le g\), \(\Theta:V\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), \(U'=V\setminus R\), and let \(L_k=\{v:\Theta(v)=k\}\). The level properties are: (LP1) \(R=L_n\), every \(\Psi_x\)-negative node lies in \(R\), \(\delta_x(R)=\delta_g(R)\), and \(\varrho_x(R)=0\); (LP2') \(\Theta(v)\ge\Theta(u)-1\) for every increasable edge \(uv\) induced by \(U'\); (LP2'') \(\Theta(v)\le\Theta(u)+1\) for every decreasable edge \(uv\) induced by \(U'\); and (LP3) \(\Theta\) is contiguous, \(|R|=j+1\), \(L_j\) is the lowest nonempty level, and \(|L_j|=1\). The LP2 conditions apply only to edges induced by \(U'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm maintains a top-level root set containing all negative-imbalance nodes, saturated outward and zero inward boundary conditions for that root set, one-step level inequalities on increasable and decreasable edges inside the nonroot subgraph, and contiguous levels with a unique node at the lowest occupied level j. The edge inequalities are required only inside the nonroot set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{LP1}\wedge\mathrm{LP2'}\wedge\mathrm{LP2''}\wedge\mathrm{LP3}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed global arc-connectivity through arc deletion and outgoing cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ with $|V|\ge 2$, its arc-connectivity is
\[\lambda(D):=\min\{|C|:C\subseteq A,\ D-C\text{ is not strongly connected}\}=\min_{\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V}|\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U)|.\]
A cut attaining this value is a minimum cut. The digraph $D$ is $k$-arc-connected, or strongly $k$-connected, when $\lambda(D)\ge k$. In particular, $D$ is $1$-arc-connected if and only if it is strongly connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arc-connectivity is the minimum number of arcs whose deletion destroys strong connectivity, equivalently the minimum size of an outgoing cut of a nonempty proper vertex subset. A minimizing cut is a minimum cut. A digraph is k-arc-connected when its arc-connectivity is at least k, and 1-arc-connectivity is equivalent to strong connectivity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda(D)=\min_{\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V}|\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U)|,\qquad D\text{ is }k\text{-arc-connected}\iff\lambda(D)\ge k.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected loopless multigraph with \(n=|V|\ge 2\).
Each contraction chooses an extant edge uniformly at random.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One trial returns a fixed minimum cut with probability at least \(2/(n(n-1))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted random contraction; integer weights may be represented by parallel edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
While more than two supervertices remain, choose an extant edge uniformly at random, contract its endpoints, retain parallel edges, and delete self-loops. Output the edges between the final two supervertices. For any fixed global minimum cut, the probability that no edge of that cut is contracted is at least
\[
\prod_{i=3}^{n}\left(1-\frac{2}{i}\right)=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}.
\]
Running \(r\) independent trials and returning the lightest result raises the success probability to at least \(1-(1-2/(n(n-1)))^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly contract edges until two supervertices remain. Repetition amplifies the inverse-quadratic probability that a trial preserves and returns a minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Karger Random-Contraction Family

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A sparse \(k\)-connectivity certificate is a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) satisfying \(|F|\le k(|V|-1)\) and
\[
\min\{k,\lambda_H(u,v)\}=\min\{k,\lambda_G(u,v)\}
\quad\text{for all distinct }u,v\in V.
\]
Consequently, every pairwise edge connectivity below \(k\) is preserved exactly, while every connectivity at least \(k\) remains at least \(k\). Thus, when \(k\ge\lambda(G)\), computing a global minimum cut in \(H\) yields the same value as in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sparse certificate keeps only linearly many edges per connectivity level while preserving all cuts below the chosen threshold, including a sufficiently small global minimum cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Certificate Minimum-Cut Methods

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some spanning tree in the support of a sufficiently large fractional packing crosses a global minimum cut at most twice.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative weight assigned to spanning tree T.
Edges of T crossing shore S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional spanning-tree packing principle underlying minimum-cut search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fractional spanning-tree packing assigns weights \(x_T\ge0\) such that
\[
\sum_{T\ni e}x_T\le1\quad\text{for every }e\in E.
\]
For any global minimum-cut shore \(S\),
\[
\sum_Tx_T\,|T\cap\delta(S)|\le\lambda.
\]
If the packing has total weight \(\tau\ge\lambda/2\), the weighted average crossing count is at most two; hence some tree \(T\) with \(x_T>0\) satisfies \(|T\cap\delta(S)|\le2\). Minimum-cut methods exploit this by searching cuts that one-respect or two-respect packed trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large fractional spanning-tree packing contains a tree crossed at most twice by some global minimum cut, reducing cut search to tree-structured candidates.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Packing Minimum-Cut Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional-packing inequality and averaging implication are mathematically plausible and the property is relevant to tree-packing minimum-cut methods, but no source is supplied. The plain statement also says only that some global minimum cut is crossed at most twice, whereas the LaTeX statement establishes the support-tree conclusion for any fixed global minimum-cut shore.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each fixed \(k\), minimum \(k\)-cut is exactly solvable in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: Partition of the vertices into k nonempty parts.
Edges whose endpoints occupy different parts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact complexity regime when the number of required components is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The fixed-\(k\) minimum-cut problem computes
\[
\operatorname{OPT}_k(G)=\min\left\{w(\delta(\Pi)):\Pi=(V_1,\ldots,V_k),\;V_i\ne\varnothing,\;\biguplus_{i=1}^{k}V_i=V\right\}.
\]
When \(k\) is a constant independent of the input size, exact algorithms run in time \(n^{O(k)}\), and therefore in polynomial time for every fixed \(k\). The exponent may depend on \(k\); this statement does not assert fixed-parameter tractability with respect to \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any constant number of required components, an exact minimum k-cut can be found in polynomial time, although the exponent may depend on k.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-k Minimum Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction between fixed k and input-dependent k is stated correctly, and complexity_bound fits this regime leaf. The nontrivial exact running-time claim n^{O(k)} has no authoritative algorithm or theorem citation, so it cannot yet be accepted.

\(k\), encoded as part of the input, satisfies \(2\le k\le|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variable-\(k\) minimum-cut optimization problem is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Input number of required nonempty parts.
A partition into k nonempty parts.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity regime in which the requested number of components belongs to the input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The variable-\(k\) problem receives both \(G\) and \(k\) and seeks
\[
\min\left\{w(\delta(\Pi)):\Pi=(V_1,\ldots,V_k),\;V_i\ne\varnothing,\;\biguplus_{i=1}^{k}V_i=V\right\}.
\]
Unlike the fixed-\(k\) regime, allowing \(k\) to grow with the instance makes exact minimum \(k\)-cut NP-hard. Thus a running-time guarantee of the form \(n^{O(k)}\) is not a polynomial-time algorithm for this regime, because its exponent is input-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When k is part of the input rather than a constant, exact minimum k-cut is NP-hard; fixed-k polynomial bounds do not remain polynomial uniformly.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-k Minimum Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The variable-k regime is clearly separated from the fixed-k regime and complexity_bound is the appropriate content kind. The NP-hardness claim requires a specific authoritative theorem citation and a source-supported decision-problem and weight-encoding formulation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterative splitting output has weight at most \((2-2/k)\operatorname{OPT}_k(G)\).

notation.meaning: Weight of the final crossing edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical repeated-splitting approximation for weighted undirected minimum k-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\mathcal{P}=\{V\}\). While \(|\mathcal{P}|<k\), for every part \(U\in\mathcal{P}\) compute a global minimum cut of the induced graph \(G[U]\); choose a part and such a cut having minimum weight, and replace \(U\) by its two nonempty shores. After exactly \(k-1\) splits, output all edges joining different parts of \(\mathcal{P}\). The resulting cut satisfies
\[
w(\delta(\mathcal{P}))\le\left(2-\frac{2}{k}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_k(G).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly split the current part having the cheapest internal minimum cut; after k parts are formed, the result is a 2−2/k approximation.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum k-Cut Approximation Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The iterative splitting algorithm and claimed 2-2/k guarantee are appropriate for the approximation-family leaf, but the nontrivial approximation theorem and exact choice rule have no inspectable source. Source verification is required before accepting the formula and variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be the vertices reachable from \(s\) in \(D_f\). Since \(t\notin S\), the pair \((S,V\setminus S)\) is an \(s\)-\(t\) cut. Absence of residual arcs leaving \(S\) implies that every original arc in \(\delta^+(S)\) is saturated and every original arc in \(\delta^-(S)\) carries zero flow. Therefore
\[
|f|=f(\delta^+(S))-f(\delta^-(S))=c(\delta^+(S)).
\]
Feasibility of \(f\), residual reachability, and these equalities are directly checkable and certify simultaneous flow and cut optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal value of pairwise connectivity synthesis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the exact minimum total capacity and the half-integrality guarantee for integral demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V$ be finite, let $r$ be a symmetric nonnegative demand function on distinct pairs of $V$, let $E^*$ be the complete undirected edge set, and define $R(v):=\max_{x\in V\setminus\{v\}}r(v,x)$. Among all $g:E^*\to\mathbb{R}_+$ satisfying $\lambda_g(u,v)\ge r(u,v)$ for every distinct $u,v\in V$, the minimum of $\sum_{e\in E^*}g(e)$ equals $\frac12\sum_{v\in V}R(v)$. If $r$ is integer-valued, an optimal $g$ may be chosen half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For symmetric pairwise demands, the least possible total capacity of a feasible complete-graph capacity assignment is one half of the sum, over all vertices, of their largest incident demands. When all demands are integers, some optimal capacity assignment has values in half-integers.

Conversely, every nontrivial bipartition produced by one of these permitted deletions pulls back to a global minimum cut of \(G\). Here a cactus is a connected graph in which every edge belongs to at most one cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Preserving Sparse Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold connectivity certificate for finite undirected multigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,F)\) of \(G\) satisfying \(|F|\le k(|V|-1)\) and, for every \(S\subseteq V\), \[\min\{k,|\delta_H(S)|\}=\min\{k,|\delta_G(S)|\}.\] Consequently, for every \(u,v\in V\), \[\min\{k,\lambda_H(u,v)\}=\min\{k,\lambda_G(u,v)\}.\] Thus \(H\) preserves each cut size and each local edge-connectivity value after truncation at \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning subgraph with at most k(n−1) edges preserves every cut size, and hence every pairwise edge connectivity, after truncation at k.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) with at most \(k(|V|-1)\) edges that preserves every cut size and every local edge-connectivity value after truncation at \(k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite undirected weighted formulation; weights may be signed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weighted Max-Cut value is \[\operatorname{mc}(G,w)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}w_e.\] A feasible solution is the bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\), with an edge contributing precisely when its endpoints lie in different parts. Equivalently, using labels \(x_v\in\{-1,1\}\), \[\operatorname{mc}(G,w)=\max_x\frac12\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}(1-x_ux_v).\] Complementary sets define the same cut. When all weights are nonnegative, an optimum never loses value by including an edge solely because of its sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted Max-Cut selects a bipartition maximizing the total weight of edges whose endpoints lie on opposite sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Max-Cut

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced weighted cut with the standard near-equality convention for odd order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maximum-bisection value is \[\max\left\{w(\delta(S)):S\subseteq V,\ \bigl||S|-|V\setminus S|\bigr|\le 1\right\}.\] Thus, when \(n\) is even, both sides must contain exactly \(n/2\) vertices; when \(n\) is odd, their sizes are \((n-1)/2\) and \((n+1)/2\). A feasible solution is such a balanced bipartition, and its objective is the sum of weights of edges having endpoints in different parts. Removing the balance constraint recovers weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum Bisection finds a maximum-weight cut whose two vertex sides have equal, or as nearly equal as possible, cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Bisection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The near-equal-side formulation is coherent, but the odd-order convention and permitted weight domain require an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(\mathcal P=(V_1,\ldots,V_k)\) of \(V\) into \(k\) nonempty sets, let \(\delta(\mathcal P)\) contain the edges whose endpoints lie in different parts. The Max \(k\)-Cut value is \[\operatorname{mc}_k(G,w)=\max_{\mathcal P}\sum_{e\in\delta(\mathcal P)}w_e.\] Equivalently, assign each vertex a label \(x_v\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and maximize \(\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[x_u\ne x_v]\), subject to every label being used. For \(k=2\), this is weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Max k-Cut partitions the vertices into k nonempty classes to maximize the total weight of edges joining different classes.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with signs \(\sigma_e\in\{+1,-1\}\) and nonnegative magnitudes \(a_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A signed cut may be optimized by minimizing positive edges cut plus negative edges uncut, equivalently maximizing satisfied signed adjacencies.

notation.meaning: binary side label of vertex v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical two-cluster signed-disagreement convention; other signed-cut conventions exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartition encoded by \(x_v\in\{-1,1\}\), call a positive edge satisfied when its endpoints share a side and a negative edge satisfied when they occupy opposite sides. Its disagreement cost is \[D(x)=\sum_{uv\in E:\,\sigma_{uv}=+1}a_{uv}\mathbf 1[x_u\ne x_v]+\sum_{uv\in E:\,\sigma_{uv}=-1}a_{uv}\mathbf 1[x_u=x_v].\] The signed-graph cut problem in this convention minimizes \(D(x)\), equivalently maximizes the total magnitude of satisfied edges. A zero-cost solution exists exactly when the signed graph admits a bipartition satisfying every signed adjacency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed cut seeks two clusters that keep positive edges together and place negative edges apart, minimizing the total violated edge magnitude.
knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Graph Cut Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives one valid two-cluster signed-disagreement convention, while the leaf title covers signed-graph cut problems more broadly. A source is required to establish the intended convention and scope.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut cone is the conic hull of all cut incidence vectors in \(\mathbb R^{E_n}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-graph cut cone in edge-coordinate space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\delta(S)_{ij}=1\) when exactly one of \(i,j\) lies in \(S\), and define \(\delta(S)_{ij}=0\) otherwise. The cut cone is \[\operatorname{CUT}_n=\operatorname{cone}\{\delta(S):S\subseteq[n]\}=\left\{\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\alpha_S\delta(S):\alpha_S\ge0\right\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{E_n}.\] Since \(\delta(S)=\delta([n]\setminus S)\), complementary shores generate the same ray. The zero vector arises from trivial cuts or from taking every coefficient equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut cone consists of all nonnegative linear combinations of incidence vectors of cuts of the complete graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Cone Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complete-graph cut-cone definition is standard and appropriate for the leaf, but it has no inspectable citation with a specific locator.

assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 2\) and cut vectors are indexed by the edges \(E_n\) of the complete graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete-graph cut polytope in edge-coordinate space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(S\subseteq[n]\), let \(\delta(S)\in\{0,1\}^{E_n}\) be the incidence vector of the edges with exactly one endpoint in \(S\). The cut polytope is \[\operatorname{CUTP}_n=\operatorname{conv}\{\delta(S):S\subseteq[n]\}.\] Equivalently, its points are precisely the vectors \(x=\sum_S\alpha_S\delta(S)\) with \(\alpha_S\ge0\) and \(\sum_S\alpha_S=1\). Its vertices are the distinct cut vectors, with complementary sets producing the same vector. Linear optimization over \(\operatorname{CUTP}_n\) is weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut polytope is the convex hull of all complete-graph cut vectors, and weighted Max-Cut is linear optimization over it.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut Polytope Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-polytope definition and optimization interpretation are standard and fit the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Cone–Polytope Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between conic and bounded cut representations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut polytope is the height-one section of its homogenization cone \(\widehat C_n=\operatorname{cone}\{(1,\delta(S))\}\).

notation.meaning: homogenization cone of the cut polytope
cut incidence vector induced by S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard homogenization and affine-section correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenization correspondence, distinguished from the ordinary cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the homogenized cut cone by \[\widehat C_n=\operatorname{cone}\{(1,\delta(S)):S\subseteq[n]\}\subseteq\mathbb R^{1+|E_n|}.\] Then \[\operatorname{CUTP}_n=\{x\in\mathbb R^{E_n}:(1,x)\in\widehat C_n\}.\] Indeed, the first coordinate forces the nonnegative conic coefficients to sum to one. Conversely, every \((t,y)\in\widehat C_n\) with \(t>0\) satisfies \(y/t\in\operatorname{CUTP}_n\). This exact cone-polytope correspondence uses \(\widehat C_n\); the ordinary cone \(\operatorname{cone}\{\delta(S)\}\) is its coordinate projection, not generally a height-one homogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After homogenization, the cut polytope is exactly the height-one slice of the cone generated by augmented cut vectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone–Polytope Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogenization and height-one-section correspondence is mathematically precise and correctly distinguished from the ordinary cut cone, but it lacks an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cut-polytope and cut-cone representations with the K5 boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions, valid circuit inequalities, exactness in the K5-minor-free regime, and the explicit K5 failure witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, $P_{\mathrm{cut}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^{\delta(U)}:U\subseteq V\}$ and $0\in P_{\mathrm{cut}}(G)$. Moreover, $P_{\mathrm{bipartite\ subgraph}}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E:\exists y\in P_{\mathrm{cut}}(G),\ y\ge x\}$. Every $x\in P_{\mathrm{cut}}(G)$ satisfies $0\le x_e\le1$ and $x(F)-x(C\setminus F)\le |F|-1$ for every circuit $C$ and every odd-cardinality $F\subseteq C$; these inequalities determine the cut polytope for graphs without a $K_5$ minor. The cut cone is $\operatorname{cone}\{\chi^{\delta(U)}:U\subseteq V\}$, and its elements satisfy $x_f\le x(C\setminus\{f\})$ for every circuit $C$ and $f\in C$. These cone inequalities are not sufficient in general: for distinct $u,v\in V(K_5)$, $x=\mathbf{2}-\chi^{\delta(\{u,v\})}$ satisfies them but does not belong to the cut cone of $K_5$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cut polytope and cut cone are respectively the convex hull and conic hull of cut incidence vectors. The bipartite-subgraph polytope is obtained by downward domination from the cut polytope. Circuit inequalities are valid, characterize the cut polytope in the K5-minor-free regime, and fail to characterize the cut cone on the stated K5 witness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated cut-polytope and cut-cone representations and valid inequalities hold, with the explicit }K_5\text{ failure witness}

children.title: Metric Polyhedron
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure associated with metric distance systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the metric-cone convention; strict separation of distinct points is omitted to obtain a closed polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite set \(V\), the metric polyhedron (metric cone) is
\[\operatorname{MET}(V)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{\binom V2}:x_{ij}\ge 0,\quad x_{ij}\le x_{ik}+x_{kj}\ \text{for all distinct }i,j,k\in V\right\}.\]
Its elements are symmetric finite semimetrics after setting \(x_{ii}=0\) and \(x_{ji}=x_{ij}\). Requiring \(x_{ij}>0\) for \(i\ne j\) selects genuine metrics but does not define a closed polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric cone consists of nonnegative symmetric distance arrays satisfying every triangle inequality; positive off-diagonal distances select its genuine metrics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MET}(V)\) is a closed convex polyhedral cone containing every cut semimetric.

notation.meaning: Distance assigned to the unordered pair of distinct vertices i and j.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: triangle inequalities give the customary finite metric cone

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the mathematical formulation is coherent under the stated metric-cone convention. However, no citation with an inspectable locator supports the convention, the terminology, or the asserted containment of cut semimetrics. The supplied local inventory does not contain a relevant metric-polyhedra source.

children.title: Semimetric Polyhedron
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral structure permitting semimetric distance systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Semimetric Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the bounded normalized semimetric relaxation associated with cut vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite set \(V\), define the normalized semimetric polyhedron by
\[\operatorname{SMET}(V)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{\binom V2}:x_{ij}-x_{ik}-x_{jk}\le0,\quad x_{ij}+x_{ik}+x_{jk}\le2\ \text{for all distinct }i,j,k\in V\right\}.\]
These inequalities imply \(0\le x_{ij}\le1\) when \(|V|\ge3\). Every cut vector \(\delta(S)\), defined by \(\delta(S)_{ij}=1\) exactly when one of \(i,j\) lies in \(S\), belongs to \(\operatorname{SMET}(V)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalized semimetric polyhedron is the bounded triangle-and-perimeter relaxation containing all zero-one cut vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)\subseteq\operatorname{SMET}(V)\subseteq[0,1]^{\binom V2}\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the cut determined by S.
Convex hull of all cut vectors on V.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: triangle and perimeter inequalities form the standard bounded metric relaxation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the displayed triangle and perimeter system is mathematically coherent as a bounded cut relaxation. The name SMET and its distinction from the sibling metric polyhedron are convention-sensitive, and no relevant source with a specific locator is cited.

children.title: Metric-Relaxation Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural gaps between metric relaxations and cut realizability.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Relaxation Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-dependent integrality gap for maximizing nonnegative weighted cuts over the normalized semimetric relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonnegative weights \(w\in\mathbb{R}^{\binom V2}_+\), let
\[M(w)=\max_{x\in\operatorname{SMET}(V)}\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}x_{ij},\qquad C(w)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\delta(S)_{ij}.\]
Then \(M(w)\ge C(w)\). The instance has zero relaxation gap exactly when the exposed maximizing face of \(\operatorname{SMET}(V)\) contains a cut vector. Its multiplicative gap is \(M(w)/C(w)\) when \(C(w)>0\); a strict gap occurs precisely when \(M(w)>C(w)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric relaxation is exact when an optimal relaxed face contains a cut vector; otherwise its objective exceeds the maximum-cut value.
assumptions_latex: \(C(w)>0\) when the multiplicative ratio is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(w)/C(w)\ge1\), with equality exactly in the stated zero-gap regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integrality gaps compare relaxation and integral optima

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits this gap-regime leaf. The exactness criterion and objective-dependent ratio are internally coherent, but the record cites no inspectable polyhedral source for the selected relaxation and gap convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Polytope Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard valid families for the complete-graph cut polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x=\delta(S)\) be any cut vector on a finite set \(V\). For every three distinct vertices, it satisfies the triangle and perimeter inequalities
\[x_{ij}-x_{ik}-x_{jk}\le0,\qquad x_{ij}+x_{ik}+x_{jk}\le2.\]
More generally, for every integer vector \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) with \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=1\), it satisfies the hypermetric inequality
\[\sum_{i<j}b_i b_j x_{ij}\le0.\]
Consequently all these inequalities are valid for \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)=\operatorname{conv}\{\delta(S):S\subseteq V\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Triangle, perimeter, and integer hypermetric inequalities are valid for every cut vector and hence for the entire cut polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(\sum_i b_i=1\) for the hypermetric family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every displayed inequality is valid on \(\operatorname{CUT}(V)\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the cut S.
Integer coefficient vector defining a hypermetric inequality.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: displayed inequalities are classical valid cut-polytope families

children.title: Random-Cut Baselines
children.top_down_role: Randomized cut constructions used as approximation baselines.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Cut Baselines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent fair assignment baseline for nonnegative weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have weights \(w_e\ge0\). Assign each vertex independently and uniformly to one of two sides, producing a random cut \(S\). Every edge is cut with probability \(1/2\), so
\[\mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]=\frac12\sum_{e\in E}w_e.\]
Therefore some cut has weight at least \(\frac12\sum_{e\in E}w_e\), and since \(\operatorname{OPT}\le\sum_{e\in E}w_e\), the random cut has expected value at least \(\operatorname{OPT}/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly random bipartition cuts each edge with probability one half, giving a one-half expected approximation for nonnegative weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]\ge\operatorname{OPT}/2\).

notation.meaning: Total weight of edges crossing cut S.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linearity of expectation gives the elementary random-cut baseline

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property content kind is acceptable for a baseline guarantee, and the finite nonnegative-weight assumptions make the expectation and one-half approximation statements precise. The record nevertheless has no cited Max-Cut or randomized-algorithms source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Conditional-Expectation Derandomization
children.top_down_role: Deterministic realization of guarantees from random-cut analyses.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Expectation Derandomization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic vertex-by-vertex realization of the independent random-cut baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order the vertices as \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\). Initially leave all assignments random and fair. At step \(k\), compute the conditional expected final cut weight for each choice \(v_k\in S\) and \(v_k\notin S\), given the previous choices, and fix the choice attaining the larger value. Continue through \(k=n\), then output the resulting cut \(S\). The maintained conditional expectation never decreases, and the terminal conditional expectation equals the weight of the output cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix vertices sequentially on the side whose conditional expected final cut value is larger; the resulting deterministic cut matches the initial expectation.
assumptions_latex: The conditional expectations for both choices can be computed in polynomial time.
The initial distribution assigns vertices independently and fairly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(w(\delta(S))\ge\mathbb E[w(\delta(S_0))]\), where \(S_0\) is the initial random cut.

notation.meaning: Cut sampled by the original randomized procedure.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the method of conditional expectations fixes choices without decreasing conditional value

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind exactly fits the leaf, and the sequential conditional-expectation procedure and computational assumption are clearly stated. No relevant source with a specific locator is provided for the algorithm or its guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Derandomization Guarantee Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantee inherited by exact conditional-expectation derandomization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\) be the objective value of a randomized finite-choice algorithm, and suppose \(\mathbb E[Z]\ge L\). If every random choice is fixed sequentially to a value whose conditional expectation is at least the conditional expectation before fixing that choice, then the final deterministic output has value \(Z_{\mathrm{det}}\ge L\). In particular, conditional-expectation derandomization of the fair random-cut algorithm returns a cut of weight at least \(\frac12\sum_{e\in E}w_e\ge\operatorname{OPT}/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact conditional-expectation choices preserve the randomized algorithm's expected lower bound, including the one-half Max-Cut guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The randomized algorithm has finitely many sequential random choices.
Each required conditional expectation is evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z_{\mathrm{det}}\ge L\); for random-cut derandomization, \(w(\delta(S))\ge\operatorname{OPT}/2\).

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound on the initial expectation.

knowledge_statements.title: Max-Cut Semidefinite Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vector and Gram-matrix relaxation of nonnegative weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\), the Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation is
\[\operatorname{SDP}(G)=\max\left\{\frac12\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}(1-X_{ij}):X\succeq0,\ X_{ii}=1\ \text{for all }i\in V\right\}.\]
Equivalently, write \(X_{ij}=u_i^{\mathsf T}u_j\) for unit vectors \(u_i\). Every cut encoded by signs \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\) gives the feasible rank-one matrix \(X=ss^{\mathsf T}\), whose objective equals that cut's weight. Hence \(\operatorname{SDP}(G)\ge\operatorname{OPT}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing cut signs by arbitrary unit vectors yields a semidefinite program whose value upper-bounds the maximum cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}(G)\le\operatorname{SDP}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Positive-semidefinite Gram matrix of unit vectors.
Unit vector assigned to vertex i.
Sign vector encoding an integral cut.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Hyperplane Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Goemans–Williamson rounding applied to a feasible unit-vector SDP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given unit vectors \((u_i)_{i\in V}\), sample a rotationally invariant random vector \(g\), and output
\[S=\{i\in V:g^{\mathsf T}u_i\ge0\}.\]
For an edge \(ij\), put \(\theta_{ij}=\arccos(u_i^{\mathsf T}u_j)\in[0,\pi]\). Then
\[\Pr[ij\in\delta(S)]=\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi},\qquad \mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]=\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}.\]
Repeated independent rounding may return the best sampled cut; one sample already satisfies the stated expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A random hyperplane separates two SDP vectors with probability equal to their angle divided by pi, producing a randomized cut.
assumptions_latex: The hyperplane normal \(g\) has a rotationally invariant continuous distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]=\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}\theta_{ij}/\pi\).

notation.meaning: Angle between vectors assigned to endpoints i and j.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: spherical symmetry gives the angle-over-pi separation probability

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_G\operatorname{OPT}(G)/\operatorname{SDP}(G)=\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) when combined with the rounding lower bound.

notation.meaning: Value of the standard Max-Cut semidefinite relaxation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic worst-case gap for the standard Max-Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=\min_{0\le\theta\le\pi}\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}.\]
For every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist finite nonnegatively weighted graphs \(G\) for which
\[\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(G)}{\operatorname{SDP}(G)}\le\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon.\]
Thus the standard SDP has asymptotic integrality gap at least \(1/\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\) under the convention \(\operatorname{SDP}/\operatorname{OPT}\), and no analysis using only its objective value can certify a uniformly larger approximation factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are weighted graphs whose maximum-cut value approaches only the Goemans-Williamson constant times the standard SDP value.

children.title: Approximation-Ratio Tightness
children.top_down_role: Regimes where semidefinite rounding guarantees become tight.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Ratio Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case guarantee and relaxation-relative tightness of Goemans–Williamson rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}=\min_{0<\theta\le\pi}\frac{2\theta}{\pi(1-\cos\theta)}.\]
For every feasible SDP vector solution,
\[\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}\frac{\theta_{ij}}{\pi}\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\frac12\sum_{ij\in E}w_{ij}(1-\cos\theta_{ij}).\]
Consequently random-hyperplane rounding of an optimal solution satisfies \(\mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{SDP}(G)\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{OPT}(G)\). Together with asymptotic SDP-gap instances, the factor \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\approx0.87856\) is tight relative to this relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hyperplane rounding achieves the Goemans–Williamson factor, and matching SDP gap instances make that relaxation-relative factor asymptotically tight.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph with nonnegative edge weights.
The vectors form an optimal feasible solution of the standard Max-Cut SDP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[w(\delta(S))]\ge\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\operatorname{OPT}(G)\), with asymptotic relaxation-relative tightness.

notation.meaning: Minimum scalar comparison between hyperplane separation and SDP edge contribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity-Based Optimality Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional and Unique-Games-conditional approximation barriers for polynomial-time Max-Cut algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), it is NP-hard to approximate nonnegative weighted Max-Cut within a factor exceeding \(16/17+\varepsilon\). Under the Unique Games Conjecture, it is NP-hard to achieve a factor exceeding \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon\), where \(\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}\approx0.87856\). Hence, assuming the Unique Games Conjecture and \(P\ne NP\), the Goemans–Williamson approximation ratio is optimal among polynomial-time algorithms up to an arbitrarily small additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Known NP-hardness gives a 16/17 barrier; under Unique Games, the Goemans–Williamson ratio is the exact polynomial-time frontier.
assumptions_latex: Polynomial time is measured in the standard Turing model.
The second barrier assumes the Unique Games Conjecture.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No polynomial-time \((\alpha_{\mathrm{GW}}+\varepsilon)\)-approximation exists under the Unique Games Conjecture unless \(P=NP\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound content kind fits this optimality-frontier leaf, and the unconditional and Unique-Games-conditional claims are distinguished. Exact hardness thresholds and their assumptions require theorem-level citations; the supplied inventory has no relevant Max-Cut hardness source or locator.

children.title: Integer Formulations for Max-Cut
children.top_down_role: Exact optimization formulations supporting cut generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Formulations for Max-Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vertex-side and edge-crossing binary formulation for weighted Max-Cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with weights \(w_e\in\mathbb{R}\). Introduce \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\) for each \(v\in V\) and \(x_{uv}\in\{0,1\}\) for each \(uv\in E\). Then weighted Max-Cut is represented by \[\max \sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}x_{uv}\] subject, for every \(uv\in E\), to \[x_{uv}\le y_u+y_v,\quad x_{uv}\le 2-y_u-y_v,\quad x_{uv}\ge y_u-y_v,\quad x_{uv}\ge y_v-y_u.\] At every integral feasible point, \(x_{uv}=1\) exactly when \(y_u\ne y_v\); consequently the objective equals the weight of the cut \(\{v:y_v=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary vertex variables select the two shores, while linear XOR constraints force each edge variable to indicate whether that edge crosses the cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer-program optimum equals \(\max_{S\subseteq V}\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}w_e\).

binary shore assignment of vertex v
binary crossing indicator for edge e

knowledge_statements.title: Valid-Inequality Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation-oracle specification for strengthening a fractional Max-Cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational point \(\bar x\in\mathbb{Q}^{E}\) and a specified valid-inequality family \(\mathcal F=\{a^{i\top}x\le b_i:i\in I\}\) for the cut polytope, solve \[i^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{i\in I}\bigl(a^{i\top}\bar x-b_i\bigr).\] If the maximum violation is positive, output \(a^{i^*\top}x\le b_{i^*}\) and append it to the current linear relaxation; otherwise certify that \(\bar x\) satisfies every inequality in \(\mathcal F\). Reoptimize after each addition and stop when the chosen family has no violated member or the relaxation yields an integral incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separation oracle either finds a valid cut inequality violated by the current fractional solution or certifies satisfaction of the chosen inequality family.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is explicitly specified and valid for the cut polytope.
The maximally violated member of \(\mathcal F\) can be computed.
