knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Bounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP upper bounds and incumbent lower bounds for exact maximization search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a branch-and-bound node \(N\), let \(P_N\) be the linear relaxation obtained from the Max-Cut formulation, accumulated valid inequalities, and the branching restrictions defining \(N\). Let \(U_N=\max\{w^\top x:x\in P_N\}\), with \(U_N=-\infty\) when \(P_N=\varnothing\), and let \(L\) be the value of the best known feasible cut. Every integral completion represented by \(N\) has value at most \(U_N\). Hence infeasibility of \(P_N\), or the inequality \(U_N\le L\), certifies that node \(N\) may be pruned without removing a globally improving solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node is safely pruned when its relaxation is infeasible or its LP upper bound cannot exceed the best feasible cut value.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation \(P_N\) contains every integral completion allowed at node \(N\).
The incumbent value \(L\) comes from a feasible cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(P_N=\varnothing\) or \(U_N\le L\), pruning \(N\) preserves an optimal solution.

children.title: Branch-Cut Scalability Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Cut Scalability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional worst-case boundary for exact branch-and-cut on unrestricted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider any exact Max-Cut branch-and-cut implementation whose node relaxations, separation calls, branching decisions, and bookkeeping require polynomial time per processed node. If its number of processed nodes were bounded by a polynomial in the binary input length for every weighted graph, the implementation would be a polynomial-time exact algorithm for Max-Cut. Since Max-Cut is NP-hard, \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies that no such implementation can have both polynomial per-node work and a polynomial worst-case node bound on all instances. This limitation concerns worst-case guarantees and does not preclude effective pruning on particular graph classes or empirical instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, an exact polynomial-work-per-node branch-and-cut method cannot process only polynomially many nodes on every Max-Cut instance.
assumptions_latex: The implementation returns an exact optimum.
All work per processed node is polynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case number of processed nodes is not polynomially bounded over all Max-Cut inputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Graph Dynamic Programming for Max-Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bag-assignment dynamic programming over a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rooted nice tree decomposition \((T,(B_t)_{t\in T})\) of \(G\), maintain for every node \(t\) and assignment \(a:B_t\to\{0,1\}\) a value \(F_t(a)\): the maximum weight contributed by edges introduced in the subtree of \(t\), among vertex assignments agreeing with \(a\). Initialize leaf tables at zero; apply introduce-vertex, introduce-edge, forget-vertex, and join transitions, adding \(w_{uv}\) at the unique introduce-edge node precisely when \(a(u)\ne a(v)\). At a forget node maximize over the forgotten vertex's two labels; at a join node add the two compatible child values. Output the maximum root-table entry and recover a cut by backtracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming stores the best partial cut for each bag labeling, combines compatible states, and backtracks from the optimal root state.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite weighted undirected graph.
A rooted nice tree decomposition is supplied.
Every edge is introduced exactly once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The backtracked labeling defines a maximum-weight cut of \(G\).

notation.meaning: optimal partial value conditional on bag assignment a

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical decision and optimization hardness for unrestricted simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the decision problem by input \((G,K)\), where \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected unweighted graph and \(K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\), and ask whether some \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies \(|\delta(S)|\ge K\). This decision problem is NP-complete. Membership in NP uses the shore \(S\) as a certificate, whose crossing edges are countable in polynomial time. Consequently, computing \(\max_{S\subseteq V}|\delta(S)|\) on unrestricted graphs is NP-hard; the weighted optimization problem with nonnegative integer weights is NP-hard as well because it contains the unweighted case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deciding whether a general graph has a cut of at least a prescribed size is NP-complete, so exact general-graph Max-Cut is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, simple, undirected, and given explicitly.
The threshold \(K\) is encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unweighted Max-Cut decision is NP-complete, and exact Max-Cut optimization is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: edges with exactly one endpoint in S

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Max-Cut Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial exact solvability for planar graphs without external-field terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite planar undirected graph with a planar embedding and nonnegative rational edge weights \(w_e\). A maximum-weight cut of \(G\) can be computed in time polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\) and the binary encoding length of \(w\), by transforming the planar cut problem into an appropriate parity-subgraph or minimum-weight perfect-matching problem in an associated planar-dual construction. Thus planarity separates this zero-field edge-only regime from unrestricted NP-hard Max-Cut. The conclusion does not automatically extend to formulations with arbitrary vertex-side rewards or external-field terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegatively weighted planar Max-Cut is exactly polynomial-time solvable through planar duality and matching, provided no vertex-side field terms are added.
assumptions_latex: The objective contains only edge-crossing terms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A maximum-weight cut of \(G\) is computable in polynomial time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is appropriately restricted to planar edge-only Max-Cut, but the exact weighted planar reduction and the external-field boundary need authoritative, specifically located support.

children.title: Dense-Graph Approximation Schemes
children.top_down_role: Approximation behavior for dense Max-Cut instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Approximation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PTAS regime for Max-Cut on uniformly dense graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed density constant \(\alpha>0\) and accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a polynomial-time approximation scheme for unweighted Max-Cut on graphs \(G=(V,E)\) satisfying \(|E|\ge\alpha |V|^2\). Given such a graph, the scheme returns a cut \(S\subseteq V\) with \[|\delta(S)|\ge (1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G).\] For fixed \(\alpha\) and \(\varepsilon\), its running time is polynomial in \(|V|\), although the polynomial or its constant factor may depend superpolynomially on \(1/\varepsilon\) and \(1/\alpha\). This statement is an approximation guarantee, not exact solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every fixed accuracy and density threshold, dense unweighted graphs admit polynomial-time cuts worth at least one minus epsilon times optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple unweighted graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns \(S\) with \(|\delta(S)|\ge(1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}(G)\) in polynomial time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dense-graph PTAS claim is plausibly and explicitly scoped to fixed density and accuracy, but neither the approximation theorem nor its parameter-dependent runtime is cited.

children.title: Bounded-Treewidth Exact Solvability

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Treewidth Exact Solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact weighted Max-Cut on graphs supplied with bounded-width decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have rational edge weights and let a tree decomposition of width at most \(k\) be supplied. Max-Cut on \(G\) is solvable exactly by dynamic programming over a nice form of the decomposition. A state records the two-shore assignment of the current bag; transitions introduce or forget vertices and edges or combine compatible child tables. Since a bag has at most \(k+1\) vertices, it has at most \(2^{k+1}\) assignments. After standard conversion to a nice decomposition, an optimal cut and its value can be obtained using \(2^{O(k)}(|V|+|E|)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a width-k tree decomposition, weighted Max-Cut is exactly solvable by bag-label dynamic programming in single-exponential parameter time and linear graph-size dependence.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and undirected with rational edge weights.
A tree decomposition of width at most \(k\) is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weighted Max-Cut is solvable in \(2^{O(k)}(|V|+|E|)\) arithmetic operations.

children.title: Width-Parameter Dependence

knowledge_statements.title: Width-Parameter Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-space and arithmetic-operation dependence on the width of a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with rational edge weights, and suppose a tree decomposition of \(G\) of width at most \(k\) is supplied. After conversion to a nice decomposition with introduce-edge nodes, each bag contains at most \(k+1\) vertices, so the direct Max-Cut dynamic program has at most \(2^{k+1}\) binary shore-assignment states per bag. Introduce, forget, introduce-edge, and join transitions can be evaluated in \(2^{O(k)}\) arithmetic operations per decomposition node. Using a nice decomposition of size \(2^{O(k)}(|V|+|E|)\), the total number of arithmetic operations is \(2^{O(k)}(|V|+|E|)\). Thus Max-Cut is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the width of a supplied decomposition; a bit-complexity bound additionally depends polynomially on the encoding length of the rational weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a supplied width-k decomposition, the bag table has at most 2^(k+1) shore assignments, yielding an exact algorithm using 2^O(k) times the graph size in arithmetic operations; bit complexity also reflects the weight encoding.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and undirected with rational edge weights.
A tree decomposition of \(G\) of width at most \(k\) is supplied.
The decomposition is converted to a nice form with introduce-edge nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state count is at most \(2^{k+1}\) per bag, and exact Max-Cut uses \(2^{O(k)}(|V|+|E|)\) arithmetic operations.

children.title: Signed-Cut Objective Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Cut Objective Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between signed cut maximization and minimum weighted parity frustration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have nonzero signed weights \(w_e\), and let \(z_v\in\{0,1\}\). Write \(d_e=1\) when \(w_e>0\) and \(d_e=0\) when \(w_e<0\). For \(e=uv\), define the violated-preference indicator as \(q_e(z)=\mathbf 1\{z_u\oplus z_v\ne d_e\}\). Then \[\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}\mathbf 1\{z_u\ne z_v\}=\sum_{e:w_e>0}w_e-\sum_{e\in E}|w_e|q_e(z).\] Hence maximizing the signed cut objective is exactly equivalent to minimizing total weighted frustration: positive edges prefer opposite shores, whereas negative edges prefer the same shore.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed cut objective equals a constant minus the weight of edges whose preferred same-or-opposite parity is violated.
assumptions_latex: Each edge weight \(w_e\) is nonzero and real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Signed-cut maximizers are precisely minimizers of \(\sum_{e\in E}|w_e|q_e(z)\).

notation.meaning: preferred endpoint parity of edge e
indicator that labeling z violates edge e's preferred parity

children.title: Balance versus Frustration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Signed-graph structure governing compatible versus conflicting cut preferences.

knowledge_statements.title: Balance versus Frustration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-frustration characterization of parity-balanced signed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each edge \(e=uv\) of a finite undirected graph carry a desired parity \(d_e\in\{0,1\}\) and a positive penalty \(c_e>0\). Define \[\operatorname{fr}(G,d,c)=\min_{z:V\to\{0,1\}}\sum_{uv\in E}c_{uv}\mathbf 1\{z_u\oplus z_v\ne d_{uv}\}.\] Call the signed parity system balanced when there exists \(z:V\to\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(z_u\oplus z_v=d_{uv}\) for every edge. Then \(\operatorname{fr}(G,d,c)=0\) if and only if the system is balanced. Otherwise every labeling violates at least one positive-penalty edge, and the frustration value is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A signed parity graph has zero minimum frustration exactly when one binary vertex labeling satisfies every edge's preferred parity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{fr}(G,d,c)=0\) if and only if \((G,d)\) is balanced.

notation.meaning: desired endpoint parity on edge e

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\).

notation.meaning: Edges having exactly one endpoint in S
Total weight of an edge set F

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected formulation; the unweighted problem is obtained by unit edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\), a bisection is a bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\) satisfying \(\bigl||S|-|V\setminus S|\bigr|\le 1\). The minimum-bisection value is the least total weight of edges crossing such a bipartition. Equivalently, choosing the smaller side gives
\[\operatorname{bis}(G):=\min\left\{w(\delta(S)):S\subseteq V,\ |S|=\lfloor |V|/2\rfloor\right\}.\]
Any feasible set attaining this minimum is a minimum bisection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum bisection divides the vertices into two parts whose sizes differ by at most one while minimizing the total weight of crossing edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Bisection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted minimum-bisection definition is mathematically coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf, but no cited source or inspectable locator supports this formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sep}_{\beta}(G)=\min_{S:\ \beta |V|\le |S|\le(1-\beta)|V|}w(\delta(S)).\]

notation.meaning: Edges crossing from S to its complement
Required minimum fraction on each side

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-balanced, weighted-edge separator with an explicit balance parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n=|V|\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is \(\beta\)-balanced when both sides of its induced bipartition contain at least \(\beta n\) vertices, equivalently \(\beta n\le |S|\le(1-\beta)n\). The minimum \(\beta\)-balanced-separator value is
\[\operatorname{sep}_{\beta}(G):=\min\left\{w(\delta(S)):S\subseteq V,\ \beta n\le |S|\le(1-\beta)n\right\}.\]
A minimizing crossing edge set \(\delta(S)\), or its defining bipartition, is a minimum balanced separator under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced separator minimizes crossing-edge weight among bipartitions placing at least a prescribed fraction of the vertices on each side.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Separator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parameterized cardinality-balance definition fits the leaf, but balanced-separator conventions vary and no source with a specific locator is supplied.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected weighted graph with \(|V|\ge2\).
Only nonempty proper subsets \(S\subsetneq V\) are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{RCut}(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}w(\delta(S))\left(\frac1{|S|}+\frac1{|V\setminus S|}\right).\]

notation.meaning: Total weight of edges crossing the bipartition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-way ratio-cut convention without an additional constant factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nontrivial bipartition \((S,\bar S)\), its ratio-cut objective is the crossing weight normalized by the cardinalities of both parts:
\[\operatorname{RCut}(S,\bar S):=w(\delta(S))\left(\frac{1}{|S|}+\frac{1}{|\bar S|}\right).\]
The ratio-cut value of \(G\) is \(\operatorname{RCut}(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\operatorname{RCut}(S,\bar S)\). Thus cuts isolating a small vertex set receive a larger penalty than cuts of the same crossing weight having more balanced cardinalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ratio cut minimizes crossing weight multiplied by the sum of the reciprocal cardinalities of the two nonempty sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Ratio Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-way ratio-cut definition is internally consistent and appropriately classified as a definition, but its normalization convention lacks cited support.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with symmetric nonnegative edge weights.
Both sides of every feasible cut have positive weighted volume.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{NCut}(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}w(\delta(S))\left(\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(S)}+\frac1{\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S)}\right).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-way normalized-cut objective using weighted degree volume.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nontrivial bipartition \((S,\bar S)\) with positive volume on both sides, define
\[\operatorname{NCut}(S,\bar S):=w(\delta(S))\left(\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}(S)}+\frac{1}{\operatorname{vol}(\bar S)}\right).\]
The normalized-cut value is the minimum of this quantity over all such bipartitions. Unlike ratio cut, normalized cut measures the size of a part by its incident weighted degree rather than by its number of vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized cut minimizes crossing weight times the sum of reciprocal weighted volumes of the two sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted-volume normalized-cut formulation is coherent and fits the leaf, but no source with a specific locator verifies the convention and feasible-domain treatment.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights.
The feasible cut has positive volume on both sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\phi(G)=\min_{S:\ 0<\operatorname{vol}(S)\le\operatorname{vol}(V)/2}\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\operatorname{vol}(S)}.\]

notation.meaning: Weighted volume of a vertex set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric two-sided conductance for weighted undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The conductance of a nontrivial cut \(S\subsetneq V\) is
\[\phi(S):=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\min\{\operatorname{vol}(S),\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S)\}}.\]
The graph conductance is \(\phi(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\phi(S)\), where cuts with a zero-volume side are excluded. By replacing a feasible side with its complement when necessary, the same objective is
\[\phi(G)=\min_{S:\ 0<\operatorname{vol}(S)\le\operatorname{vol}(V)/2}\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\operatorname{vol}(S)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conductance minimizes crossing-edge weight divided by the smaller weighted volume of the two sides.
knowledge_statements.title: Conductance Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conductance objective and its equivalent smaller-volume form are mathematically consistent, but the record has no supporting citation or locator.

Minimum edge expansion of the graph

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-normalized edge expansion with weighted crossing edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The edge expansion of a nontrivial cut \(S\subsetneq V\) is
\[h(S):=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{\min\{|S|,|V\setminus S|\}}.\]
The edge-expansion objective for the graph is \(h(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}h(S)\). Choosing the smaller side of each bipartition yields the equivalent one-sided form
\[h(G)=\min_{S:\ 1\le |S|\le |V|/2}\frac{w(\delta(S))}{|S|}.\]
For unit weights this counts boundary edges per vertex on the smaller side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge expansion minimizes crossing-edge weight divided by the cardinality of the smaller side.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Expansion Objectives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cardinality-normalized edge-expansion definition fits the leaf, but the weighted convention requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Volume-versus-Cardinality Normalization
children.top_down_role: Regimes where volume and cardinality normalization produce differing behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected weighted graph in which every vertex has the same positive weighted degree \(d\).
\(S\) is a nonempty proper subset of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\phi(S)=\frac{h(S)}{d},\qquad \phi(G)=\frac{h(G)}{d}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact comparison on weighted regular graphs; irregular graphs require degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If every vertex has weighted degree \(d>0\), then every vertex set satisfies \(\operatorname{vol}(S)=d|S|\). Consequently, for every nontrivial cut,
\[\phi(S)=\frac{w(\delta(S))}{d\min\{|S|,|V\setminus S|\}}=\frac{h(S)}{d}.\]
Taking the minimum over cuts gives \(\phi(G)=h(G)/d\). Hence volume and cardinality normalization select exactly the same minimizing cuts on a weighted \(d\)-regular graph, although their objective values differ by the fixed factor \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a weighted regular graph, conductance equals edge expansion divided by the common degree, so both normalizations have the same optimal cuts.
knowledge_statements.title: Volume-versus-Cardinality Normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regular-graph comparison is mathematically consistent and property is the correct content kind, but no citation supports the stated relationship.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative capacities \(c_e\).
Feasible cuts have two nonempty sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Phi_{\mathrm{unif}}(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\frac{c(\delta(S))}{|S|\,|V\setminus S|}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All unordered vertex pairs have unit demand; no global scaling factor is included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under unit demand between every unordered pair of distinct vertices, the demand separated by a cut \((S,V\setminus S)\) is \(|S|\,|V\setminus S|\). Its uniform sparsity is therefore
\[\Phi_{\mathrm{unif}}(S):=\frac{c(\delta(S))}{|S|\,|V\setminus S|}.\]
The uniform sparsest-cut value is \(\Phi_{\mathrm{unif}}(G):=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\Phi_{\mathrm{unif}}(S)\). Multiplying every objective value by a fixed graph-dependent factor gives equivalent alternative normalization conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform sparsest cut minimizes cut capacity divided by the number of all-pairs unit demands separated by the cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Sparsest Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The all-pairs unit-demand definition is coherent and fits uniform sparsest cut, but alternative global normalizations exist and the selected convention is uncited.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform sparsest cut and uniform multicommodity flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the complete unit-demand specialization of sparsest cut and names the corresponding undirected multicommodity-flow specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be the complete undirected demand graph and let \(b(f)=1\) for every \(f\in E(H)\). The uniform sparsest-cut problem is to find a nonempty proper subset \(X\subsetneq V(G)\) minimizing \[\frac{u(\delta_G(X))}{|X|\,|V(G)\setminus X|}.\] The corresponding special case of the undirected multicommodity-flow problem is called the uniform multicommodity-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete undirected demand graph with unit demand on every demand edge, uniform sparsest cut minimizes cut capacity divided by the product of the two shore sizes. The corresponding undirected multicommodity-flow specialization is uniform multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq V(G)}\frac{u(\delta_G(X))}{|X|\,|V(G)\setminus X|}

assumptions_latex: Each unordered vertex pair \(\{u,v\}\) has nonnegative demand \(d_{uv}\), and some cut separates positive total demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Phi(c,d)=\min_{S:\ D(S)>0}\frac{c(\delta(S))}{D(S)},\qquad D(S)=\sum_{u\in S,\,v\notin S}d_{uv}.\]

notation.meaning: Total pair demand separated by S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected capacitated graph with arbitrary symmetric pair demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cut \((S,V\setminus S)\), let its separated demand be
\[D(S):=\sum_{u\in S,\,v\in V\setminus S}d_{uv}.\]
Whenever \(D(S)>0\), the cut sparsity is \(c(\delta(S))/D(S)\). The nonuniform sparsest-cut value is
\[\Phi(c,d):=\min_{S\subseteq V:\ D(S)>0}\frac{c(\delta(S))}{D(S)}.\]
Uniform sparsest cut is the special case \(d_{uv}=1\) for all distinct pairs, subject to the chosen global normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonuniform sparsest cut minimizes crossing capacity divided by the total prescribed pair demand separated by the cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Sparsest Cut

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonuniform sparsest-cut definition is internally consistent, but no authoritative source and specific locator support the capacity-demand formulation.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected capacitated graph with nonnegative pair demands.
The maximum concurrent-flow value \(\lambda^*\) and sparsest-cut value \(\Phi^*\) are finite and positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[1\le \operatorname{gap}(G,c,d):=\frac{\Phi^*}{\lambda^*}.\]

notation.meaning: Maximum simultaneous fraction of every demand routable within capacities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent multicommodity-flow lower bound and its multiplicative gap from sparsest cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\lambda^*\) be the largest scalar \(\lambda\ge0\) for which every pair demand \(d_{uv}\) can be routed simultaneously at amount \(\lambda d_{uv}\) without exceeding any edge capacity. Let \(\Phi^*\) be the corresponding nonuniform sparsest-cut value. Every cut bounds concurrent flow, so \(\lambda^*\le\Phi^*\). The instance flow-cut gap is
\[\operatorname{gap}(G,c,d):=\frac{\Phi^*}{\lambda^*}\ge1.\]
A flow-cut gap family studies this ratio over a specified class of graphs and demand systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The flow-cut gap is the sparsest-cut value divided by maximum concurrent flow; every cut constraint implies this ratio is at least one.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow–Cut Gap Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inequality is plausible under the stated concurrent-flow interpretation, but the exact multicommodity-flow model is not formalized or sourced. The leaf concerns a gap family, so classifying the record as duality also requires source-backed confirmation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{MaxAgree}:=\max_{\mathcal P}\left(\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^+}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\sim_{\mathcal P}v]+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^-}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\not\sim_{\mathcal P}v]\right).\]

notation.meaning: Vertices u and v occupy the same cluster of partition P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted complete signed-graph formulation of correlation clustering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A positive pair agrees with a partition \(\mathcal P\) when its endpoints share a cluster, while a negative pair agrees when its endpoints lie in different clusters. The agreement weight is
\[A(\mathcal P):=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^+}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\sim_{\mathcal P}v]+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^-}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\not\sim_{\mathcal P}v].\]
Agreement maximization asks for an unrestricted partition attaining \(\max_{\mathcal P}A(\mathcal P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agreement maximization clusters vertices to maximize the weight of positive pairs kept together plus negative pairs placed apart.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted complete signed-graph formulation; equivalent to agreement maximization for fixed total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The disagreement weight of a partition \(\mathcal P\) is
\[D(\mathcal P):=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^+}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\not\sim_{\mathcal P}v]+\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E^-}w_{uv}\mathbf 1[u\sim_{\mathcal P}v].\]
Disagreement minimization asks for \(\min_{\mathcal P}D(\mathcal P)\). If \(W\) is the total pair weight and \(A(\mathcal P)\) is the agreement weight, then \(A(\mathcal P)+D(\mathcal P)=W\); hence minimizing disagreement and maximizing agreement have exactly the same optimal partitions in this complete labeled model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disagreement minimization minimizes the weight of positive pairs split apart plus negative pairs placed together; it is equivalent to maximizing agreements.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-LP and Gram-matrix SDP relaxations for weighted correlation clustering on a complete signed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be finite, let \(E^+\mathbin{\dot\cup}E^-=\binom{V}{2}\), and let \(w_{ij}\ge 0\). The metric relaxation minimizes \[\sum_{ij\in E^+}w_{ij}d_{ij}+\sum_{ij\in E^-}w_{ij}(1-d_{ij})\] subject to \(d_{ii}=0\), \(0\le d_{ij}\le 1\), and \(d_{ij}\le d_{ik}+d_{kj}\) for all \(i,j,k\in V\). A compatible vector SDP introduces a Gram matrix \(X\succeq0\) satisfying \(X_{ii}=1\), \(0\le X_{ij}\le1\), and \(d_{ij}=1-X_{ij}\), together with the metric inequalities on \(d\). Every partition is feasible by assigning one orthonormal unit vector to each block, so that \(X_{ij}=1\) within blocks and \(X_{ij}=0\) between blocks. Consequently, both relaxations lower-bound the minimum disagreement objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric LP optimizes fractional separation distances. A compatible SDP represents same-block indicators by a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix; assigning orthonormal vectors to distinct blocks embeds every clustering, so both relaxations lower-bound minimum disagreement.

Modularity Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted undirected Newman–Girvan modularity with the configuration-model null term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be an undirected weighted graph with symmetric adjacency matrix \(A\), degrees \(d_i=\sum_jA_{ij}\), and \(2m=\sum_i d_i>0\). For a partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\), its modularity is \[Q(\mathcal P)=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i,j\in V}\left(A_{ij}-\frac{d_id_j}{2m}\right)\mathbf 1\{i,j\text{ belong to the same block of }\mathcal P\}.\] Modularity maximization is the combinatorial optimization problem \(\max_{\mathcal P}Q(\mathcal P)\), where the maximum ranges over all set partitions of \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modularity maximization selects a vertex partition whose within-block edge weight most exceeds the configuration-model expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\mathcal P\text{ partition of }V}Q(\mathcal P)\).

children.title: Resolution-Limit Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Scale-dependent failures in modularity-based community recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolution-Limit Phenomena
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact merge boundary exposing the global-scale resolution limit of configuration-model modularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For disjoint blocks \(A,B\) in a partition, let \(e(A,B)\) be their total connecting edge weight and \(\operatorname{vol}(A)=\sum_{i\in A}d_i\). Under Newman–Girvan modularity, replacing \(A,B\) by \(A\cup B\) changes the objective by \[\Delta Q=\frac{e(A,B)}{m}-\frac{\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)}{2m^2}.\] Thus modularity strictly prefers merging whenever \(2m e(A,B)>\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)\). Because this threshold depends on the graph-wide quantity \(m\), enlarging remote parts of a graph can make two locally unchanged communities merge-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modularity merges adjacent blocks when their connecting weight exceeds a threshold depending on total graph weight; remote graph growth can therefore erase otherwise unchanged small communities.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected weighted graph with \(m>0\).
\(A\) and \(B\) are distinct blocks of the current partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2m e(A,B)>\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)\Longrightarrow Q(\mathcal P\setminus\{A,B\}\cup\{A\cup B\})>Q(\mathcal P)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Model Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of modularity values and maximizers on the chosen expected-edge matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an undirected weighted adjacency matrix \(A\) with total weight \(m>0\). For a symmetric null-model matrix \(P\), define \(Q_P(\mathcal P)=(2m)^{-1}\sum_{ij}(A_{ij}-P_{ij})\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}\). If another null model is \(P'=P+\Delta P\), then every partition satisfies \[Q_{P'}(\mathcal P)-Q_P(\mathcal P)=-\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i,j}\Delta P_{ij}\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}.\] Consequently, a nonconstant partition-dependent perturbation can reverse the ordering of two partitions and change the maximizing clustering even though \(A\) is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing expected edge weights shifts each partition according to its within-block null-model mass, so the same observed graph can have a different modularity maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(A,P,P'\) are symmetric matrices on the same finite vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{P'}(\mathcal P)-Q_P(\mathcal P)=-(2m)^{-1}\sum_{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j}\Delta P_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: i and j share a partition block

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise merge regimes for resolution-parameter modularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\gamma>0\), define generalized modularity by \[Q_\gamma(\mathcal P)=\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i,j}\left(A_{ij}-\gamma\frac{d_id_j}{2m}\right)\mathbf 1\{i\sim_{\mathcal P}j\}.\] For distinct blocks \(A,B\) with positive volumes, merging them has gain \(\Delta Q_\gamma=e(A,B)/m-\gamma\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B)/(2m^2)\). Hence the merge, tie, and separation regimes occur respectively at \(\gamma<\gamma_{AB}\), \(\gamma=\gamma_{AB}\), and \(\gamma>\gamma_{AB}\), where \(\gamma_{AB}=2m e(A,B)/(\operatorname{vol}(A)\operatorname{vol}(B))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each pair of blocks has a critical resolution value: below it merging improves modularity, at it merging ties, and above it keeping the blocks separate is locally better.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sign}(\Delta Q_\gamma)=\operatorname{sign}(\gamma_{AB}-\gamma)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Count Graph Clustering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum weighted k-cut formulation with exactly k nonempty clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(w_e\ge0\), and let \(1\le k\le |V|\). A fixed-count graph clustering is a partition \(\mathcal P=(C_1,\ldots,C_k)\) of \(V\) into exactly \(k\) nonempty sets. In the minimum \(k\)-cut formulation its cost is \[\operatorname{cut}(\mathcal P)=\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}\mathbf 1\{u\text{ and }v\text{ lie in different }C_r\},\] and the optimization problem is to minimize this quantity over all such partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-count clustering partitions the vertices into exactly k nonempty clusters and, in the minimum k-cut model, minimizes total weight crossing between clusters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{(C_1,\ldots,C_k)}\operatorname{cut}(C_1,\ldots,C_k)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Cut Clustering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree hierarchical clustering with the standard weighted cut-based Dasgupta objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite undirected similarity graph with \(w_{uv}\ge0\). A hierarchical clustering is a rooted tree \(T\) whose leaves are exactly \(V\). For leaves \(u,v\), let \(T_{uv}\) be the subtree rooted at their least common ancestor and let \(|T_{uv}|\) denote its number of leaves. The cut-based hierarchical cost is \[\operatorname{cost}_G(T)=\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}|T_{uv}|.\] Hierarchical cut clustering seeks a tree minimizing this cost; binary trees suffice under the usual refinement convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hierarchy is a leaf-labeled rooted tree. Similar vertices are penalized by the size of the smallest cluster containing both, and the objective minimizes total weighted penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{T\text{ rooted with leaf set }V}\sum_{uv\in E}w_{uv}|T_{uv}|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial-Laplacian Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rayleigh relaxation of unnormalized two-way spectral partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with adjacency matrix \(A\), degree matrix \(D\), combinatorial Laplacian \(L=D-A\), and all-ones vector \(\mathbf1\). Relaxing a discrete two-block indicator to a real vector gives \[\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Lx:x^{\mathsf T}x=1,\ x^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=0\}=\lambda_2(L).\] Every minimizer is an eigenvector associated with the second-smallest eigenvalue. A discrete partition is subsequently obtained by thresholding such a vector; the relaxation value itself is the minimum Rayleigh quotient on \(\mathbf1^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unnormalized spectral partitioning minimizes Laplacian energy over unit vectors orthogonal to constants. Its solutions are second-eigenvalue eigenvectors, which are then rounded into cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, undirected, and weighted nonnegatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\perp\mathbf1,\ \|x\|_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Lx=\lambda_2(L)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Normalized-Laplacian Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric normalized-Laplacian relaxation for normalized-cut partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with positive degree matrix \(D\), Laplacian \(L=D-A\), and \(L_{\mathrm{sym}}=D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\). The normalized relaxation is \[\min\{y^{\mathsf T}L_{\mathrm{sym}}y:y^{\mathsf T}y=1,\ y^{\mathsf T}D^{1/2}\mathbf1=0\}=\lambda_2(L_{\mathrm{sym}}).\] Its minimizers are second eigenvectors of \(L_{\mathrm{sym}}\). With \(x=D^{-1/2}y\), the constraints become \(x^{\mathsf T}Dx=1\) and \(x^{\mathsf T}D\mathbf1=0\), displaying the degree-weighted geometry underlying normalized cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric normalized relaxation minimizes normalized-Laplacian energy orthogonally to the degree-weighted constant direction; a second eigenvector supplies the relaxed cut coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, undirected, and weighted nonnegatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{y\perp D^{1/2}\mathbf1,\ \|y\|_2=1}y^{\mathsf T}L_{\mathrm{sym}}y=\lambda_2(L_{\mathrm{sym}})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Walk Laplacian Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-eigenvector form of the degree-normalized spectral relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a connected undirected weighted graph with \(D\) positive diagonal and let \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}=D^{-1}L=I-D^{-1}A\). The degree-weighted relaxation is \[\min\{x^{\mathsf T}Lx:x^{\mathsf T}Dx=1,\ x^{\mathsf T}D\mathbf1=0\}=\lambda_2,\] where \(\lambda_2\) is the second-smallest generalized eigenvalue of \(Lx=\lambda Dx\), equivalently the second eigenvalue of \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}x=\lambda x\). Any minimizing generalized eigenvector can be thresholded to obtain a discrete partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The random-walk relaxation uses degree-weighted normalization. Its minimizers solve the second generalized Laplacian eigenproblem and may be rounded by thresholding.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, undirected, and weighted nonnegatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Lx=\lambda_2Dx\) and \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}x=\lambda_2x\) for every minimizing eigenvector \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Laplacian Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Similarity equivalence of normalized and random-walk Laplacians, including the regular-graph specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected weighted graph with every degree positive, \[L_{\mathrm{rw}}=D^{-1/2}L_{\mathrm{sym}}D^{1/2},\qquad L_{\mathrm{sym}}=D^{1/2}L_{\mathrm{rw}}D^{-1/2}.\] Hence the two matrices are similar, have identical eigenvalues, and their right eigenvectors correspond by \(y=D^{1/2}x\). If the graph is \(d\)-regular, then \(D=dI\) and \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}=L_{\mathrm{sym}}=d^{-1}L\); consequently all three Laplacians have the same eigenvectors, while the combinatorial eigenvalues are multiplied by \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive degrees make the symmetric normalized and random-walk Laplacians similar. On regular graphs they both equal a scalar multiple of the combinatorial Laplacian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(L_{\mathrm{rw}})=\sigma(L_{\mathrm{sym}})\), and if \(D=dI\), then \(L_{\mathrm{rw}}=L_{\mathrm{sym}}=d^{-1}L\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary similarity relation between normalized Laplacian operators

knowledge_statements.title: Fiedler-Vector Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-way unnormalized spectral partitioning by thresholding a Fiedler vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\). Form \(L=D-A\), compute a nonzero vector \(f\) satisfying \(Lf=\lambda_2(L)f\) and \(f^{\mathsf T}\mathbf1=0\), and choose a threshold \(t\). Output \[S_t=\{i\in V:f_i\le t\},\qquad V\setminus S_t.\] The threshold must make both sets nonempty; common conventions use \(t=0\), a median of the coordinates, or the threshold minimizing a specified cut score over the sorted coordinates. Repeated eigenvalues require selecting and recording a particular vector in the \(\lambda_2(L)\)-eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute a second combinatorial-Laplacian eigenvector and split vertices at a nontrivial threshold, optionally choosing the best threshold among the sorted coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, connected, undirected, and weighted nonnegatively.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=S_t\mathbin{\dot\cup}(V\setminus S_t)\) with \(\varnothing\ne S_t\ne V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite weighted undirected graph, order the vertices so that \(f(v_1)\leq\cdots\leq f(v_n)\). For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\), form \(S_i=\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}\) and compute \(\phi(S_i)=w(S_i,V\setminus S_i)/\min\{\operatorname{vol}(S_i),\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S_i)\}\). Discard sets with zero denominator and output a minimizing sweep set. If \(u_2\) is a second eigenvector of the symmetric normalized Laplacian \(\mathcal L=I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\) and the swept coordinate is \(f=D^{-1/2}u_2\), then the output satisfies \(\phi(S_{i^*})\leq\sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,w)\) be a finite connected weighted undirected graph, let \(D\) and \(A\) be its degree and adjacency matrices, let \(\mathcal L=I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\), and define \(h(G)=\min_{\varnothing\neq S\subsetneq V}w(S,V\setminus S)/\min\{\operatorname{vol}(S),\operatorname{vol}(V\setminus S)\}\). If \(\lambda_2\) is the second-smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathcal L\), then \[\frac{\lambda_2}{2}\leq h(G)\leq\sqrt{2\lambda_2}.\] Moreover, if \(u_2\) is a second eigenvector of \(\mathcal L\), a sweep of the coordinate \(D^{-1/2}u_2\) produces a nontrivial set \(S\) satisfying \(\phi(S)\leq\sqrt{2\lambda_2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimum two-way conductance lies between half the normalized spectral gap and the square root of twice that gap. Sweeping the degree-normalized coordinate of a second symmetric normalized-Laplacian eigenvector produces a cut satisfying the same upper bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Cheeger Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiway conductance bounds using the kth normalized-Laplacian eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite weighted undirected graph, define \(\rho_G(k)=\min_{S_1,\ldots,S_k}\max_{1\leq i\leq k}\phi(S_i)\), where the minimum ranges over \(k\) nonempty pairwise disjoint vertex sets. If \(0=\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues of the normalized Laplacian, then for every \(2\leq k\leq n\), \[\frac{\lambda_k}{2}\leq \rho_G(k)\leq Ck^2\sqrt{\lambda_k},\] where \(C>0\) is a universal constant. Thus \(k\) disjoint sparse regions are quantitatively controlled by the bottom \(k\)-dimensional spectral subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The kth normalized-Laplacian eigenvalue controls the best possible maximum conductance among k disjoint nonempty vertex sets.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite, weighted, and undirected, with positive degrees.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Cheeger Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cheeger inequality with independent edge weights and positive vertex measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w_{uv}=w_{vu}\geq0\), let \(\mu_v>0\), set \(L_w=\operatorname{diag}(d)-W\), and let \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\leq\cdots\) be the generalized eigenvalues of \(L_wx=\lambda Mx\), where \(M=\operatorname{diag}(\mu)\). Define \(h_{w,\mu}=\min_S w(S,V\setminus S)/\min\{\mu(S),\mu(V\setminus S)\}\) and \(q_{\max}=\max_v d_v/\mu_v\). If the weighted graph is connected, then \[\frac{\lambda_2}{2}\leq h_{w,\mu}\leq\sqrt{2q_{\max}\lambda_2}.\] The usual normalized Cheeger inequality is recovered when \(\mu_v=d_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With arbitrary positive vertex measure, conductance is bounded below by half the generalized spectral gap and above using the maximum weighted exit rate.
assumptions_latex: \(W\) is finite, symmetric, and entrywise nonnegative.
\(\mu_v>0\) for every vertex, and the support graph is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_2/2\leq h_{w,\mu}\leq\sqrt{2q_{\max}\lambda_2}\).

children.title: Directed Cheeger Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cheeger Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A directed conductance inequality obtained through stationary time-reversal symmetrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be an irreducible finite Markov transition matrix with stationary distribution \(\pi\), and let \(P^*=\Pi^{-1}P^{\mathsf T}\Pi\) be its time reversal. Define \(M=(P+P^*)/2\) and \(\Phi(P)=\min_{0<\pi(S)\leq1/2}\sum_{i\in S,j\notin S}\pi_iP_{ij}/\pi(S)\). Stationarity implies \(\Phi(P)=\Phi(M)\). If \(\gamma=1-\lambda_2(M)\), then \[\frac{\gamma}{2}\leq\Phi(P)\leq\sqrt{2\gamma}.\] Hence the relevant real spectral gap is that of the additive reversiblization, not an ordering of the generally complex eigenvalues of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed stationary conductance equals that of the additive reversiblization and therefore obeys an ordinary Cheeger inequality for the reversiblized spectral gap.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a finite irreducible Markov transition matrix.
\(\pi\) is its strictly positive stationary distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(P)=\Phi((P+P^*)/2)\) and \(\gamma/2\leq\Phi(P)\leq\sqrt{2\gamma}\).

notation.meaning: Time reversal in the stationary inner product.

children.title: Reversibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Directed regimes distinguished by reversible versus nonreversible behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Reversibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why the reversible second-eigenvalue formulation does not transfer directly to directed chains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the deterministic directed cycle on \(n\geq3\) states, let \(P_{i,i+1\bmod n}=1\). Its stationary distribution is uniform and its directed conductance is positive, of order \(n^{-1}\), but the eigenvalues of \(P\) are \(e^{2\pi i j/n}\), all on the unit circle. Consequently, there is no canonically ordered real second eigenvalue whose gap can satisfy the reversible Cheeger statement. The additive reversiblization \((P+P^*)/2\) instead has real gap \(1-\cos(2\pi/n)\), of order \(n^{-2}\), restoring the square-root conductance scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic directed cycle has positive conductance but complex unit-modulus eigenvalues, so reversible Cheeger theory requires symmetrization or another nonreversible spectral surrogate.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the one-step deterministic transition matrix on the directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reversible formula cannot use a real ordered \(\lambda_2(P)\); additive reversiblization yields gap \(1-\cos(2\pi/n)\).

notation.meaning: Time-reversed transition matrix under the uniform stationary distribution.

children.title: Degree-Heterogeneity Effects
children.top_down_role: Spectral partitioning distortions caused by uneven degree profiles.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is finite, connected, weighted, and undirected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\), \(\lambda_k(L)/d_{\max}\leq\lambda_k(\mathcal L)\leq\lambda_k(L)/d_{\min}\); hence these comparison constants are not uniform when \(d_{\max}/d_{\min}\) is unbounded.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: generalized Courant-Fischer comparison using degree-matrix bounds
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of uniform spectral-scale comparison under an unbounded weighted-degree ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=D-A\) and \(\mathcal L=D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2}\) for a finite connected weighted undirected graph with \(0<d_{\min}\leq d_v\leq d_{\max}\). If the eigenvalues of each Laplacian are ordered nondecreasingly, then for every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\), \[\frac{\lambda_k(L)}{d_{\max}}\leq\lambda_k(\mathcal L)\leq\frac{\lambda_k(L)}{d_{\min}}.\] Consequently, the comparison constants between the normalized and unnormalized eigenvalue scales differ by the degree ratio \(d_{\max}/d_{\min}\), so this comparison is not uniform over graph families with unbounded degree ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalized and unnormalized Laplacian eigenvalues obey a degree-dependent comparison. When the maximum-to-minimum degree ratio is unbounded, that comparison supplies no uniform conversion between their spectral scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Heterogeneity Effects

notation.meaning: Inverse participation ratio of a unit vector.

Effective support as a fraction of the number of vertices.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-participation-ratio condition for concentration of a normalized graph eigenvector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite vertex set \(V\) and a vector \(u\in\mathbb R^V\) with \(\lVert u\rVert_2=1\), define \(\operatorname{IPR}(u)=\sum_{v\in V}u_v^4\), \(s_{\mathrm{eff}}(u)=1/\operatorname{IPR}(u)\), and the normalized participation ratio \(p(u)=s_{\mathrm{eff}}(u)/|V|\). A sequence of unit eigenvectors \((u_n)\) on graphs with \(|V_n|\to\infty\) is IPR-localized when \(s_{\mathrm{eff}}(u_n)=o(|V_n|)\), equivalently when \(p(u_n)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of unit eigenvectors is localized in the inverse-participation-ratio sense when its effective support is sublinear in the number of vertices, equivalently when its normalized participation ratio tends to zero.

children.title: Localization-Regularization Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric and entrywise nonnegative.
Degrees are defined by row sums, including diagonal weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularized degrees are \(d_v+\tau\), their ratio is \((d_{\max}+\tau)/(d_{\min}+\tau)\), and this ratio is at most \(2\) whenever \(\tau\geq d_{\max}\).

notation.meaning: Regularized adjacency and row-sum degree matrices.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic row-sum calculation for uniform rank-one augmentation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform rank-one adjacency regularization and its exact effect on the degree ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be a symmetric nonnegative adjacency matrix, with degrees defined by \(d_v=\sum_{j=1}^n A_{vj}\). For \(\tau>0\), define \(A_\tau=A+(\tau/n)\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\), let \(D_\tau\) be the diagonal matrix of row sums of \(A_\tau\), and set \(\mathcal L_\tau=I-D_\tau^{-1/2}A_\tau D_\tau^{-1/2}\). Then \(D_\tau=D+\tau I\), every regularized degree is \(d_v+\tau\), and \[\frac{\max_v(d_v+\tau)}{\min_v(d_v+\tau)}=\frac{d_{\max}+\tau}{d_{\min}+\tau}.\] In particular, if \(\tau\geq d_{\max}\), this ratio is at most \(2\). This degree-ratio bound alone does not imply delocalization of every eigenvector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform rank-one adjacency regularization adds tau to every row-sum degree. The resulting degree ratio is exact and is at most two when tau is at least the maximum original degree, but that fact alone does not guarantee eigenvector delocalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Localization-Regularization Regimes

children.title: Repeated-Eigenvalue Regimes
children.top_down_role: Spectral partitioning settings with non-simple relevant eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Eigenvalue Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis nonuniqueness and projector invariance for a repeated symmetric-Laplacian eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=L^{\mathsf T}\) and suppose an eigenvalue \(\lambda\) has multiplicity \(m>1\), with eigenspace \(E_\lambda\). If \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(E_\lambda\), then every other orthonormal eigenbasis matrix for that eigenspace is \(UQ\) for some orthogonal \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\). Individual eigenvectors and their coordinate orderings are therefore not intrinsic. In contrast, the projector \(P_\lambda=UU^{\mathsf T}\), row distances \(\lVert U_{i,:}-U_{j,:}\rVert_2\), and row inner products are invariant under the basis replacement \(U\mapsto UQ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A repeated eigenvalue determines an eigenspace, not unique eigenvectors; projectors and Euclidean relationships in the full eigenspace remain basis invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every orthonormal basis change is \(U\mapsto UQ\), while \(UU^{\mathsf T}\) and all embedded row distances remain unchanged.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the repeated eigenvalue.
An orthonormal basis matrix for the eigenspace.

children.title: Basis-Selection Instability
children.top_down_role: Partition sensitivity to basis choices within repeated eigenspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Selection Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected equal components show instability of rounding one vector from a repeated eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the disjoint union of two nonempty connected graphs \(G_1\) and \(G_2\). The normalized Laplacian has eigenvalue \(0\) with multiplicity two and eigenspace spanned by \(z_1=D^{1/2}\mathbf1_{V(G_1)}\) and \(z_2=D^{1/2}\mathbf1_{V(G_2)}\). Every nonzero combination \(a z_1+b z_2\) is a zero eigenvector. Consequently, a procedure selecting one numerical eigenvector and thresholding its coordinates can return different cuts after an orthogonal rotation within this eigenspace, even though the graph and invariant spectral projector are unchanged. The full two-dimensional embedding is stable up to rotation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two disconnected components, arbitrary rotations of the repeated zero eigenspace change individual eigenvectors and their threshold cuts, while the full eigenspace remains invariant.
assumptions_latex: \(G=G_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}G_2\), with both components nonempty and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Single-vector threshold rounding is basis dependent, whereas the projector onto \(\operatorname{span}\{z_1,z_2\}\) is basis independent.

notation.meaning: Degree-weighted component indicator for component i.

children.title: Subspace-Stable Clustering
children.top_down_role: Clustering representations invariant to eigenspace basis selection.

assumptions_latex: The admissible family \(\mathcal P\) of vertex partitions is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi_{UQ}(P)=\Phi_U(P)\) for every \(Q\in O(k)\) and \(P\in\mathcal P\); under the stated objective-gap condition, the minimizing clustering is unchanged by sufficiently small projector perturbations.

notation.meaning: Spectral embedding matrix whose rows represent vertices.
Within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances for partition \(P\).
Orthogonal group acting on the selected eigenspace basis.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Orthogonal basis invariance of Euclidean clustering objectives and finite-gap stability are standard.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite spectral embeddings; stability concerns the invariant subspace rather than a particular eigenvector basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\in\mathcal P\), define \(\Phi_U(P)=\sum_{C\in P}\sum_{i\in C}\lVert U_{i,:}-\bar U_C\rVert_2^2\), where \(\bar U_C=|C|^{-1}\sum_{i\in C}U_{i,:}\). For every orthogonal \(Q\in O(k)\), \(\Phi_{UQ}(P)=\Phi_U(P)\). Suppose \(P_*\) uniquely minimizes \(\Phi_U\) and \(\gamma=\min_{P\ne P_*}(\Phi_U(P)-\Phi_U(P_*))>0\). If another orthonormal embedding \(\widetilde U\) satisfies \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}|\Phi_{\widetilde U}(P)-\Phi_U(P)|<\gamma/2\), then \(P_*\) also uniquely minimizes \(\Phi_{\widetilde U}\). Thus clustering can remain stable even when individual bases rotate inside a repeated eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Euclidean clustering is invariant under eigenspace basis rotations and remains unchanged under perturbations smaller than half its objective gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Subspace-Stable Clustering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property is mathematically precise, basis-invariant, and appropriate for the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the objective-gap stability claim.

notation.meaning: Weighted edge-boundary cost of a partition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrestricted rounding, not of rounding schemes having proved separation or approximation guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the disjoint union of \(k\) connected weighted graphs, each containing an edge of positive weight. The component partition has \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(G)=0\). A rounding map may nevertheless output a nonempty \(k\)-partition \(P\) that splits one connected component and combines vertices from different components; choosing the split across a positive-weight edge gives \(\operatorname{cut}(P)>0\). Hence \(\operatorname{cut}(P)/\operatorname{OPT}_k(G)=+\infty\), with the ratio interpreted as infinite when its numerator is positive and denominator is zero. Therefore spectral relaxation quality alone cannot bound multiway rounding distortion without conditions connecting embedded geometry to the rounding map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted rounding can cut a positive edge even when disconnected components give zero optimum, so its multiplicative distortion can be infinite.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Rounding Distortion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-optimum example correctly exhibits unbounded distortion for unrestricted rounding and fits a failure-boundary container, but it has no cited source.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Triangle inequalities plus spreading constraints form the standard balanced-partition metric relaxation.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality-balanced metric relaxation; alternative volume-weighted spreading constraints require a separate formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A spreading-metric relaxation is
\[\min \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}w_{ij}d_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad d_{ii}=0,\ d_{ij}=d_{ji},\ 0\le d_{ij}\le 1,\ d_{ij}\le d_{i\ell}+d_{\ell j},\ \sum_{j\in V}d_{ij}\ge |V|-b\quad(i,j,\ell\in V).\]
For any partition into blocks of size at most \(b\), setting \(d_{ij}=0\) within blocks and \(d_{ij}=1\) between blocks satisfies every constraint, and the objective equals the partition's cut weight. Consequently the relaxation optimum is a lower bound on the corresponding integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semimetric with triangle and spreading constraints relaxes balanced partitioning; every bounded-size partition gives a feasible zero-one metric of equal cut cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Spreading-Metric Relaxations

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A distribution over dominating tree metrics exists with expected pairwise stretch \(O(\log n)\).

notation.meaning: Shortest-path metric of a sampled weighted tree containing \(V\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: This is the standard probabilistic dominating-tree approximation theorem for finite metrics.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probabilistic dominating-tree approximation; the universal constant is left unspecified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There is a probability distribution over weighted tree metrics \(d_T\) on trees whose vertex sets contain \(V\), and a universal constant \(C>0\), such that for every \(u,v\in V\),
\[d(u,v)\le d_T(u,v)\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \mathbb E[d_T(u,v)]\le C\log n\,d(u,v).\]
Thus every finite metric admits a random noncontractive tree representation with expected pairwise distortion at most \(C\log n\). The expectation is taken over the sampled tree, separately for each fixed pair \((u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite metric is dominated by a random tree metric whose expected stretch for each pair is logarithmic in the number of points.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Metric Approximations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite \(\ell_1\) embeddings represented through the cut cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty proper \(S\subset V\), let \(\delta_S(u,v)=1\) when exactly one of \(u,v\) lies in \(S\), and let \(\delta_S(u,v)=0\) otherwise. A cut embedding of distortion \(D\ge1\) is a family \(\lambda_S\ge0\) such that
\[d(u,v)\le \sum_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}\lambda_S\delta_S(u,v)\le Dd(u,v)\qquad(u,v\in V).\]
The middle expression is an \(\ell_1\) metric, and every \(\ell_1\) metric on \(V\) has such an exact cut decomposition. Hence low-distortion cut embedding and low-distortion embedding into \(\ell_1\) are equivalent finite-metric formulations.

children.title: Graph Coarsening Strategies
children.top_down_role: Graph-reduction strategies used to form multilevel hierarchies.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Coarsening Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted aggregation coarsening with exact preservation of aggregate-respecting cut costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(G_0=G\). At level \(\ell\), choose a surjective aggregation map \(\pi_\ell:V_\ell\to V_{\ell+1}\) whose fibers are the selected aggregates. For distinct coarse vertices \(A,B\), set
\[w_{\ell+1}(A,B)=\sum_{\substack{\{u,v\}\in E_\ell\\ \pi_\ell(u)=A,\ \pi_\ell(v)=B}}w_\ell(u,v).\]
Discard self-loops. Stop when a prescribed vertex-count or contraction threshold is met, and output the graphs and aggregation maps. Every coarse partition lifts by assigning each fine vertex to its aggregate's block, and its lifted cut weight equals the coarse cut weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly contract disjoint aggregates and sum interaggregate edge weights; every coarse partition then lifts with exactly the same cut cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G_0=(V_0,E_0,w_0)\) is a finite weighted undirected graph.
At each level, a contraction rule selects pairwise disjoint vertex aggregates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces a weighted hierarchy in which coarse cut weights equal the fine cut weights of lifted aggregate-respecting partitions.

notation.meaning: Map sending fine vertices to their aggregates.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weighted aggregation by summing interaggregate edges is the standard contraction invariant.

children.title: Uncoarsening Schedules
children.top_down_role: Hierarchy-expansion regimes used during multilevel partition recovery.

assumptions_latex: A hierarchy \(G_0,\ldots,G_L\) with aggregation maps is given.
A feasible partition \(P_L\) has been computed on the coarsest graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The schedule returns a feasible fine-level partition and never increases cut cost when every accepted refinement move is nonincreasing.

notation.meaning: Aggregation map from level \(\ell\) to level \(\ell+1\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Projection followed by local refinement is the defining multilevel uncoarsening schedule.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-by-level projection with feasibility-preserving local refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\ell=L-1,L-2,\ldots,0\), initialize \(P_\ell\) by assigning \(v\in V_\ell\) to the block containing \(\pi_\ell(v)\) in \(P_{\ell+1}\). Apply a specified local refinement oracle to \(P_\ell\), accepting only moves that preserve the balance constraints and do not increase cut weight; stop refinement when no accepted move remains or a level budget is exhausted. Output \(P_0\). Because projection preserves the coarse cut and every accepted move is nonincreasing, the cut-weight sequence across each projection-refinement stage is nonincreasing, while feasibility is maintained at every level.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the coarse partition down one level at a time and apply feasible nonincreasing local moves, yielding a no-worse fine partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Uncoarsening Schedules

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The level-by-level projection and refinement schedule is coherent and algorithm is the correct content kind, but the claimed projection and feasibility invariants lack a cited source.

children.title: Hierarchy-Quality Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Partition-quality effects of coarsening choices and hierarchy depth.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy-Quality Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact search-space tradeoff for contraction-based minimization, independent of a particular coarsening heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible fine-level partitions and let \(\mathcal F_\pi=\{P\in\mathcal F:P\text{ is constant on every aggregate of }\pi\}\). Then \(\mathcal F_\pi\subseteq\mathcal F\), and exact preservation of aggregate-respecting cut costs yields
\[\min_{P\in\mathcal F}\operatorname{cut}(P)\le \min_{P\in\mathcal F_\pi}\operatorname{cut}(P).\]
Merging additional aggregates can only shrink \(\mathcal F_\pi\), so the restricted optimum is nondecreasing while the number of coarse vertices is nonincreasing. Subsequent uncoarsening refinement may recover partitions excluded from the coarse search space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: More contraction makes coarse problems smaller but restricts admissible partitions, so the exact restricted optimum can only worsen for cut minimization.
assumptions_latex: Each coarse vertex represents an indivisible aggregate of original vertices.
Cut weight is minimized over partitions satisfying fixed feasibility constraints.
Cut costs of aggregate-respecting partitions are preserved by contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coarsening restricts the feasible search space, so its optimum cannot improve upon the unrestricted fine optimum, although it reduces instance size.

children.title: Kernighan–Lin Refinement
children.top_down_role: Pair-exchange refinement regimes for graph partitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Kernighan–Lin Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical weighted, exactly balanced two-way pair-swap pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize all vertices as unlocked and set \(G_0=0\). At step \(t\), among unlocked \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\), choose a pair maximizing the exact cut reduction \(g(a,b)\) produced by exchanging them; record the pair, lock both vertices, update the remaining gains, and set \(G_t=G_{t-1}+g(a,b)\). Continue until no unlocked cross-pair exists. Choose \(t^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_t G_t\). If \(G_{t^*}>0\), commit precisely the first \(t^*\) recorded swaps; otherwise restore the initial partition. Repeat passes until a pass has no positive-gain prefix, and output the resulting balanced bipartition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernighan-Lin greedily locks cross-block vertex pairs, then commits the prefix of swaps giving the largest positive cumulative cut reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite weighted undirected graph.
An exactly balanced bipartition \((A,B)\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pass outputs the best positive-gain prefix of locked pair exchanges, or leaves the partition unchanged when no prefix has positive gain.

notation.meaning: Cut reduction obtained by swapping \(a\) and \(b\).
Cumulative gain after the first \(t\) swaps.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The locked maximum-gain pair-swap pass is the classical Kernighan-Lin refinement rule.

children.title: Fiduccia–Mattheyses Refinement
children.top_down_role: Single-vertex move refinement regimes with gain management.

knowledge_statements.title: Fiduccia–Mattheyses Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance-constrained two-way single-vertex refinement; bucket implementation details are abstracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize every vertex as unlocked and place each movable vertex in a gain structure keyed by its current cut reduction \(g(v)\). Repeatedly select an unlocked vertex of maximum gain whose move keeps the block weights within the permitted balance interval, move and lock it, update the gains of affected unlocked neighbors, and record the cumulative gain \(G_t\). Stop when no feasible unlocked move remains. Choose a recorded prefix maximizing \(G_t\); commit that prefix if its gain is positive and undo its suffix, otherwise undo the entire pass. Repeat passes until no positive-gain prefix exists, and output the final feasible bipartition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiduccia-Mattheyses uses a gain structure for locked single-vertex moves and retains only the best feasible positive-gain prefix of each pass.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite weighted graph or hypergraph.
A feasible bipartition and a permitted balance interval are given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pass commits the feasible prefix of locked single-vertex moves with maximum positive cumulative gain, or makes no change if none exists.

notation.meaning: Immediate cut reduction from moving vertex \(v\).
Cumulative gain of the first \(t\) recorded moves.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Gain ordering, locking, and best-prefix rollback define the classical Fiduccia-Mattheyses pass.

children.title: Refinement-Regime Comparison
children.top_down_role: Structural settings favoring pair-exchange or single-vertex refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Refinement-Regime Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison by move neighborhood and balance regime, excluding implementation-specific running-time claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a partition \(P\), Kernighan–Lin searches sequences drawn from \(N_{\mathrm{KL}}(P)\), where each elementary move exchanges one vertex from each block and therefore preserves equal cardinality. Fiduccia–Mattheyses searches sequences drawn from \(N_{\mathrm{FM}}(P)\), where each elementary move transfers one vertex and is feasible only when the resulting block weights remain within the balance interval. Consequently, a partition can be locally optimal for one neighborhood but not the other. Pair swaps directly explore compensated exchanges under exact balance, whereas single moves directly exploit available balance slack; best-prefix rollback permits both methods to traverse individually nonimproving moves within a pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernighan-Lin explores balance-preserving pair swaps, while Fiduccia-Mattheyses explores feasible single moves; their local optima therefore need not coincide.
assumptions_latex: Both methods refine a finite weighted bipartition using exact cut gains.
Kernighan–Lin enforces exact balance by pair swaps, while Fiduccia–Mattheyses permits feasible single-vertex moves within a balance interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The methods optimize different move neighborhoods; exact-balance pair swaps and tolerance-based single moves yield distinct local-optimality regimes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The comparison follows from the algorithms' distinct feasible move neighborhoods.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Based Partition Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localized two-way refinement reduced to an auxiliary minimum terminal cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct an auxiliary capacitated network \(H\) with terminals \(s,t\) and one node for every vertex in \(R\). For each original edge with both endpoints in \(R\), add the corresponding capacity between its endpoint nodes. For every edge from \(u\in R\) to a fixed vertex outside \(R\), add its weight to the terminal capacity that charges assigning \(u\) to the opposite block. Compute a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow and an associated minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut, and assign each vertex in \(R\) according to its terminal side. Accept the induced partition only if it satisfies the prescribed balance constraint and decreases cut weight; otherwise retain the input partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode a local two-way reassignment as a terminal network, solve a minimum cut, and accept the induced partition only when balanced and improving.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite undirected graph with nonnegative capacities.
A bipartition \((A,B)\) and a refinement region \(R\subseteq V\) are fixed.
Vertices in \(V\setminus R\) retain their current blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum terminal cut gives the least-capacity reassignment represented by the auxiliary network, and accepting only feasible improving candidates preserves refinement validity.

notation.meaning: Source and sink terminals representing the two fixed sides.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stars exhibit an unbounded gap between ordinary and equitable chromatic numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the star \(S_n=K_{1,n}\), ordinary coloring gives \(\chi(S_n)=2\). In any proper coloring, the center's color class is a singleton and every other class contains only leaves. Equitability therefore forces each leaf-only class to contain at most two vertices. Hence at least \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) leaf colors and one center color are necessary, and partitioning the leaves into pairs and at most one singleton attains this bound. Consequently, \[\chi_{=}(S_n)=\left\lceil\frac n2\right\rceil+1,\] so \(\chi_{=}(S_n)-\chi(S_n)\) is unbounded.

knowledge_statements.title: List Edge Coloring

The circular clique \(K_{p/q}\) has vertex set \(\mathbb Z_p\), with \(ij\) an edge exactly when \(q\le |i-j|_p\le p-q\), where \(|i-j|_p=\min\{|i-j|,p-|i-j|\}\). knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering-sensitive upper bound produced by sequential greedy vertex coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be an ordering of the vertices of a finite simple graph \(G\). Color the vertices sequentially, assigning to \(v_i\) the least positive color not already used on its earlier neighbors. If \(b_i=|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|\), then the resulting coloring is proper and uses at most \(1+\max_i b_i\) colors. Consequently, every ordering certifies \(\chi(G)\le 1+\max_i b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Greedy coloring along an ordering uses at most one more color than the largest number of earlier neighbors of any vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le 1+\max_{1\le i\le n}|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|.\)

notation.meaning: number of neighbors of v_i preceding it

children.title: Degeneracy Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chromatic bound obtained from a degeneracy ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty finite simple graph \(G\), define its degeneracy by \(d(G)=\max_{\varnothing\ne H\subseteq G}\delta(H)\), where \(H\) ranges over subgraphs. Repeatedly deleting a vertex of current degree at most \(d(G)\) and reversing the deletion order gives an ordering in which every vertex has at most \(d(G)\) earlier neighbors. Greedy coloring in this order therefore yields \(\chi(G)\le d(G)+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every d-degenerate graph has a deletion ordering that greedy coloring uses to produce at most d+1 colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a nonempty finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le d(G)+1\), where \(d(G)=\max_{\varnothing\ne H\subseteq G}\delta(H)\).
