knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Graph Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties underlying vertex-critical coloring arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple graph \(G\) is \(k\)-critical if \(\chi(G)=k\) and every proper subgraph is \((k-1)\)-colorable. Every \(k\)-critical graph is connected and has minimum degree at least \(k-1\). Indeed, for each vertex \(v\), every \((k-1)\)-coloring of \(G-v\) uses all \(k-1\) colors on \(N(v)\); otherwise that coloring extends to \(G\). For \(k\ge3\), a \(k\)-critical graph has no cut vertex.

Given \(Q\), validity is checkable using at most \(\binom r2\) adjacency tests.

knowledge_statements.title: Planar Coloring Theorem Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-color bound and the triangle-free planar strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite simple planar graph. The Four Color Theorem states that \(G\) has a proper vertex coloring with at most four colors, so \(\chi(G)\le4\). Under the additional hypothesis that \(G\) contains no triangle, Grötzsch's theorem strengthens the bound to \(\chi(G)\le3\). Both bounds are sharp: \(K_4\) is planar and requires four colors, while odd cycles are triangle-free planar graphs requiring three colors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every planar graph is 4-colorable, and every triangle-free planar graph is 3-colorable; complete graphs and odd cycles show sharpness.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple planar graph.
For the strengthened conclusion, \(G\) is triangle-free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)\le4\), and if \(G\) is triangle-free then \(\chi(G)\le3\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines edge colorings of a graph and relates them to vertex colorings of its line graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph. An edge-colouring is a partition of \(E\) into matchings, called colours. If a feasible coloring uses labels \(1,

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-simplex Gram-matrix relaxation of finite graph \(k\)-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the semidefinite feasibility system \[X\succeq0,
\qquad X_{vv}=1\quad(v\in V),
\qquad X_{uv}=-\frac{1}{k-1}\quad(uv\in E).\] A proper \(k\)-coloring makes this system feasible by assigning to each color one vertex of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb R^{k-1}\) and taking \(X\) as the resulting Gram matrix. Therefore feasibility is necessary for \(k\)-colorability, and infeasibility is a certificate that \(\chi(G)>k\). Allowing the edge conditions as inequalities gives the corresponding vector-coloring relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper k-coloring produces a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix from regular-simplex color vectors; infeasibility therefore rules out k-colorability.

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential first-fit coloring under a prescribed vertex ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \((v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) order \(V\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), assign \(v_i\) the least positive integer not assigned to any earlier neighbor: \[c(v_i)=\min\bigl(\mathbb N_{>0}\setminus\{c(v_j):j<i,\ v_jv_i\in E\}\bigr).\] The output \(c\) is a proper coloring. If \(d_i^-\) is the number of neighbors of \(v_i\) preceding it, then the algorithm uses at most \(1+\max_i d_i^-\) colors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process vertices in order, giving each the smallest color absent from its earlier neighbors; the result is proper and uses at most one plus the maximum earlier-neighbor count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is proper and \(|c(V)|\le 1+\max_i d_i^-\).

notation.meaning: number of neighbors of v_i occurring earlier in the ordering

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard first-fit coloring definition and ordering bound

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind and local container fit, and the first-fit rule and ordering bound are standard. However, no citation or inspectable locator is supplied. Also, the expression \(\max_i d_i^-\) is undefined when \(V=\varnothing\); a source-backed version should either assume \(V\ne\varnothing\) or handle the empty graph separately.

children.title: Smallest-Last Methods
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy-oriented vertex orderings used for constructive coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Smallest-Last Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy ordering followed by reverse-order greedy coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. Repeatedly choose a minimum-degree vertex in the current induced graph, delete it, and record the deletion sequence \((w_1,\ldots,w_n)\). Then greedily color vertices in the reverse order \((w_n,\ldots,w_1)\). If \(d=\max_i\deg_{G[\{w_i,\ldots,w_n\}]}(w_i)\), the resulting coloring is proper and uses at most \(d+1\) colors; this \(d\) equals the degeneracy of \(G\). Ties may be resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a current minimum-degree vertex repeatedly, then greedily color in reverse deletion order. The method uses at most degeneracy plus one colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reverse deletion ordering yields a proper coloring with at most \(d+1\) colors.

notation.meaning: degeneracy attained along the deletion sequence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm content kind matches Smallest-Last Methods, and the stated deletion-order degeneracy guarantee is standard for a nonempty finite graph. No supporting citation or locator is provided, and the displayed maximum defining \(d\) needs an explicit nonempty-graph convention or hypothesis.

children.title: Recursive Largest-First Methods
children.top_down_role: Color-class construction based on recursive largest-first selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Largest-First Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: RLF constructs one independent color class at a time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple. While uncolored vertices remain, initialize a color class \(S\) with an uncolored vertex of maximum uncolored degree. Let \(A\) be uncolored vertices nonadjacent to every vertex of \(S\). While \(A\ne\varnothing\), add to \(S\) a vertex maximizing its number of uncolored neighbors outside \(A\), breaking ties by minimum degree in \(G[A]\), and recompute \(A\). Assign one new color to all vertices of \(S\), remove them, and repeat. Each produced \(S\) is independent, so the output is a proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLF repeatedly grows an independent color class, favoring eligible vertices that exclude many remaining candidates, and removes each completed class before constructing the next.
assumptions_latex: All stated selection ties are resolved arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated color classes partition \(V\) into independent sets and therefore define a proper coloring.

notation.meaning: eligible uncolored vertices nonadjacent to S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct knowledge kind for this leaf, but the exact RLF selection and tie-breaking variant lacks a source. The phrase "uncolored neighbors outside \(A\)" is state-dependent and does not explicitly distinguish vertices excluded by adjacency to \(S\) from vertices already placed in \(S\); an authoritative algorithm statement is needed to fix the intended candidate sets.

children.title: Constructive Ordering Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph structures and performance patterns distinguishing the two ordering families.

knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Ordering Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordering quality controls the color guarantee of sequential coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and an ordering \(\pi=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\), define its backward width by \[b(\pi)=\max_i|N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}|.\] Greedy coloring along \(\pi\) uses at most \(b(\pi)+1\) colors. Consequently, any constructive regime producing an ordering with \(b(\pi)\le k\) supplies a polynomially checkable certificate that its greedy coloring uses at most \(k+1\) colors. A reverse smallest-last ordering has backward width equal to at most the degeneracy of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any constructed ordering with at most k earlier neighbors per vertex makes greedy coloring use at most k+1 colors; reverse smallest-last ordering realizes the degeneracy guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|c_\pi(V)|\le b(\pi)+1\), and reverse smallest-last order has \(b(\pi)\le\operatorname{degen}(G)\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of earlier neighbors in ordering π

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary greedy-ordering and degeneracy bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Property is a reasonable primary kind for the ordering-width relation in this container, although the record also characterizes the ordering as a certificate. The greedy bound and reverse smallest-last claim are mathematically standard, but neither has a cited source or inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.title: DSATUR Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential coloring ordered dynamically by saturation degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. Initially all vertices are uncolored. At each iteration choose an uncolored vertex \(v\) maximizing the saturation degree \(\sigma(v)=|\{c(u):u\in N(v),\ u\text{ colored}\}|\); break ties by maximum degree in the uncolored subgraph, then arbitrarily. Assign \(v\) the least positive color absent from its colored neighborhood. Stop when every vertex is colored. The resulting map \(c:V\to\mathbb N_{>0}\) is a proper coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly color the vertex seeing the most distinct neighbor colors, using residual degree for ties and the smallest available color. The completed coloring is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure terminates after \(|V|\) assignments and returns a proper coloring \(c\).

notation.meaning: number of distinct colors present in the colored neighborhood of v
partial and ultimately complete vertex coloring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits DSATUR Coloring and the construction yields a proper coloring. The residual-degree tie break is one DSATUR variant rather than a universally fixed definition, so the exact rule requires a specific source and locator.

children.title: Coloring Search-Tree Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching designs for exact coloring search trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Search-Tree Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete branching scheme for exact fixed-\(k\) coloring feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and a proper partial coloring \(c:S\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\), choose an uncolored vertex \(v\in V\setminus S\). Its feasible colors are \[F(v)=\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus\{c(u):u\in S\cap N(v)\}.\] Create one child for every \(a\in F(v)\), extending the assignment by \(c(v)=a\). A node with \(F(v)=\varnothing\) is infeasible; a node with \(S=V\) certifies feasibility. Exhausting all children without a complete assignment certifies that the parent has no \(k\)-coloring extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an uncolored vertex and branch over every color not used by a colored neighbor. Empty domains fail; complete assignments certify k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The children partition all proper \(k\)-coloring extensions of the current partial assignment.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the branching leaf, and the children exhaust the extensions of the stated proper partial \(k\)-coloring. The record has no citation or inspectable locator supporting this exact search-tree formulation.

children.title: Coloring Bounds for Pruning
children.top_down_role: Upper and lower bounding mechanisms used to restrict exact search.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Bounds for Pruning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower and upper bounds certify safe branch-and-bound pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a node of an exact chromatic-number search, let \(L\) be a valid lower bound on every completion reachable from that node and let \(U\) be the number of colors in a known complete coloring of \(G\). Then \(L\le\chi(G)\le U\) at the root, and the node may be pruned whenever \(L\ge U\), since it cannot improve the incumbent. A clique \(Q\) compatible with the node gives the verifiable lower bound \(L\ge|Q|\); any explicit proper coloring gives the verifiable upper bound \(U=|c(V)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compatible clique supplies a lower bound and a proper coloring an upper bound. A search node is safely discarded when its lower bound cannot beat the incumbent.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) bounds every completion at the node and \(U\) is an incumbent coloring value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L\ge U\), pruning the node preserves the optimal chromatic number.

notation.meaning: node lower bound on the attainable color count
clique used as a lower-bound certificate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: branch-and-bound dominance and clique/coloring certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate kind for clique and incumbent bounds used in pruning. No supporting source is supplied. The sentence \(L\ge |Q|\) should also be sourced or restated as an update such as \(L\leftarrow\max\{L,|Q|\}\), because an arbitrary valid lower bound \(L\) need not already dominate the clique bound.

children.title: Coloring Search Pruning Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dominance, infeasibility, and structural pruning opportunities.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Search Pruning Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound pruning predicates for partial exact-coloring search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search node represented by a proper partial coloring with color domains \(D(v)\) on uncolored vertices, pruning is sound if at least one of the following holds: \(D(v)=\varnothing\) for some uncolored \(v\); propagation derives a violated edge or cardinality constraint; a valid node lower bound \(L\) satisfies \(L\ge U\), where \(U\) is the incumbent value; or the node is dominated by an already explored equivalent state whose admissible completions include its own. Each predicate excludes every completion that could improve \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune on an empty color domain, propagated contradiction, lower bound no better than the incumbent, or certified dominance by an equivalent state.
assumptions_latex: All propagation, bounding, and dominance tests are valid for the represented subtree.
\(U\) is the value of a known feasible coloring.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every node satisfying a listed predicate may be removed without eliminating a coloring better than \(U\).

notation.meaning: current feasible color domain of uncolored vertex v
node lower bound and incumbent upper bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constraint and branch-and-bound pruning predicates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is the correct role for a list of pruning predicates. Empty domains, contradictions, and bound pruning are standard, but the dominance predicate does not state what information from the explored state certifies disposal of the dominated subtree. A specific source is required for that regime and none is cited for the other predicates.

children.title: Restricted Master Coloring Models
children.top_down_role: Restricted column formulations used during exact coloring search.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Master Coloring Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-covering restricted master problem for column-generation coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple, and let \(\mathcal S'\) be a finite collection of stable sets. The restricted master relaxation is \[\min\ \sum_{S\in\mathcal S'}x_S\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{S\in\mathcal S':v\in S}x_S\ge1\ \ (v\in V),\qquad x_S\ge0\ \ (S\in\mathcal S').\] Requiring \(x_S\in\{0,1\}\) gives the restricted integer master. If \(\mathcal S'\) contains all stable sets, the integer optimum equals \(\chi(G)\); with fewer columns it is an upper restriction and may be infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cover every vertex by selected stable-set columns while minimizing their number. With all stable sets and binary variables, the optimum is the chromatic number.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal S'\) is a stable set of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the complete stable-set family \(\mathcal S\), the binary master optimum is \(\chi(G)\).

notation.meaning: current restricted family of stable-set columns
selection variable for stable-set column S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard set-covering formulation of graph coloring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind for this restricted-master formulation. The set-covering model and complete-family chromatic-number equivalence are standard and internally consistent, but no source or specific locator supports them.

children.title: Stable-Set Pricing Problems
children.top_down_role: Pricing subproblems that generate color-class columns.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Pricing Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pricing oracle for the set-covering coloring master relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the restricted master relaxation with dual multipliers \(\pi_v\ge0\) on the vertex-covering constraints, the reduced cost of a stable-set column \(S\) is \[\bar c_S=1-\sum_{v\in S}\pi_v.\] Hence pricing is the maximum-weight stable-set problem \[z(\pi)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in S}\pi_v:S\subseteq V\text{ is stable}\right\}.\] A negative-reduced-cost column exists exactly when \(z(\pi)>1\). If \(z(\pi)\le1\), the current restricted-master solution is optimal for the full linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using vertex dual prices as weights, solve a maximum-weight stable-set problem. A column improves the master exactly when its weight exceeds one.
assumptions_latex: The restricted master relaxation is feasible and solved to LP optimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z(\pi)>1\) yields an improving column, while \(z(\pi)\le1\) certifies full-master LP optimality.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier for covering vertex v
reduced cost of stable-set column S
maximum dual weight of a stable set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: LP duality for set-covering column generation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Duality is the correct kind for the pricing relation, and the reduced-cost sign and threshold are consistent with the stated minimization covering master. The exact full-master optimality claim has no cited source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching structures that preserve tractable or reusable pricing subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Pricing-Compatible Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ryan–Foster-style branching that preserves stable-set pricing structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a fractional coloring master solution, choose distinct nonadjacent vertices \(u,v\) for which \(\sum_{S\ni u,v}x_S\) is fractional. Create two exhaustive branches. In the together branch, retain only columns \(S\) satisfying \(u\in S\iff v\in S\). In the separate branch, retain only columns satisfying \(|S\cap\{u,v\}|\le1\). Apply the same restrictions when generating new stable-set columns. Every integral coloring satisfies exactly one branch, and pricing remains a maximum-weight stable-set problem with the corresponding together-or-separate restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on whether two nonadjacent vertices share a color. Restrict both existing and generated stable-set columns accordingly, preserving exhaustive search and structured pricing.
assumptions_latex: The master columns represent stable color classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two branches cover all integral colorings and preserve constrained stable-set pricing.

notation.meaning: master variable for stable-set column S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Ryan–Foster-style branching for set-partitioning or covering columns

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the pricing-compatible branching leaf. The together/separate restrictions are plausible Ryan-Foster-style rules, but their use with the stated set-covering coloring master, the fractional branching quantity, and preservation of the pricing problem require a coloring-specific source and locator.

children.title: Integer Programming Encodings
children.top_down_role: Integer optimization encodings for exact graph coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Programming Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary assignment formulation of the chromatic-number problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and simple and set \(K=|V|\). For \(v\in V\) and \(c\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), let \(x_{vc}\) indicate assignment of color \(c\), and let \(y_c\) indicate its use. Then \[\min\sum_{c=1}^K y_c\] subject to \[\sum_{c=1}^Kx_{vc}=1,\quad x_{vc}\le y_c,\quad x_{uc}+x_{vc}\le1\ \ (uv\in E),\quad x_{vc},y_c\in\{0,1\}\] encodes proper colorings. Its optimum equals \(\chi(G)\). The optional inequalities \(y_c\ge y_{c+1}\) remove color-label symmetry without changing the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables assign one color to each vertex, forbid equal colors across edges, and activate used colors. Minimizing activations yields the chromatic number.
assumptions_latex: The available color index set has size \(K=|V|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer-program optimum is \(\chi(G)\).

notation.meaning: binary assignment of color c to vertex v
binary indicator that color c is used

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Integer Programming p. 103

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the correct kind, and the binary formulation is mathematically standard. The cited locator identifies only a general integer-programming chapter and does not specifically support the graph-coloring formulation or symmetry inequalities. Full-text support is pending. In addition, the constraint display should explicitly quantify \(v\in V\), \(c\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), and \(uv\in E\) for the respective constraint families.

children.title: SAT Encodings
children.top_down_role: Boolean satisfiability encodings for coloring feasibility and optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: SAT Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct CNF encoding of fixed-k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(k\ge 1\). Introduce a Boolean variable \(x_{v,c}\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(c\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Form the CNF formula \(F_k(G)\) containing
\[
\bigvee_{c=1}^{k}x_{v,c}\quad(v\in V),
\]
\[
\neg x_{v,c}\vee\neg x_{v,d}\quad(v\in V,\ c<d),
\]
and
\[
\neg x_{u,c}\vee\neg x_{v,c}\quad(uv\in E,\ 1\le c\le k).
\]
Then \(F_k(G)\) is satisfiable if and only if \(G\) has a proper coloring using at most \(k\) colors; satisfying assignments and such colorings translate directly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex-color variables, exactly-one color clauses, and edge-conflict clauses form a satisfiable CNF exactly when the graph is k-colorable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_k(G)\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \chi(G)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Boolean variable asserting that vertex v receives color c.

children.title: Constraint-Programming Encodings
children.top_down_role: Constraint-programming representations for exact coloring.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Programming Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-domain constraint model for fixed-k-colorability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(k\ge1\), introduce one finite-domain variable \(C_v\) for each \(v\in V\), with domain \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Post the binary disequality constraint
\[
C_u\ne C_v
\]
for every edge \(uv\in E\). Equivalently, these constraints may be grouped as an all-different constraint on each clique, provided every edge constraint is represented. The constraint network has a feasible assignment if and only if \(G\) admits a proper coloring with at most \(k\) colors, and every feasible assignment specifies such a coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign each vertex a finite-domain color variable and impose disequality across every edge; feasible assignments are precisely proper k-colorings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists(C_v)_{v\in V}\text{ satisfying all constraints}\iff\chi(G)\le k.\)

notation.meaning: Finite-domain color variable for vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-k coloring over a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite graph \(G\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and a rooted nice tree decomposition \((T,\{B_t\})\) of width \(w\). For each node \(t\), store all proper maps \(\varphi:B_t\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) extendible to the vertices introduced in the subtree of \(t\). At introduce nodes, retain maps respecting newly exposed edges; at forget nodes, project over the forgotten vertex; at join nodes, intersect the two child tables on their common bag. Accept exactly when the root table is nonempty. Back-pointers recover a coloring. The running time is \(O(|V(T)|k^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(w))\), with \(O(k^{w+1})\) table space per processed node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic programming stores extendible bag colorings, combines them along a nice tree decomposition, and decides k-colorability in time exponential only in the width.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\{B_t\})\) is a supplied nice tree decomposition of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is accepted}\iff\chi(G)\le k\), with time \(O(|V(T)|k^{w+1}\operatorname{poly}(w))\).

notation.meaning: Width of the supplied tree decomposition.
A proper coloring of a current bag.

knowledge_statements.title: Promised-Colorable Graph Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation guarantee under a promised chromatic-number upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a promise parameter \(k\ge2\). A polynomial-time \(\rho\)-approximate coloring algorithm for promised \(k\)-colorable graphs is an algorithm that, on every finite \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\) satisfying \(\chi(G)\le k\), outputs a proper coloring of \(G\) using at most
\[
\rho(n,k)\,\chi(G)
\]
colors. A commonly used weaker bicriteria guarantee requires only at most \(f(n,k)\) colors under the same promise. No output guarantee is imposed on graphs violating the promise, although the algorithm must still halt in polynomial time on every encoded input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The input is promised k-colorable, and the algorithm must efficiently return a proper coloring with a stated multiplicative or bicriteria color bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph on \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{number of output colors}\le\rho(n,k)\chi(G)\), or \(\le f(n,k)\) for a bicriteria guarantee.

notation.meaning: Multiplicative approximation factor under the promise.
Bicriteria upper bound on output colors.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Coloring Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized rounding of a feasible vector-coloring solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input unit vectors \((u_v)_{v\in V}\) satisfying \(\langle u_v,u_w\rangle\le-1/(k-1)\) for every edge \(vw\in E\), together with an integer \(r\ge1\). Sample independent standard Gaussian vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) and assign
\[
c(v)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le i\le r}\langle g_i,u_v\rangle,
\]
breaking ties deterministically. Mark every vertex incident to a monochromatic edge, retain the induced proper coloring on the unmarked vertices, and pass the marked induced subgraph to a specified repair or recursive coloring procedure. The output is proper when the repair uses colors disjoint from \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\); approximation bounds require a separate estimate on the marked set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random Gaussian directions round vector colors; conflicting vertices are removed and repaired separately, producing a proper coloring when fresh repair colors are used.
assumptions_latex: The displayed vector-coloring constraints are feasible.
The repair procedure returns a proper coloring of the marked subgraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is proper on unmarked vertices, and combining it with disjoint repair colors gives a proper coloring of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Unit vector assigned to vertex v by the semidefinite relaxation.
Rounded preliminary color of vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Lemma Coloring Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric Lovász-local-lemma criterion for random list coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have maximum degree \(\Delta\), and suppose every vertex \(v\) has a list \(L(v)\) of exactly \(q\) colors. Choose each vertex color independently and uniformly from its list. For each edge \(uv\), let \(A_{uv}\) be the event that the endpoints receive the same color. Then \(\Pr(A_{uv})\le1/q\), and each event depends on at most \(2\Delta-2\) other edge events. Consequently, if
\[
e(2\Delta-1)\le q,
\]
the symmetric Lovász local lemma implies positive probability that no bad event occurs; hence \(G\) has a proper coloring from the prescribed lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent random list colors yield a proper coloring with positive probability when the symmetric local-lemma dependency criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) admits a proper coloring \(c\) with \(c(v)\in L(v)\) for every \(v\).

notation.meaning: Allowed color list at vertex v.
Bad event that adjacent vertices u and v receive one common color.

knowledge_statements.title: Chromatic-Number Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical complexity boundary for unrestricted finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each fixed integer \(k\ge3\), the decision problem
\[
\text{given }G,\text{ decide whether }\chi(G)\le k
\]
is NP-complete. Membership in NP follows because a vertex-to-color assignment is polynomially verifiable. NP-hardness for \(k=3\) is the classical graph 3-colorability result; for every fixed \(k>3\), adjoining a clique of size \(k-3\) adjacent to every original vertex transfers 3-colorability to \(k\)-colorability. Therefore computing the exact chromatic number of an unrestricted finite graph is NP-hard. In contrast, the cases \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) are decidable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed k-colorability is NP-complete for every k at least three, while one- and two-colorability are polynomial-time decidable; exact chromatic number is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, simple, and represented explicitly.
\(k\) is fixed rather than part of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\text{-COLORABILITY is NP-complete for fixed }k\ge3\), and exact computation of \(\chi(G)\) is NP-hard.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Inapproximability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard near-polynomial inapproximability threshold for chromatic number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time algorithm can, on every finite \(n\)-vertex graph \(G\), output a proper coloring using at most
\[
n^{1-\varepsilon}\chi(G)
\]
colors. Equivalently, under the same assumption, the chromatic number cannot be approximated within a factor \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) in polynomial time. The guarantee concerns worst-case unrestricted graphs and multiplicative approximation measured against the optimum chromatic number; it does not rule out stronger guarantees on promised or structurally restricted graph classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, unrestricted chromatic number has no polynomial-time approximation within n raised to one minus any fixed positive constant.
assumptions_latex: The input is an unrestricted finite graph on \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No polynomial-time \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\)-approximation for \(\chi(G)\) exists.

notation.meaning: Number of vertices in the input graph.

children.title: List-Coloring Complexity
children.top_down_role: Hardness and tractability boundaries for list-coloring variants.

knowledge_statements.title: List-Coloring Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness of fixed-size list coloring on unrestricted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an integer \(k\ge3\). The problem of deciding whether a finite graph \(G\), supplied with a list \(L(v)\) of exactly \(k\) permitted colors for each vertex \(v\), has a proper list coloring is NP-complete. It belongs to NP because a proposed coloring can be checked against all lists and edges in polynomial time. NP-hardness already holds for instances with the identical list \(L(v)=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) at every vertex, since those instances are exactly the ordinary fixed-\(k\) colorability problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every fixed list size at least three, deciding list-colorability is NP-complete, even when every vertex receives the same list.
assumptions_latex: Every input list has exactly \(k\) colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed-\(k\) LIST-COLORABILITY is NP-complete.

notation.meaning: Set of colors permitted at vertex v.

children.title: Edge-Coloring Complexity
children.top_down_role: Hardness and tractability boundaries for edge-coloring variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Coloring Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp NP-completeness result for cubic graph edge coloring.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite simple cubic graph \(G\), deciding whether its edges admit a proper coloring with three colors is NP-complete. Because every cubic graph has maximum degree \(\Delta(G)=3\) and Vizing's theorem gives \(\chi'(G)\in\{3,4\}\), this is equivalently the problem of deciding whether \(G\) is Class 1 rather than Class 2. A proposed three-edge-coloring is verifiable in polynomial time by checking that every pair of incident edges receives distinct colors. Consequently, computing the edge-chromatic number remains NP-hard even on cubic simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determining whether a cubic simple graph has edge-chromatic number three is NP-complete, so exact edge coloring is NP-hard on cubic graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple cubic graph.
Proper edge colorings assign distinct colors to incident edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deciding whether \(\chi'(G)=3\) is NP-complete; computing \(\chi'(G)\) on cubic graphs is NP-hard.

children.title: Cross-Variant Complexity Transfers
children.top_down_role: Reductions and structural correspondences connecting the two complexity landscapes.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Variant Complexity Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-graph transfer between edge-coloring and vertex-coloring variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(H\), let its line graph \(L(H)\) have one vertex for each edge of \(H\), with two vertices adjacent exactly when their corresponding edges share an endpoint. Then, for every \(k\ge1\),
\[
H\text{ has a proper }k\text{-edge-coloring}\iff L(H)\text{ has a proper }k\text{-vertex-coloring}.
\]
Moreover, assigning each edge \(e\) a color list \(S(e)\) yields the identical list-coloring instance on \(L(H)\). The construction is polynomial in the explicit graph size, so decision and optimization reductions transfer from edge-coloring or list-edge-coloring to vertex-coloring or list-coloring restricted to line graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The line graph turns edges into vertices and preserves ordinary and list coloring, giving polynomial-time transfers between edge and vertex variants.
assumptions_latex: The line graph is represented explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi'(H)=\chi(L(H))\), and list-edge-colorings of \(H\) equal list-colorings of \(L(H)\) under corresponding lists.

notation.meaning: Permitted color list for edge e.

children.title: Bipartite Graph Coloring
children.top_down_role: Coloring structure, recognition context, and tractable regimes for bipartite graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-time two-coloring and odd-cycle certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). For every unvisited connected component, choose a root, assign it color \(0\), and perform breadth-first search. Whenever an edge \(uv\) reaches an uncolored vertex \(v\), set \(c(v)=1-c(u)\); if an edge has \(c(u)=c(v)\), use the two search-tree paths to their lowest common ancestor together with \(uv\) to output an odd cycle. If no conflict occurs, \(c\) is a proper two-coloring. Thus the algorithm certifies either bipartiteness or non-bipartiteness in time \(O(|V|+|E|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Breadth-first search alternates two colors in each component and returns either a proper two-coloring or an odd cycle witnessing failure.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph represented by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs either a proper two-coloring of \(G\) or an odd cycle, in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

notation.meaning: Binary color assigned to vertex v.

children.title: Chordal Graph Coloring
children.top_down_role: Coloring structure and tractable regimes arising from chordality.

knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal greedy coloring from a perfect elimination ordering of a finite chordal graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal, and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be a perfect elimination ordering, so the later neighbors of each \(v_i\) form a clique. Process the vertices in the reverse order \(v_n,\ldots,v_1\), assigning each vertex the smallest positive color unused by its already colored neighbors. The resulting coloring is proper and uses exactly \(\omega(G)=\chi(G)\) colors. Given the ordering and adjacency lists, the coloring can be implemented in polynomial time; a perfect elimination ordering can also be recognized and constructed in linear time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse greedy coloring along a perfect elimination ordering colors every chordal graph optimally, using exactly its clique number of colors.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple chordal graph.
\(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is a perfect elimination ordering of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{reverse-greedy}(G)=\chi(G)=\omega(G)\).

children.title: Structural Tractability Contrast
children.top_down_role: Contrasting the structural mechanisms that make coloring tractable in the two classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Tractability Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts the structural certificates underlying polynomial coloring of bipartite and chordal graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G\), bipartiteness supplies a partition \(V(G)=A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B\) into stable sets, yielding \(\chi(G)\leq 2\), with equality when \(E(G)\neq\varnothing\). Chordality instead supplies a perfect elimination ordering; reverse greedy coloring along that ordering yields \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)\). Thus both classes admit polynomial-time optimal coloring, but through different certificates: parity-compatible bipartition for bipartite graphs and clique-structured elimination for chordal graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite coloring is certified by a two-part partition, whereas chordal coloring is certified by a perfect elimination ordering and clique structure.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph belonging to the stated graph class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow\chi(G)\leq2\), while \(G\text{ chordal}\Rightarrow\chi(G)=\omega(G)\) via reverse greedy elimination.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical bipartite and chordal coloring characterizations

children.title: Interval Graph Coloring

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring from an interval representation using the chordal elimination order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be the intersection graph of closed intervals \(I_v=[\ell_v,r_v]\). Order the vertices by nondecreasing right endpoint, breaking ties arbitrarily; this is a perfect elimination ordering. Greedily color in the reverse of this order, always choosing the smallest color absent from already colored neighbors. The coloring is optimal and uses \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)\) colors, where \(\omega(G)=\max_{t\in\mathbb R}|\{v:t\in I_v\}|\). Sorting endpoints followed by greedy coloring gives a polynomial-time implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sorting intervals by right endpoint gives an elimination order whose reverse greedy coloring uses exactly the maximum overlap number.
assumptions_latex: \(\{I_v:v\in V(G)\}\) is an interval representation of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G)=\omega(G)=\max_{t\in\mathbb R}|\{v:t\in I_v\}|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical interval-graph representation and perfect-elimination coloring result

children.title: Permutation Graph Coloring
children.top_down_role: Coloring structure and tractable methods for permutation graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Permutation Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring through the inversion-poset representation of a permutation graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_\pi\) have vertices \(1,\ldots,n\), with \(ij\in E(G_\pi)\) exactly when \(i<j\) and \(\pi(i)>\pi(j)\). A color class is precisely an increasing subsequence of \(\pi\). Therefore a proper coloring is a partition of \(\pi\) into increasing subsequences, and a minimum such partition can be constructed by a chain-partition algorithm for the associated order. Its number of colors equals the length of a longest decreasing subsequence, which is also \(\omega(G_\pi)\); hence \(\chi(G_\pi)=\omega(G_\pi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coloring a permutation graph is equivalent to partitioning its permutation into increasing subsequences; the optimum equals the longest decreasing subsequence length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G_\pi)=\omega(G_\pi)=\operatorname{LDS}(\pi)\).

notation.meaning: length of a longest decreasing subsequence of pi

children.title: Comparability Graph Coloring

knowledge_statements.title: Comparability Graph Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal coloring of a comparability graph using ranks in an inducing partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(V,\prec)\) be a finite partially ordered set and let \(G(P)\) join two distinct elements exactly when they are comparable. Define \(r(v)\) as the maximum cardinality of a chain ending at \(v\), and color \(v\) by \(r(v)\). If \(u\prec v\), then \(r(u)<r(v)\), so this is a proper coloring. It uses \(h(P)\) colors, where \(h(P)\) is the maximum chain cardinality. Every maximum chain is a clique, hence \(\chi(G(P))=\omega(G(P))=h(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank each poset element by the longest chain ending there; these ranks optimally color its comparability graph.
assumptions_latex: \(P=(V,\prec)\) is a finite partially ordered set.
\(G(P)\) is the comparability graph induced by \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G(P))=\omega(G(P))=h(P)\).

notation.meaning: maximum size of a chain ending at v

children.title: Representation-Based Class Relations

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Based Class Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Class inclusions and equivalences relevant to representation-based coloring algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite simple graphs, every interval graph is chordal. A graph is a permutation graph exactly when both it and its complement are comparability graphs. Consequently interval graphs, permutation graphs, and comparability graphs are perfect, although their certificates differ: interval intersection models yield endpoint elimination, permutation diagrams yield simultaneous comparability orientations of the graph and complement, and posets yield transitive orientations. These representations support polynomial-time optimal coloring but do not make the three named classes identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interval graphs are chordal; permutation graphs are exactly graphs whose graph and complement are comparability graphs, and all three classes are perfect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ interval}\Rightarrow G\text{ chordal}\), and \(G\text{ permutation}\Longleftrightarrow G,\overline G\text{ comparability}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact coloring parameterized by the width of a supplied tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) have \(n\) vertices and a supplied tree decomposition of width at most \(k\). For any integer \(q\geq1\), dynamic programming over a nice form of the decomposition stores the proper color assignments of each bag and decides \(q\)-colorability in time \(O(nq^{k+1}\operatorname{poly}(k))\) and space \(O(q^{k+1}\operatorname{poly}(k))\). Since every graph of treewidth at most \(k\) is \((k+1)\)-colorable, testing \(q=1,\ldots,k+1\) determines \(\chi(G)\); thus coloring is polynomial-time solvable for fixed \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A width-k tree decomposition supports exact coloring by bag dynamic programming, with exponential dependence confined to k.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph on \(n\) vertices.
A tree decomposition of \(G\) of width at most \(k\) is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertex and edge colorings and chromatic numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proper vertex and edge colorings, their minimum numbers of colors, and associated terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vertex coloring of a graph $G=(V,E)$ is a partition of $V$ into stable sets, equivalently a map $\phi:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}$ whose color classes $\phi^{-1}(i)$ are stable. Its minimum number of colors is $\chi(G)$. The graph is $k$-colorable when $\chi(G)\le k$ and $k$-chromatic when $\chi(G)=k$. An edge coloring is a partition of $E$ into matchings, equivalently a map $\phi:E\to\{1,\ldots,k\}$ whose color classes are matchings. Its minimum number of colors is $\chi'(G)$, with $\chi'(G)=\chi(L(G))$. The analogous notions of $k$-edge-colorability, $k$-edge-chromaticity, and minimum coloring use $\chi'(G)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex coloring partitions the vertices into stable sets, and the chromatic number is the least number of such color classes. An edge coloring partitions the edges into matchings, and the edge-chromatic number is the least number of those classes. A graph is k-colorable or k-edge-colorable when the corresponding minimum is at most k, and k-chromatic or k-edge-chromatic when it equals k. The edge-chromatic number of a graph equals the chromatic number of its line graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \chi'(G)=\chi(L(G))

knowledge_statements.title: Greedy Ordering Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Crown graphs exhibit an unbounded gap between good and bad greedy vertex orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\geq2\), let \(G_n\) be the crown graph with bipartition \(\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}\) and \(\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}\), containing every cross-edge except \(a_ib_i\). Then \(\chi(G_n)=2\). Under the greedy order \(a_1,b_1,a_2,b_2,\ldots,a_n,b_n\), first-fit assigns both \(a_i\) and \(b_i\) color \(i\), and therefore uses \(n\) colors. Hence the number of colors produced by greedy coloring cannot be bounded as a function of \(\chi(G)\) independently of the vertex order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite crown graph needs two colors, yet a bad alternating vertex order makes first-fit greedy use arbitrarily many colors.
assumptions_latex: Greedy coloring uses the smallest available positive integer color.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G_n)=2\) but \(\operatorname{FirstFit}(G_n;a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_n,b_n)=n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Color Symmetry Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit multiplicity in labeled-color assignment formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a labeled \(k\)-color assignment formulation with variables \(x_{vc}\), every permutation \(\sigma\in S_k\) maps a feasible assignment to another by \(x'_{v,c}=x_{v,\sigma^{-1}(c)}\), without changing feasibility or any color-symmetric objective. If a coloring uses exactly \(r\) nonempty color classes, then it has \(k!/(k-r)!\) distinct labeled encodings obtained by injectively assigning those classes to the \(k\) labels. Thus one combinatorial coloring may generate a large orbit of equivalent integer solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permuting color labels creates many equivalent assignment solutions; an r-class coloring has k!/(k-r)! labeled encodings among k colors.
assumptions_latex: Constraints and objective are invariant under permutations of the \(k\) color labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{Orb}(x)|=k!/(k-r)!\) for a coloring with \(r\) nonempty classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring Relaxation Weakness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded integrality gap in a standard color-indexed linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the formulation with \(x_{vc},y_c\in\{0,1\}\), objective \(\min\sum_{c=1}^k y_c\), constraints \(\sum_c x_{vc}=1\), and \(x_{uc}+x_{vc}\leq y_c\) for every edge \(uv\) and color \(c\). Relax the variables to \([0,1]\). For \(G=K_n\) and \(k=n\), the assignment \(x_{vc}=1/n\) and \(y_c=2/n\) is feasible and has value \(2\), whereas every integer solution has value \(n\). The relaxation therefore has integrality gap at least \(n/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete graph, the standard color-indexed LP can have value two although the integer chromatic number is n.
assumptions_latex: The color-indexed formulation uses \(k=n\) labeled colors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{IP}}(K_n)/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{LP}}(K_n)\geq n/2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Induced Relaxation Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple color-order symmetry breaking does not repair the color-indexed relaxation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Augment the color-indexed relaxation by the common label-order constraints \(y_1\geq y_2\geq\cdots\geq y_n\). Since the integer optimum is \(n\), ordering the color-use variables removes some equivalent integer labelings but leaves the integrality gap at least \(n/2\). Stronger symmetry handling or stronger valid inequalities are therefore required to eliminate this failure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intersection Graph of a Set Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a graph by the nonempty-intersection relation among distinct sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a set and let \(\mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_n\}\) be a family of distinct nonempty subsets of \(S\) with \(\bigcup_{i=1}^n S_i=S\). The intersection graph of \(\mathcal S\) has one vertex for each \(S_i\), with distinct vertices \(S_i,S_j\) adjacent exactly when \(S_i\cap S_j\ne\varnothing\). A graph \(G\) is an intersection graph on \(S\) if it is the intersection graph of some such family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intersection graph of a family of distinct nonempty subsets has one vertex per set and joins two distinct vertices exactly when their sets intersect. A graph is an intersection graph on S when some such family of subsets of S represents it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_iS_j\in E\iff i\ne j\text{ and }S_i\cap S_j\ne\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree-Two Reduction and Expansion for τ-Critical Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the complete local alternatives at a degree-two vertex and the converse vertex-splitting construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be $\tau$-critical, let $d_G(x)=2$, and let $N_G(x)=\{y,z\}$. If $yz\in E(G)$, then $G[\{x,y,z\}]$ is a connected component of $G$. If $yz\notin E(G)$, then no vertex other than $x$ is adjacent to both $y$ and $z$, and contracting both $xy$ and $xz$ produces a $\tau$-critical graph $G'$. Conversely, if $G'$ is $\tau$-critical and $w\in V(G')$, splitting $w$ into vertices $y,z$ of degree at least one and adjoining a new vertex $x$ adjacent to both $y$ and $z$ produces a $\tau$-critical graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degree-two vertex x of a τ-critical graph, adjacent neighbors x,y,z form a whole component. If the neighbors are nonadjacent, they have no other common neighbor and contracting xy and xz preserves τ-criticality. Conversely, splitting any vertex of a τ-critical graph into two nonisolated vertices and adding a new common degree-two neighbor preserves τ-criticality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: yz\in E(G)\Rightarrow G[\{x,y,z\}]\text{ is a component};\quad yz\notin E(G)\Rightarrow(N_G(y)\cap N_G(z)=\{x\}\text{ and }G/\{xy,xz\}\text{ is }\tau\text{-critical}),\text{ with the stated splitting operation as a converse}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complement, complete graph, and line graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both the complement and line graph are simple even when the original graph has repeated edges or loops; complement involution is asserted only for simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $G=(V,E)$, its complement $\bar G$ is the simple graph on $V$ whose edges are the pairs of distinct vertices nonadjacent in $G$; if $G$ is simple, then $\overline{\bar G}=G$. A graph is complete iff it is simple and every two distinct vertices are adjacent, and $K_n$ denotes the complete graph on $n$ vertices, unique up to isomorphism. The line graph $L(G)$ is the simple graph with vertex set $E$ in which two edge-elements of $G$ are adjacent iff they meet at a vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement joins precisely the distinct nonadjacent vertex pairs and is involutive on simple graphs. A complete graph is simple with every distinct vertex pair adjacent. The line graph has one vertex for each edge-element of the original graph and joins two of them exactly when the corresponding edges meet.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(\bar G)=\{\{u,v\}:u\ne v\text{ and }u,v\text{ are nonadjacent in }G\},\quad G\text{ simple}\Rightarrow\overline{\bar G}=G,\quad V(L(G))=E.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's incidence-matrix conventions and its convention that a clique is a maximal complete subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph, the degree $d_i$ of vertex $i$ is the number of incident edges and, under the stated incidence-matrix convention, $d_i=\sum_k b_{ik}$. For a digraph, $d_i^{(\mathrm{out})}$ and $d_i^{(\mathrm{in})}$ count outgoing and incoming arcs, respectively, with signed incidence sum $d_i^{(\mathrm{out})}-d_i^{(\mathrm{in})}$. The complete graph $K_n$ has every pair of distinct vertices adjacent and $n(n-1)/2$ edges; the complete digraph has $n(n-1)$ arcs; and $K_{p,q}$ has bipartition sizes $p,q$ and $pq$ edges. A graph $G'=(N',A')$ is a subgraph of $G=(N,A)$ when $N'\subseteq N$ and $A'\subseteq A$ with endpoints in $N'$. The subgraph induced by $N'$ contains every edge of $A$ whose endpoints lie in $N'$. A complete subgraph is complete, and a maximal complete subgraph is called a clique. Deleting $A'\subseteq A$ produces $(N,A\setminus A')$; the complement $\bar G$ contains precisely the edges of the complete graph on $N$ that are absent from $G$. Contracting an edge $(i,j)$ replaces $i,j$ by one vertex and transfers their other incident edges; parallel edges may result, yielding a multigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex degree counts incident edges; directed out-degree and in-degree count outgoing and incoming arcs, with their difference represented by the signed incidence sum. Complete graphs, complete digraphs, and complete bipartite graphs have respectively n(n−1)/2, n(n−1), and pq edges or arcs. A subgraph uses subsets of the original vertices and edges, while an induced subgraph contains all original edges between its chosen vertices. Under the source's convention, a clique is a maximal complete subgraph. Edge deletion removes selected edges, complementation selects the missing edges on the same vertices, and edge contraction merges the endpoints and may create parallel edges, hence a multigraph.
assumptions_latex: \text{the stated unsigned or signed incidence-matrix convention applies to the corresponding degree identity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E(K_n)|=\frac{n(n-1)}2,\qquad |A(\overrightarrow K_n)|=n(n-1),\qquad |E(K_{p,q})|=pq

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clique indicators and separating graph distributions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines clique indicators, their disjunctive representation of clique detection, and positive and negative distributions used for monotone-circuit lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For S\subseteq[n], define C_S(G)=1 if and only if S is a clique in G. Then \operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}=\bigvee_{S\subseteq[n],\,|S|=k}C_S. Distribution \mathcal Y chooses K\subseteq[n] uniformly with |K|=k and returns the graph whose only edges form the clique on K. Distribution \mathcal N chooses c:[n]\to[k-1] uniformly and places an edge \{u,v\} exactly when c(u)\ne c(v). Consequently, \operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}=1 on \mathcal Y and \operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}=0 on \mathcal N with probability one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator C_S accepts exactly when S forms a clique, and k-clique detection is the OR of all indicators for k-element sets. The planted isolated k-clique distribution is always positive, while the random complete (k−1)-partite distribution is always negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}=\bigvee_{|S|=k}C_S,\qquad \Pr[\operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}(\mathcal Y)=1]=\Pr[\operatorname{CLIQUE}_{k,n}(\mathcal N)=0]=1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite graphs and their complements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(X\subseteq V\) is stable if no two vertices of \(X\) are adjacent, and \(\alpha(G)=\max\{|X|:X\text{ is stable}\}\). A set \(X\subseteq V\) is a clique if \(G[X]\) is complete, and \(\omega(G)=\max\{|X|:X\text{ is a clique}\}\). Stable sets of \(G\) are cliques of \(\bar G\), so \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\bar G)\). The chromatic number \(\chi(G)\) is the minimum number of stable sets partitioning \(V\); the chromatic index \(\chi'(G)\) is the minimum number of matchings partitioning \(E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable sets contain no adjacent pair, while cliques induce complete subgraphs; their maximum sizes are the stability and clique numbers. Complementation exchanges stable sets and cliques, giving alpha of G equal to omega of its complement. The chromatic number is the minimum number of stable classes partitioning the vertices, and the chromatic index is the minimum number of matchings partitioning the edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)=\omega(\bar G)

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Cardinality Clique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unweighted maximum-clique optimization in a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(C\subseteq V\) is a clique when every two distinct vertices in \(C\) are adjacent. The maximum cardinality clique problem is
\[\text{maximize }|C|\quad\text{subject to }C\subseteq V\text{ and }\{u,v\}\in E\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in C.\]
Any feasible set attaining the optimum is a maximum clique, and the optimum value is the clique number \(\omega(G)\). Maximality under inclusion is not sufficient for maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum cardinality clique is a largest vertex set whose distinct pairs are all adjacent; its size is the clique number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(G)=\max\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ \{u,v\}\in E\text{ for all distinct }u,v\in C\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Weight Clique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization definition for a finite, vertex-weighted simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}\). A clique is a set \(C\subseteq V\) such that \(uv\in E\) for every two distinct vertices \(u,v\in C\). Its weight is \(w(C)=\sum_{v\in C}w(v)\). The maximum-weight clique value and solution set are
\[\omega_w(G)=\max\{w(C):C\subseteq V,\ C\text{ is a clique}\},\qquad \operatorname{MWC}(G,w)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{C\text{ clique}}w(C).\]
The empty clique is permitted and has weight \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a clique whose total vertex weight is largest; the empty clique is allowed, so the optimum is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega_w(G)=\max\{\sum_{v\in C}w(v):C\text{ is a clique of }G\}\).

notation.meaning: sum of the weights of vertices in C

Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\). Construct \(G^w\) by replacing each \(v\in V\) with a clique \(K_v\) of \(w(v)\) copies. For distinct \(u,v\), join every vertex of \(K_u\) to every vertex of \(K_v\) exactly when \(uv\in E\). Then
\[\omega(G^w)=\omega_w(G).\]
Moreover, a clique \(C\) of \(G\) lifts to \(\bigcup_{v\in C}K_v\), while every maximum clique of \(G^w\) projects to a clique of \(G\) having the same weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive integer vertex weights can be encoded by clique modules, preserving the optimum and permitting solution projection in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(G^w)=\omega_w(G)\), with weight-preserving lifting and projection of optimal cliques.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum Cardinality Stable Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality optimization over pairwise nonadjacent vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. A stable set is a subset \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \(uv\notin E\) for all distinct \(u,v\in S\). The stability number and family of maximum stable sets are
\[\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ S\text{ is stable}\},\qquad \operatorname{MSS}(G)=\{S:S\text{ is stable and }|S|=\alpha(G)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a largest vertex subset containing no adjacent pair; its cardinality is the graph's stability number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq V,\ S\text{ is stable}\}\).

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of a stable set in G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-cardinality independent-set formulation and weakness of its edge LP relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The binary edge-inequality formulation for maximum-cardinality independent set and its complete-graph relaxation failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(I\subseteq V\) is independent (stable) if no edge has both endpoints in \(I\). Maximum independent set is represented by
\[
\max \sum_{v\in V}x_v\quad\text{s.t.}\quad x_u+x_v\le 1\quad(\{u,v\}\in E),\qquad x_v\in\{0,1\}\quad(v\in V),
\]
with \(I^*=\{v\in V:x_v^*=1\}\) for an optimal solution \(x^*\). After replacing integrality by \(0\le x_v\le1\), the assignment \(x_v=\tfrac12\) is feasible, so \(z_{LP}(G)\ge |V|/2\). For \(G=K_n\) with \(n\ge2\), \(\alpha(K_n)=1\) while \(z_{LP}(K_n)\ge n/2\); hence this relaxation has an unbounded multiplicative gap on complete graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent or stable set contains no adjacent pair of vertices. Its maximum cardinality is modeled with one binary variable per vertex and an inequality allowing at most one endpoint of every edge to be selected. The unit-interval relaxation always admits the all-one-half solution. On complete graphs, the integer optimum is one while the relaxation value is at least half the number of vertices, so the relaxation gap grows without bound.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph.}
x_v\in\{0,1\}\text{ in the integer formulation; }0\le x_v\le1\text{ in the LP relaxation.}
G=K_n\text{ with }n\ge2\text{ for the failure boundary.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:x_u+x_v\le1\ (\{u,v\}\in E),\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\},\qquad z_{LP}(G)\ge |V|/2;\qquad \alpha(K_n)=1,\ z_{LP}(K_n)\ge n/2.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Weight Stable Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted optimization over stable vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}\). For a stable set \(S\subseteq V\), put \(w(S)=\sum_{v\in S}w(v)\). The maximum-weight stable-set value and its optimizers are
\[\alpha_w(G)=\max\{w(S):S\subseteq V,\ S\text{ is stable}\},\qquad \operatorname{MWSS}(G,w)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{S\text{ stable}}w(S).\]
The empty stable set is allowed and has weight \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a stable set with maximum total vertex weight; allowing the empty set makes the optimum nonnegative even when weights are negative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_w(G)=\max\{\sum_{v\in S}w(v):S\text{ is stable in }G\}\).

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a stable set in G

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Cardinality Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality minimization over vertex sets meeting every edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph. A vertex cover is a set \(C\subseteq V\) such that \(C\cap\{u,v\}\neq\varnothing\) for every edge \(uv\in E\). The vertex-cover number and family of minimum covers are
\[\tau(G)=\min\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ C\text{ is a vertex cover}\},\qquad \operatorname{MVC}(G)=\{C:C\text{ is a vertex cover and }|C|=\tau(G)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a smallest vertex set meeting every edge; its size is the vertex-cover number.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(G)=\min\{|C|:C\subseteq V,\ C\cap\{u,v\}\neq\varnothing\text{ for every }uv\in E\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum cardinality of a vertex cover

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary integer-programming formulation of minimum vertex cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines vertex covers and represents the minimum-cardinality problem as a binary integer program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(S\subseteq V\) is a vertex cover if every edge has at least one endpoint in \(S\). The minimum-cardinality vertex-cover problem is
\[
\min \sum_{v\in V}x_v\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_u+x_v\ge 1\ \text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E,\qquad x_v\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for every }v\in V.
\]
Under \(S=\{v\in V:x_v=1\}\), feasible binary vectors correspond exactly to vertex covers, and the objective value is \(|S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an undirected graph, a vertex cover contains at least one endpoint of every edge. Using one binary variable per vertex yields an integer program whose edge constraints enforce coverage and whose objective minimizes the cover cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{|S|:S\subseteq V\text{ is a vertex cover}\}=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:x_u+x_v\ge1\ \forall\{u,v\}\in E,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal and maximal versus minimum and maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion or subgraph order is used for minimality and maximality, whereas minimum and maximum refer to cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a family of sets or graphs. An element \(F\in\mathcal F\) is minimal if no proper subset or proper subgraph of \(F\) belongs to \(\mathcal F\), and maximal if \(F\) is not a proper subset or proper subgraph of any member of \(\mathcal F\). A minimum element has minimum cardinality in \(\mathcal F\), and a maximum element has maximum cardinality. Consequently, inclusion-minimal need not mean minimum-cardinality, and inclusion-maximal need not mean maximum-cardinality; in particular, a minimal vertex cover need not be minimum and a maximal matching need not be maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimal and maximal describe local extremality under containment or the subgraph relation. Minimum and maximum instead describe globally smallest or largest cardinality. Thus minimal vertex covers can be larger than minimum vertex covers, and maximal matchings can be smaller than maximum matchings.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F\text{ is a family of sets or graphs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}F\text{ minimal}&\iff \nexists F'\in\mathcal F\text{ with }F'\subsetneq F\text{ or }F'\text{ a proper subgraph of }F,\\F\text{ maximal}&\iff \nexists F'\in\mathcal F\text{ with }F\subsetneq F'\text{ or }F\text{ a proper subgraph of }F',\end{aligned}\quad\text{while minimum and maximum refer to cardinality; neither pair is equivalent in general.}

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Weight Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative-cost minimization over vertex covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite simple graph and let \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). For \(C\subseteq V\), put \(w(C)=\sum_{v\in C}w(v)\). The minimum-weight vertex-cover value is

Any feasible \(C\) attaining this minimum is a minimum-weight vertex cover.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost selection required to cover a prescribed edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(c:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), let \(p:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and let \(K\ge0\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u\in S\text{ or }v\in S\}\). The partial vertex-cover problem is
\[\min_{S\subseteq V}\left\{\sum_{v\in S}c(v):\sum_{e\in E(S)}p(e)\ge K\right\}.\]
The instance is feasible exactly when \(K\le\sum_{e\in E}p(e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select minimum-cost vertices whose incident edges have total covered weight at least a prescribed target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{PVC}(G,c,p,K)=\min\{c(S):S\subseteq V,\ p(E(S))\ge K\}\).

notation.meaning: edges having at least one endpoint in S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Partial vertex cover has multiple formulations, and no source establishes that this weighted target formulation is the intended local sense. The conclusion also uses c(S) and p(E(S)) without defining those aggregate abbreviations.

children.title: Budgeted Vertex Cover

knowledge_statements.title: Budgeted Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum edge coverage subject to a vertex-cost budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(c:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), let \(p:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), and let \(B\ge0\). With \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u\in S\text{ or }v\in S\}\), the budgeted vertex-cover problem is
\[\max_{S\subseteq V}\left\{\sum_{e\in E(S)}p(e):\sum_{v\in S}c(v)\le B\right\}.\]
Each edge is counted once even when both endpoints belong to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a vertex-cost budget, select vertices maximizing the total weight of edges incident to at least one selected vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{BVC}(G,c,p,B)=\max\{p(E(S)):S\subseteq V,\ c(S)\le B\}\).

notation.meaning: edges covered by the selected vertices
maximum covered-edge weight under the budget

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation establishes this weighted maximum-coverage formulation as the intended meaning of budgeted vertex cover. The conclusion additionally uses c(S) and p(E(S)) without defining those aggregate abbreviations.

children.title: Coverage–Cost Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective and feasibility regimes linking coverage targets to resource limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Coverage–Cost Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bicriteria formulation unifying partial and budgeted weighted vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let vertex costs and edge profits be nonnegative. For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(c(S)=\sum_{v\in S}c_v\) and \(p(S)=\sum_{e\in E:e\cap S\ne\varnothing}p_e\). For \(B,Q\in\mathbb R_+\), define
\[F(B)=\max\{p(S):S\subseteq V,\ c(S)\le B\},\qquad K(Q)=\min\{c(S):S\subseteq V,\ p(S)\ge Q\}.\]
With an infeasible minimum interpreted as \(+\infty\), \(K(Q)\le B\) if and only if \(F(B)\ge Q\). Thus either value function determines the attainable coverage–cost frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative B and Q, minimum cost for coverage Q is at most B exactly when maximum coverage under budget B is at least Q.
assumptions_latex: \(c_v\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\), and \(p_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(Q)\le B\iff F(B)\ge Q\).

notation.meaning: maximum covered edge profit under vertex-cost budget B
minimum vertex cost attaining edge profit at least Q

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct equivalence of the standard partial and budgeted vertex-cover formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Clique–Stable-Set Complementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-system and optimum-value correspondence under graph complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), the set \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if every two distinct vertices of \(S\) are adjacent in the complement \(\overline G\), equivalently, \(S\) is a clique of \(\overline G\). Hence the stable sets of \(G\) and cliques of \(\overline G\) are identical as vertex subsets, and
\[\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G),\qquad \omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set is stable in a graph exactly when it is a clique in the complement; the corresponding optimum cardinalities agree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a clique in \(\overline G\); moreover, \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\).

notation.meaning: complement of G on the same vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set–Vertex-Cover Complementation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementation within the common vertex set, including nonnegative vertex weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(S\subseteq V\), the set \(S\) is stable in \(G\) if and only if \(V\setminus S\) is a vertex cover of \(G\). Consequently, complementation is a bijection between stable sets and vertex covers. For nonnegative vertex weights \(w\),
\[\tau_w(G)=w(V)-\alpha_w(G),\]
where \(w(V)=\sum_{v\in V}w_v\), \(\tau_w(G)\) is the minimum weight of a vertex cover, and \(\alpha_w(G)\) is the maximum weight of a stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complement of a stable set is a vertex cover and conversely; minimum cover weight equals total weight minus maximum stable-set weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ stable}\iff V\setminus S\text{ is a vertex cover}\), and \(\tau_w(G)=w(V)-\alpha_w(G)\).

notation.meaning: minimum weight of a vertex cover

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching problems represented as stable-set problems on line graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The line graph \(L(G)\) has vertex set \(E(G)\), with two vertices adjacent exactly when their corresponding edges share an endpoint in \(G\). Therefore \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a matching in \(G\) if and only if the corresponding vertex subset is stable in \(L(G)\). This bijection preserves cardinality and edge weights, so
\[\nu(G)=\alpha(L(G))\quad\text{and}\quad \nu_w(G)=\alpha_w(L(G)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edges form a matching in G exactly when their corresponding vertices form a stable set in the line graph, preserving size and weight.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite loopless undirected graph.
\(w:E(G)\to\mathbb R\) assigns the same weight to each edge and its line-graph vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is a matching in }G\iff M\text{ is stable in }L(G)\), and \(\nu_w(G)=\alpha_w(L(G))\).

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a matching in G

children.title: Edge Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Edge Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic linear relaxation constraints for incidence vectors of stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every incidence vector \(x\) of a stable set satisfies
\[x_u+x_v\le1\qquad\text{for every }uv\in E.\]
Together with \(0\le x_v\le1\) for all \(v\in V\), these constraints define the edge relaxation
\[Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^V:x_u+x_v\le1\text{ for every }uv\in E\},\]
which contains the stable-set polytope \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable set cannot contain both endpoints of an edge; the resulting edge relaxation contains the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of stable-set incidence vectors
