knowledge_statements.title: Clique Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clique constraints for the stable-set polytope and its clique relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty clique \(K\) of \(G\), any stable-set incidence vector \(x\) satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1.\]
The clique relaxation is
\[Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{+}^{V}:\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1\text{ for every clique }K\right\}.\]
Every stable-set incidence vector belongs to this relaxation, and therefore \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\). Singleton cliques supply the upper bounds \(x_v\le1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At most one vertex of any clique can belong to a stable set; all such inequalities define the clique relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction, total-dual-integrality certificate, stable-set polytope description, and clique containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A), and let \mathcal C be a crossing collection with \delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U)=\varnothing for every U\in\mathcal C. Define G on vertex set A by making distinct arcs adjacent exactly when they both enter some U\in\mathcal C. Then the system 0\leq x(a)\leq1\ (a\in A),\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\leq1\ (U\in\mathcal C) is totally dual integral, its integer points are precisely the incidence vectors of stable sets of G, and \operatorname{STAB}(G) is described by clique inequalities. Consequently G is perfect, and every clique of G is contained in \delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U) for some U\in\mathcal C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a directed graph and a crossing collection of sets with no outgoing arcs, form a graph whose vertices are arcs and whose adjacency means that two arcs enter a common set. The displayed bound and entering-set system is totally dual integral and describes the stable-set polytope by clique inequalities. Hence every Edmonds–Giles graph is perfect, and each clique lies in the set of arcs entering some member of the crossing collection.
assumptions_latex: V(G)=A,\quad aa'\in E(G)\iff\exists U\in\mathcal C:\ a,a'\in\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U)

children.title: Edge-to-Clique Dominance Relations

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-to-Clique Dominance Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict relaxation dominance of clique inequalities over edge inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under nonnegativity, each clique inequality \(\sum_{v\in K}x_v\le1\) implies every edge inequality \(x_u+x_v\le1\) with \(u,v\in K\). Hence
\[Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G).\]
The inclusion is strict whenever \(G\) has a clique \(K\) with \(|K|\ge3\): assigning \(x_v=1/2\) on \(K\) and \(x_v=0\) elsewhere satisfies every edge inequality but violates the clique inequality for \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique inequalities imply their constituent edge inequalities and are strictly stronger when the graph contains a clique of size at least three.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{clq}}(G)\subseteq Q_{\mathrm{edge}}(G)\), strictly if \(\omega(G)\ge3\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid stable-set inequalities indexed by simple odd cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be a simple odd cycle of length \(|V(C)|=2k+1\) in \(G\). Every stable set contains at most \(k\) vertices of \(C\); hence its incidence vector satisfies the odd-cycle inequality
\[\sum_{v\in V(C)}x_v\le k=\left\lfloor\frac{|V(C)|}{2}\right\rfloor.\]
The inequality remains valid when \(C\) has chords, although additional edges may make it redundant or dominated by stronger inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every odd cycle of length 2k+1 contributes a valid inequality limiting a stable set to at most k cycle vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a simple cycle of odd length \(2k+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V(C)}x_v\le k\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Hole Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cycle inequalities restricted to chordless cycles of length at least five.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An odd hole is an induced cycle \(H\cong C_{2k+1}\) with \(k\ge2\). Since \(\alpha(H)=k\), every point of \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in V(H)}x_v\le k.\]
For the induced subgraph \(H\) itself, this inequality defines a facet of \(\operatorname{STAB}(H)\). In the ambient graph it is a valid induced-subgraph inequality, though facetness may require lifting or additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each induced odd cycle of length at least five yields a rank inequality, facet-defining for the stable-set polytope of that cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) and facet-defining for \(\operatorname{STAB}(H)\).

notation.meaning: an induced odd cycle, or odd hole

children.title: Induced-Cycle Strengthening Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Induced-Cycle Strengthening Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity criterion for strengthening the edge relaxation on chordless cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=G[U]\) be an induced cycle. If \(|U|=2k\), summing its \(2k\) edge inequalities and dividing by two gives \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\), so the cycle-rank bound is already implied by the edge relaxation. If \(|U|=2k+1\), the edge inequalities imply only \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k+1/2\); the point given by \(x_v=1/2\) for \(v\in U\) and \(x_v=0\) for \(v\notin U\) demonstrates that the strengthened valid inequality \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le k\) is not implied by the edge relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even-cycle rank bounds follow from edge constraints, whereas odd induced cycles require a strictly stronger integral rank inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|U|\) is even, the cycle-rank inequality is implied by the edge relaxation; if \(|U|\) is odd, \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\lfloor |U|/2\rfloor\) is a strict strengthening of that relaxation.

notation.meaning: edge-inequality relaxation of the stable-set polytope
vertex set of the induced cycle

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Induced-subgraph rank inequalities for the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every nonempty vertex subset \(U\subseteq V\), define its rank as the stability number \(\alpha(G[U])\). Every stable-set incidence vector satisfies
\[\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\alpha(G[U]).\]
These are the rank inequalities of \(G\). They specialize to clique inequalities when \(\alpha(G[U])=1\) and to odd-hole inequalities when \(G[U]\cong C_{2k+1}\), for which the right-hand side is \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every induced subgraph bounds the number of selected vertices by its stability number, subsuming clique and odd-hole inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in U}x_v\le\alpha(G[U])\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

notation.meaning: subgraph of G induced by U

children.title: Lifted Inequality Families

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Inequality Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of a valid face inequality for a binary polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{I\cup J}\), and suppose \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I\le b\) is valid when \(x_J=0\). Order \(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_m)\). At step \(t\), keep \(x_{j_s}=0\) for \(s>t\) and set
\[\lambda_{j_t}=b-\max\left\{a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{s<t}\lambda_{j_s}x_{j_s}:x\in X,\ x_{j_t}=1,\ x_{j_s}=0\text{ for }s>t\right\}.\]
After all steps, output \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_jx_j\le b\), which is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting computes coefficients for formerly fixed binary variables, extending a valid face inequality to the full binary polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I\le b\) is valid on \(\{x\in X:x_J=0\}\).
Each maximization slice used by the lifting order is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x_I+\sum_{j\in J}\lambda_jx_j\le b\) is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\).

notation.meaning: indices present in the initial face inequality

children.title: Rank-to-Lifting Strength Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between base rank inequalities and their lifted extensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-to-Lifting Strength Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of a valid rank inequality from an induced subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq V(G)\), and suppose \(a^\top x\leq \beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G[U])\). Order \(V(G)\setminus U=\{v_1,\ldots,v_k\}\). At step \(i\), after coefficients for \(v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\) have been fixed, set \[a_{v_i}:=\beta-\max\left\{\sum_{u\in U\cup\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}}a_u x_u:x\in\operatorname{STAB}(G[U\cup\{v_1,\ldots,v_i\}]),\ x_{v_i}=1\right\}.\] The resulting lifted inequality is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) and restricts to the original rank inequality on the face \(x_{V(G)\setminus U}=0\). Its coefficients, and thus its global strength, may depend on the lifting order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential lifting preserves validity and the original inequality on its induced-subgraph face, but different lifting orders can produce different global inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V(G)}a_vx_v\leq\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of incidence vectors of stable sets of G

children.title: Stable-Set Polytope Facets
children.top_down_role: Facet classes and structural conditions within stable-set polytope geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Polytope Facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-algebraic criterion for a valid inequality to define a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), and let \(P=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Because \(0\) and every unit vector belong to \(P\), the polytope is full-dimensional. A nonzero valid inequality \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) defines a facet of \(P\) if and only if its tight face \[F=\{x\in P:a^\top x=\beta\}\] has dimension \(n-1\). Equivalently, there exist \(n\) affinely independent stable-set incidence vectors \(\chi^{S_1},\ldots,\chi^{S_n}\) satisfying \(a^\top\chi^{S_i}=\beta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid stable-set inequality is facet-defining exactly when its tight stable-set vectors contain n affinely independent points.
assumptions_latex: \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) is a nonzero valid inequality for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^\top x\leq\beta\) defines a facet if and only if \(\dim(F)=|V|-1\).

notation.meaning: incidence vector of the stable set S
face on which the inequality is tight

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-dimensionality and affine-independence criterion are standard and correctly stated, but the record has no citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Polytope Adjacency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combinatorial characterization of adjacency between stable-set vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) and \(T\) be distinct stable sets of a finite simple graph \(G\). Their incidence vectors \(\chi^S\) and \(\chi^T\) are adjacent vertices of \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) if and only if the subgraph induced by their symmetric difference, \(G[S\triangle T]\), is connected. Thus adjacency of two stable-set vertices can be tested solely on the vertices selected by exactly one of the two stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two stable-set vertices are adjacent precisely when the graph induced by the symmetric difference of their stable sets is connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi^S\) and \(\chi^T\) are adjacent in \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) if and only if \(G[S\triangle T]\) is connected.

notation.meaning: symmetric difference of S and T

children.title: Facet–Adjacency Relations

knowledge_statements.title: Facet–Adjacency Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ridge-incidence criterion for adjacency of stable-set-polytope facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) have dimension \(d=|V(G)|\), and let \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) be distinct facets of \(P\). The facets are adjacent in the facet-adjacency graph exactly when their intersection is a ridge of \(P\): \[F_1\sim F_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \dim(F_1\cap F_2)=d-2.\] Equivalently, the two corresponding vertices of the polar polytope are joined by an edge whenever a polar representation is taken with the origin in the interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two facets are adjacent exactly when they meet in a codimension-two face; under polarity, their corresponding polar vertices are adjacent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_1\sim F_2\) if and only if \(\dim(F_1\cap F_2)=|V(G)|-2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ridge criterion and qualified polarity statement are mathematically appropriate for this condition container, but no supporting polyhedral reference is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Stable-Set Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Box-bounded edge relaxation paired with the standard fractional vertex-cover formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) and weights \(w\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{V}\), define the edge-based fractional stable-set polytope by \[\operatorname{FRAC}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:0\leq x_v\leq1\ (v\in V),\ x_u+x_v\leq1\ (uv\in E)\}.\] The fractional stable-set relaxation is \(\max\{w^\top x:x\in\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\}\). Every stable-set incidence vector is feasible, so \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\); consequently, the relaxation optimum is an upper bound on the maximum-weight stable-set value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The box-bounded edge relaxation imposes one inequality per edge, contains the stable-set polytope, and upper-bounds the maximum-weight stable-set value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\subseteq\operatorname{FRAC}(G)\) and \(\alpha_w(G)\leq\max_{x\in\operatorname{FRAC}(G)}w^\top x\).

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a stable set

children.title: Fractional Vertex-Cover Relaxation

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Vertex-Cover Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard linear relaxation of minimum-weight vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) with costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{V}\), the fractional vertex-cover relaxation is \[\tau_f(G,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vy_v:y_u+y_v\geq1\ (uv\in E),\ y_v\geq0\ (v\in V)\right\}.\] Bounds \(y_v\leq1\) may be added without changing the optimum. Every vertex-cover incidence vector is feasible, hence \(\tau_f(G,c)\leq\tau(G,c)\). Under the substitution \(x_v=1-y_v\), its feasible region with box bounds is complementary to the edge-based fractional stable-set relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional vertex cover replaces binary choices by nonnegative variables covering every edge; its optimum lower-bounds integral vertex cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_f(G,c)\leq\tau(G,c)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fractional vertex covers and their matching dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines fractional vertex covers and fractional matchings and records the complement relation, optimum-value identities, and half-integrality of the fractional matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a fractional vertex cover is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^V\) such that \(0\le x_v\le1\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(x_u+x_v\ge1\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). A vector \(x\) is a fractional vertex cover if and only if \(\mathbf1-x\) is a fractional stable set; consequently, \(\tau^*(G)+\alpha^*(G)=|V|\). Moreover, \(\tau^*(G)=\nu^*(G)\), where \(\nu^*(G)=\max\{y(E):0\le y_e\le1\ (e\in E),\ y(\delta(v))\le1\ (v\in V)\}\). Every vertex of the fractional matching polytope is half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional vertex cover assigns values between zero and one to the vertices so that the endpoints of every edge have total value at least one. Complementing it gives a fractional stable set, so their optimum values sum to the number of vertices. Linear-programming duality equates the fractional vertex-cover number with the fractional matching number. Every extreme point of the fractional matching polytope is half-integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau^*(G)+\alpha^*(G)=|V|,\qquad \tau^*(G)=\nu^*(G),\qquad \operatorname{vert}(P_{FM}(G))\subseteq\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^E.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Matching Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP dual of the fractional vertex-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-programming dual of the fractional vertex-cover relaxation is \[\nu_f(G,c)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}z_e:z_e\geq0\ (e\in E),\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}z_e\leq c_v\ (v\in V)\right\}.\] A feasible vector \(z\) is a fractional matching with vertex capacities \(c\). Since both programs are feasible and have finite optima, strong linear-programming duality gives \(\nu_f(G,c)=\tau_f(G,c)\). For unit costs, each vertex is incident to total matching weight at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual packs nonnegative edge weights subject to vertex capacities, and its optimum equals the fractional vertex-cover optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_f(G,c)=\tau_f(G,c)\).

notation.meaning: set of edges incident with v
fractional weight assigned to edge e

children.title: Vertex-Cover–Matching Duality Regimes
children.top_down_role: Graph classes and structural settings governing the dual relationship.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover–Matching Duality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fractional equality generally and integral equality for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every finite graph \(G\) with unit vertex costs, strong linear-programming duality yields \(	au_f(G)=
u_f(G)\). If \(G\) is bipartite, the vertex-edge incidence system is totally dual integral, so integral optima exist and \[	au(G)=	au_f(G)=
u_f(G)=
u(G),\] which is König's vertex-cover–matching theorem. For nonbipartite graphs the fractional equality remains valid, but integral equality can fail; for example, on an odd cycle \(C_{2k+1}\), \(	au(C_{2k+1})=k+1\) while \(
u(C_{2k+1})=k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fractional cover and matching values always agree. Integral equality holds for bipartite graphs but can fail on odd cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph with unit vertex costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_f(G)=\nu_f(G)\), and if \(G\) is bipartite then \(\tau(G)=\nu(G)\).

children.title: Half-Integral Extreme Points
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral regimes exhibiting half-integral relaxation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Extreme Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half-integrality of the standard vertex-cover linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[P_{VC}(G)=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:y_u+y_v\geq1\ (uv\in E),\ y_v\geq0\ (v\in V)\}.\] Every extreme point \(y\) of \(P_{VC}(G)\) is half-integral: \[y_v\in\left\{0,\tfrac12,1\right\}\qquad(v\in V).\] Consequently, for every nonnegative cost vector, the fractional vertex-cover program has an optimal solution whose coordinates belong to \(\{0,\tfrac12,1\}\). Under the complementary substitution \(x_v=1-y_v\) with box bounds, the corresponding extreme solutions of the edge stable-set relaxation are likewise half-integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme solution of the vertex-cover LP uses only 0, one-half, and 1; an optimal half-integral solution therefore always exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ext}(P_{VC}(G))\subseteq\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^{V}\).

notation.meaning: set of extreme points of P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The half-integrality theorem and its optimal-solution consequence are correctly scoped, but this nontrivial theorem requires an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance families organized by the size or behavior of relaxation gaps.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp worst-case gap for the standard unweighted vertex-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite graph \(G\) containing at least one edge, let \(\tau(G)\) and \(\tau_f(G)\) denote the integral and fractional minimum vertex-cover values. Threshold rounding an optimal fractional cover at \(\tfrac12\) gives \[1\leq\frac{\tau(G)}{\tau_f(G)}\leq2.\] If \(G\) is bipartite, the ratio equals \(1\). The upper bound is asymptotically sharp: for the complete graph \(K_n\), \(\tau(K_n)=n-1\), \(\tau_f(K_n)=n/2\), and the ratio is \(2-2/n\), which tends to \(2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unweighted vertex-cover LP has integrality gap at most two, is exact on bipartite graphs, and has ratios approaching two on complete graphs.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph containing at least one edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1\leq\tau(G)/\tau_f(G)\leq2\), the ratio is \(1\) for bipartite \(G\), and its supremum over finite graphs is \(2\).

notation.meaning: minimum cardinality of a vertex cover

children.title: Structural Sources of Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Graph features associated with weak integral approximation by fractional solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Sources of Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cycle obstruction to integrality and dense-graph amplification of the gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The edge constraints of the vertex-cover relaxation are integral on bipartite graphs, whereas an odd cycle permits a fractional half assignment. Specifically, on \(C_{2k+1}\), the vector \(y_v=\tfrac12\) for every vertex has value \(k+\tfrac12\), while every integral cover has value \(k+1\). Dense overlap can amplify this obstruction: on \(K_n\), the same half assignment has value \(n/2\), whereas an integral cover has value \(n-1\). Thus odd cycles witness the loss of bipartite integrality, and complete graphs form a family whose vertex-cover gap approaches two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd cycles create half-integral nonintegrality; dense collections of such conflicts, exemplified by complete graphs, amplify the vertex-cover gap toward two.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The odd-cycle and complete-graph calculations are correct and fit the failure-boundary container, but no inspectable source supports the structural interpretation or formulas.

children.title: Clique Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation problems associated with clique inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Clique Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of clique inequalities via maximum-weight clique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a rational vector \(x\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}^{V}\), assign weight \(x_v\) to vertex \(v\) and compute a maximum-weight clique \(Q\). If \(\sum_{v\in Q}x_v>1\), output the violated valid inequality \(\sum_{v\in Q}X_v\leq1\); otherwise certify that every clique inequality is satisfied. This is an exact reduction between clique separation and maximum-weight clique. Hence the separation problem is NP-hard on general graphs, while it is polynomial-time solvable on graph classes admitting polynomial-time maximum-weight clique algorithms, including perfect graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique separation finds a maximum-weight clique and reports its inequality when its weight exceeds one; its complexity matches maximum-weight clique.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}^{V}\) is the point to be separated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated clique inequality exists if and only if \(\max\{\sum_{v\in Q}x_v:Q\text{ is a clique}\}>1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum-weight-clique separation procedure is correctly stated and fits the algorithm container. Its NP-hardness and polynomial solvability on perfect graphs require specific supporting citations.

children.title: Odd-Cycle Separation
children.top_down_role: Separation problems associated with odd-cycle inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial separation of odd-cycle inequalities from the edge relaxation of the stable-set polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and let \(x\in[0,1]^V\) satisfy \(x_u+x_v\leq 1\) for every \(uv\in E\). Assign each edge the nonnegative length \(\ell_{uv}=1-x_u-x_v\). For every vertex, compute a minimum-length closed walk of odd edge count using a parity-expanded graph with states \((v,0)\) and \((v,1)\). If the minimum value is less than \(1\), extract and simplify the walk to an odd cycle \(C\); then \(\sum_{v\in C}x_v>(|C|-1)/2\), so its odd-cycle inequality is violated. If every such parity distance is at least \(1\), no odd-cycle inequality is violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign edge slacks as lengths and find a shortest odd closed walk in a parity-expanded graph. Length below one yields a violated odd-cycle stable-set inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A violated odd-cycle inequality is returned exactly when one exists.

notation.meaning: odd cycle extracted from an odd closed walk

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parity-expanded shortest-path formulation is mathematically plausible and fits the algorithm container, but no citation supports the extraction argument or exact separation guarantee.

children.title: Separation Complexity Contrast
children.top_down_role: Complexity and tractability differences between the two separation families.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Complexity Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity contrast between clique and odd-cycle separation for stable-set relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational vector \(x\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}^{V}\), separating clique inequalities \(\sum_{v\in K}x_v\leq 1\) requires deciding whether \(G\) has a clique of weight greater than \(1\); this is the maximum-weight-clique decision problem and is NP-complete. By contrast, when \(x\) satisfies the edge relaxation, separation of all odd-cycle inequalities \(\sum_{v\in C}x_v\leq(|C|-1)/2\) reduces to polynomially many shortest-path computations in a parity-expanded graph. Thus clique separation is NP-hard in general, whereas odd-cycle separation is polynomial-time solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clique separation encodes maximum-weight clique and is NP-hard. Odd-cycle separation over the edge relaxation is solvable in polynomial time using parity shortest paths.
assumptions_latex: Weights and candidate points are rationally encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clique separation is NP-hard, while odd-cycle separation is in polynomial time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique-versus-odd-cycle separation contrast fits the complexity-bound container, but both the NP-hardness claim and polynomial-time separation claim lack inspectable citations.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Stable-Set Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lifting of a valid stable-set inequality from an induced subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\subseteq V\) and suppose \(\sum_{u\in W}a_u x_u\leq\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G[W])\). To lift a vertex \(v\notin W\), compute \(M_v=\max\{\sum_{u\in S}a_u:S\subseteq W,\ S\cup\{v\}\text{ is stable}\}\) and set \(a_v=\beta-M_v\). Then \(\sum_{u\in W}a_u x_u+a_vx_v\leq\beta\) is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G[W\cup\{v\}])\), and \(a_v\) is the largest valid coefficient with the preceding coefficients fixed. Repeating this operation in a chosen order produces a sequentially lifted stable-set cut; coefficients may depend on that order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift an omitted vertex by solving a residual maximum-weight stable-set problem. The resulting coefficient is strongest with earlier coefficients fixed, but may depend on lifting order.
assumptions_latex: The initial inequality is valid for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G[W])\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential application yields a valid inequality for the enlarged stable-set polytope.

notation.meaning: convex hull of incidence vectors of stable sets of H

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential lifting coefficient and order-dependence claim are precise and suitable for this algorithm container, but no source supports the lifting formula and maximal-coefficient assertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Bron–Kerbosch Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive enumeration of every maximal clique without duplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain disjoint vertex sets \(R,P,X\), where \(R\) is a clique, every vertex in \(P\cup X\) is adjacent to all of \(R\), and \(P\) contains unprocessed extensions. If \(P=X=\varnothing\), output \(R\). Otherwise choose a pivot \(u\in P\cup X\) and, for each \(v\in P\setminus N(u)\), recurse with \((R\cup\{v\},P\cap N(v),X\cap N(v))\), then move \(v\) from \(P\) to \(X\). Starting from \((\varnothing,V,\varnothing)\), the procedure outputs every maximal clique of \(G\) exactly once.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bron–Kerbosch recursively extends a clique, using candidate and excluded sets. Pivoting restricts branching while preserving exact, duplicate-free enumeration of maximal cliques.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every maximal clique of \(G\) is output exactly once.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pivoted Bron–Kerbosch procedure fits the container and is stated consistently, but its duplicate-free completeness guarantee has no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Ordered Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal-clique enumeration using an outer degeneracy ordering and pivoted recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be a degeneracy ordering of \(G\), so each \(v_i\) has at most \(d\) neighbors occurring later. For each \(i\), invoke pivoted Bron–Kerbosch with \(R=\{v_i\}\), \(P=N(v_i)\cap\{v_{i+1},\ldots,v_n\}\), and \(X=N(v_i)\cap\{v_1,\ldots,v_{i-1}\}\). Output a clique only when both recursive candidate and excluded sets are empty. Each maximal clique is generated in the invocation for its earliest vertex, hence exactly once, while the initial candidate set of every invocation has size at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process vertices in degeneracy order and start Bron–Kerbosch from each vertex using only later neighbors as candidates. Every maximal clique is assigned to its earliest vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple graph of degeneracy \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All maximal cliques are enumerated once, with each root candidate set of size at most \(d\).

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Clique Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-delay enumeration bound for maximal cliques via maximal-independent-set duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(n=|V|\) and \(\overline m=|E(\overline G)|\). Maximal cliques can be enumerated with polynomial delay by constructing \(\overline G\) and applying a polynomial-delay maximal-independent-set enumeration algorithm to it, because \(K\subseteq V\) is a maximal clique of \(G\) exactly when \(K\) is a maximal stable set of \(\overline G\). Using an implementation whose delay on a graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m'\) edges is \(O(n(n+m'))\), this gives delay \(O(n(n+\overline m))\). Consequently, the total running time is polynomial in the input size and the number of reported maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal cliques can be enumerated with polynomial delay by enumerating maximal independent sets in the complement graph. The delay bound depends on the complement graph's edge count.
assumptions_latex: The complement graph is represented explicitly or supports polynomial-time adjacency operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal cliques are enumerable with polynomial delay and output-polynomial total running time.

notation.meaning: number of edges of the complement graph

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring-Bounded Clique Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum-clique branch-and-bound using proper-coloring upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a current clique \(R\), a candidate set \(P\subseteq\bigcap_{v\in R}N(v)\), and an incumbent size \(L\). Properly color \(G[P]\) with \(q\) colors. Since every clique in \(G[P]\) contains at most one vertex of each color, every extension of \(R\) has size at most \(|R|+q\); prune when this quantity is at most \(L\). Otherwise branch on a candidate \(v\), recursively considering inclusion with \((R\cup\{v\},P\cap N(v))\) and exclusion by removing \(v\) from \(P\). Update \(L\) whenever a larger clique is found and return the incumbent after all unpruned branches terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper coloring of the candidate subgraph bounds any clique extension. Branches whose bound cannot beat the incumbent are safely pruned.
assumptions_latex: The coloring used at each node is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a maximum clique of \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coloring upper bound and exact branch-and-bound logic fit the algorithm container, but no inspectable source supports the stated algorithm and correctness guarantee.

children.title: Branch-Reduce Clique Search
children.top_down_role: Exact clique search organized around branching plus structural reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Reduce Clique Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum-clique recursion combining safe reductions, inclusion, and exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(H\), exhaustively apply reductions that preserve the recoverable optimum and maintain their reconstruction data. If the reduced graph is empty, return the reconstructed clique. Otherwise choose a vertex \(v\) and evaluate two residual problems: exclusion gives a maximum clique of \(H-v\), while inclusion gives \(\{v\}\) together with a maximum clique of \(H[N(v)]\). Return the larger reconstructed solution. Equivalently, the optimum values satisfy \(\omega(H)=\max\{\omega(H-v),1+\omega(H[N(v)])\}\). Incumbent lower bounds and valid upper bounds may prune either branch without changing the returned optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After safe reductions, branch on excluding a vertex or including it and restricting to its neighborhood. The better reconstructed branch is a maximum clique.
assumptions_latex: Every applied reduction includes a correctness-preserving reconstruction rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned reconstructed vertex set is a maximum clique of \(H\).

notation.meaning: open neighborhood of v in the current graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The clique branching recurrence is standard, but the unspecified reductions and reconstruction mechanism prevent source-independent review of the complete branch-reduce algorithm.

children.title: Branch-Reduce Stable-Set Search
children.top_down_role: Exact stable-set search organized around branching plus structural reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Reduce Stable-Set Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact maximum-stable-set recursion combining safe reductions, inclusion, and exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite graph \(H\), exhaustively apply reductions that preserve the recoverable optimum and record reconstruction data. If the reduced graph is empty, return the reconstructed stable set. Otherwise select a vertex \(v\). The exclusion branch solves \(H-v\); the inclusion branch selects \(v\) and solves \(H-N[v]\). Return the larger reconstructed solution. Thus \(\alpha(H)=\max\{\alpha(H-v),1+\alpha(H-N[v])\}\). A branch may be pruned whenever a valid upper bound on its attainable stable-set size does not exceed the incumbent lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After safe reductions, branch on excluding a vertex or including it and deleting its closed neighborhood. The larger reconstructed solution is maximum.
assumptions_latex: Every reduction preserves the optimum through an explicit reconstruction rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned reconstructed vertex set is a maximum stable set of \(H\).

notation.meaning: closed neighborhood of v in the current graph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stable-set branching recurrence is standard, but the complete algorithm depends on unspecified reductions and reconstruction rules for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Shared Reduction Kernels
children.top_down_role: Reduction structures transferable through clique–stable-set correspondences.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Reduction Kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complement correspondence between clique and stable-set branch-reduction kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite simple graph \(G\) and vertex set \(S\subseteq V(G)\), \(S\) is a clique of \(G\) if and only if it is a stable set of \(\overline G\), and \(\omega(G)=\alpha(\overline G)\). Vertex deletion commutes with complementation, while the clique inclusion residual \(G[N_G(v)]\) corresponds to the stable-set inclusion residual \(\overline G-N_{\overline G}[v]\). Hence any clique reduction equipped with an optimum-preserving reconstruction map induces a stable-set reduction on the complement, and conversely. A shared kernel may therefore implement complement-equivariant reductions once and expose dual reconstruction rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph complementation exchanges cliques and stable sets and maps their deletion and inclusion residuals. Correct reductions can therefore be transferred between the two problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Clique and stable-set reduction kernels correspond under graph complementation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complement correspondence is consistent with the property container, but the general transfer claim for arbitrary reconstruction-equipped reductions requires an inspectable source or a more formal specification.

children.title: Stable-Set Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching designs used in exact stable-set search.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary vertex branching for an exact stable-set branch-and-cut tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a branch-and-cut node with undecided vertex \(v\), create two children imposing \(x_v=0\) and \(x_v=1\). In the first child delete \(v\); in the second select \(v\), delete its closed neighborhood \(N[v]\), and add one to the accumulated objective value. These children partition all integral stable-set incidence vectors because every such vector has exactly one of the values \(x_v=0\) or \(x_v=1\). Continue applying propagation, cut separation, and bounding until each node is fathomed or integral; the best feasible leaf solution is globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on whether a chosen vertex belongs to the stable set. Inclusion deletes its closed neighborhood; exclusion deletes only the vertex.
assumptions_latex: Branch-and-cut bounds are valid for every descendant node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two branches exhaust all stable sets and preserve exact global optimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Binary stable-set branching is correctly scoped as an algorithm, but the global-optimality statement relies on branch-and-cut termination, valid bounds, and fathoming rules without a supporting citation.

children.title: Stable-Set Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Cut families and separation subproblems used within exact search.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iterative separation of valid inequalities in a stable-set branch-and-cut relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a search node, solve the current linear relaxation and obtain \(x^*\). For each enabled valid family \(a^	op x\leq b\), run its separation oracle on \(x^*\). If an oracle returns \(a^	op x^*>b+\varepsilon\), add the inequality locally or globally according to its validity domain and reoptimize. Repeat until no enabled oracle finds a violation exceeding tolerance \(\varepsilon\), the node is infeasible, or a prescribed separation limit is reached. Because only inequalities valid for all feasible stable-set incidence vectors are added, separation can strengthen bounds but cannot remove any feasible integral stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the node relaxation, separate violated valid stable-set inequalities, add them, and reoptimize until no material violation remains or a limit is reached.
assumptions_latex: Every oracle returns only inequalities valid for the relevant node domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cut addition preserves all feasible stable sets while monotonically strengthening the relaxation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation loop and validity-preservation statement fit the algorithm container, but no source establishes the local/global validity conditions, oracle scope, or branch-and-cut integration.

children.title: Stable-Set Bound Management
children.top_down_role: Bound strength, incumbent quality, and search-node control.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Bound Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent and node-bound rules for an exhaustive exact maximum-weight stable-set search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each active search node \(Q\) represent a family \(\mathcal F(Q)\) of feasible stable sets, and let \(z(S)=\sum_{v\in S}w_v\). Initially, the node families collectively contain every stable set of \(G\). Maintain an incumbent value \(L\), attained by a known stable set, and a valid upper bound \(U(Q)\geq\max\{z(S):S\in\mathcal F(Q)\}\). Fathom \(Q\) if \(\mathcal F(Q)=\varnothing\) or \(U(Q)\leq L\). Otherwise, replace it by finitely many child nodes whose families collectively contain \(\mathcal F(Q)\), or add valid cuts without removing any feasible member of \(\mathcal F(Q)\); maintain valid bounds for all resulting nodes and replace \(L\) whenever a better feasible set is found. If the procedure terminates with no active node, the incumbent is an optimal maximum-weight stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prune infeasible nodes and nodes whose valid upper bounds cannot beat the incumbent, while ensuring that branching exhaustively covers every remaining feasible stable set. If the exhaustive search terminates with no active node, the incumbent is optimal.
assumptions_latex: The initial node families collectively contain every stable set of \(G\).
Every branching step preserves exhaustive coverage, every cut preserves feasible stable sets, and every reported \(U(Q)\) is valid.
The search terminates after finitely many node-processing steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\alpha_w(G)\) when the active-node collection becomes empty.

notation.meaning: maximum weight of a stable set in G
upper bound at search node Q
family of feasible stable sets represented by node Q

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Dynamic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight stable-set dynamic programming on a nice tree decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nice tree decomposition with bags \(X_t\), store \(D_t(S)\) for every independent subset \(S\subseteq X_t\), equal to the maximum weight of a partial stable set whose intersection with \(X_t\) is \(S\). At an introduce node for \(v\), add \(w_v\) exactly when \(v\in S\); at a forget node, maximize over excluding or including the forgotten vertex; at a join node, add the two child values and subtract \(\sum_{v\in S}w_v\). Initialize leaf states directly and return the maximum valid root state. For width \(t\), the running time is \(O(2^{t+1}n\operatorname{poly}(t))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree-decomposition table indexed by independent bag subsets solves maximum-weight stable set in time exponential only in the decomposition width.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) has a supplied nice tree decomposition of width \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root table yields \(\alpha_w(G)\) in \(O(2^{t+1}n\operatorname{poly}(t))\) time.

notation.meaning: optimal partial value with bag intersection S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dynamic program and its mathematical role fit the leaf, but the exact recurrence conventions and running-time bound lack an inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Kernelization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nemhauser–Trotter kernel for parameterized unweighted Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the vertex-cover relaxation \(\min\{\sum_{v\in V}x_v:x_u+x_v\geq1\text{ for }uv\in E,\ x_v\geq0\}\). It has an optimal solution \(x\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^V\). Put \(V_i=\{v:x_v=i\}\) and \(H=G[V_{1/2}]\). There exists a minimum vertex cover containing \(V_1\) and avoiding \(V_0\). Consequently, for an instance \((G,k)\), set \(k'=k-|V_1|\): then \(\tau(G)\leq k\) if and only if \(\tau(H)\leq k'\). If the relaxation value is at most \(k\), then \(|V(H)|\leq2k'\); otherwise the instance is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-integral vertex-cover LP fixes zero and one vertices and leaves an equivalent kernel containing at most twice the residual parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau(G)\leq k\iff\tau(G[V_{1/2}])\leq k-|V_1|\), with \(|V_{1/2}|\leq2(k-|V_1|)\) for non-rejected instances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The half-integral reduction and residual kernel bound are plausible and fit the container, but the persistency equivalence and kernel-size theorem require an authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Persistency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP primal-dual certificate for Nemhauser–Trotter vertex persistency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\{0,\tfrac12,1\}^V\) be feasible for the vertex-cover LP, and let \(y\in\mathbb R_+^E\) satisfy \(\sum_{e\ni v}y_e\leq1\) for every vertex. If \(\sum_vx_v=\sum_ey_e\), primal-dual equality certifies that \(x\) is optimal. Define \(V_1=\{v:x_v=1\}\) and \(V_0=\{v:x_v=0\}\). The Nemhauser–Trotter persistency property then certifies the existence of a minimum integral vertex cover \(C^*\) satisfying \(V_1\subseteq C^*\) and \(C^*\cap V_0=\varnothing\). Feasibility and equality are checkable in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching primal and dual LP values certify that all LP-one vertices can be selected and all LP-zero vertices omitted by some minimum cover.
assumptions_latex: The displayed \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy their respective LP constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C^*\in\arg\min\{|C|:C\text{ covers }E\}\) such that \(V_1\subseteq C^*\subseteq V\setminus V_0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Primal-dual equality certifies LP optimality, but the stated integral persistency conclusion additionally invokes the Nemhauser–Trotter theorem and has no supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Cover LP Rounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold rounding for the weighted vertex-cover relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonnegative vertex costs, solve \(\min\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:x_u+x_v\geq1\text{ for }uv\in E,\ x_v\geq0\}\), obtaining an optimum \(x^*\). Output \(C=\{v\in V:x_v^*\geq\tfrac12\}\). Every edge has at least one endpoint in \(C\), so \(C\) is a vertex cover. Moreover, \(c(C)=\sum_{v\in C}c_v\leq2\sum_vc_vx_v^*\leq2\operatorname{OPT}\). Thus threshold rounding is a polynomial-time factor-two approximation, including when some costs are zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Round every LP value at least one-half upward; the result covers every edge and costs at most twice the optimal integral cover.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is a vertex cover and \(c(C)\leq2\operatorname{OPT}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold-rounding algorithm and factor-two guarantee are standard and correctly scoped, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Search-Tree Vertex Cover
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary parameterized branching algorithm for Vertex Cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On input \((G,k)\), return failure if \(k<0\), and return the accumulated selected vertices if \(E(G)=\varnothing\). Otherwise choose any edge \(uv\). Since every vertex cover contains \(u\) or \(v\), recursively solve the two instances \((G-u,k-1)\) and \((G-v,k-1)\), adding the corresponding chosen endpoint; accept if either branch accepts. The search-tree recurrence is \(T(k)\leq2T(k-1)+n^{O(1)}\), giving \(O(2^kn^{O(1)})\) time and polynomial space under depth-first traversal. The algorithm returns a cover of size at most \(k\), or correctly reports that none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on an uncovered edge by selecting either endpoint, producing a correct parameterized algorithm with at most two branches per parameter decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertex Cover is decidable in \(O(2^kn^{O(1)})\) time by this branching rule.

notation.meaning: worst-case running time at budget k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branching algorithm, correctness claim, and parameterized running time fit the leaf, but the record provides no inspectable citation.

children.title: Stable-Set NP-Hardness
children.top_down_role: Classical hardness regimes for exact stable-set optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set NP-Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical decision and optimization hardness on unrestricted finite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decision problem Independent Set asks, for a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and integer \(k\), whether \(G\) contains a stable set of cardinality at least \(k\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\), since a proposed vertex set can be checked for nonadjacency in polynomial time. It is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete: under the identity graph transformation, \(G\) has a vertex cover of size at most \(b\) if and only if it has a stable set of size at least \(|V|-b\). Consequently, computing \(\alpha(G)\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent Set is NP-complete by complementing a vertex cover within the same graph, and computing the maximum stable-set size is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Graphs are finite, undirected, and given explicitly.
Vertex Cover is used as the source \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{Independent Set}\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete and computing \(\alpha(G)\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduction and complexity conclusions are standard and correctly stated, but the NP-completeness claim lacks a cited theorem or section locator.

children.title: Stable-Set Inapproximability
children.top_down_role: Limits on efficient approximation across stable-set instance families.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Inapproximability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-time approximation boundary for unrestricted Maximum Independent Set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph with \(n\) vertices, call an algorithm a \(\rho(n)\)-approximation for Maximum Independent Set if it always outputs a stable set \(S\) satisfying \(|S|\geq\alpha(G)/\rho(n)\). For every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), no polynomial-time algorithm approximates Maximum Independent Set within factor \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) on all finite graphs. The same lower bound applies to maximum-weight stable set because the unweighted problem is its unit-weight special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unless P equals NP, unrestricted maximum stable set has no polynomial-time approximation ratio n to the power one minus any fixed positive constant.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed independently of the input.
Approximation ratios use the standard multiplicative convention for maximization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm P\neq\mathrm{NP}\Rightarrow\) no polynomial-time \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\)-approximation exists for Maximum Independent Set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strong inapproximability exponent and its complexity assumption require a precise authoritative theorem citation; none is supplied.

children.title: Stable-Set Hardness Transfers
children.top_down_role: Reduction-based connections among exact and approximation hardness regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Hardness Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reductions through graph complementation and vertex-cover complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a set \(S\subseteq V\) is stable in \(G\) exactly when it is a clique in the complement \(\overline G\), and exactly when \(V\setminus S\) is a vertex cover of \(G\). Hence \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\alpha(G)+\tau(G)=|V|\). Graph complementation gives a polynomial-time, objective-preserving transfer between Maximum Independent Set and Maximum Clique. The vertex-cover correspondence transfers exact decision thresholds by \(k\mapsto|V|-k\), but its additive objective transformation does not automatically preserve multiplicative approximation ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementation transfers stable set exactly to clique, while taking the complementary vertex set transfers exact thresholds to vertex cover but not multiplicative ratios.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=\omega(\overline G)\) and \(\alpha(G)=|V|-\tau(G)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal-Set Enumeration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp worst-case count and output-sensitive enumeration of maximal stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m(G)\) denote the number of inclusion-maximal stable sets of an \(n\)-vertex graph. The Moon–Moser bound gives \(m(G)\leq g(n)\), where \(g(n)=3^{n/3}\) if \(n\equiv0\pmod3\), \(g(n)=4\cdot3^{(n-4)/3}\) if \(n\equiv1\pmod3\) and \(n\geq4\), and \(g(n)=2\cdot3^{(n-2)/3}\) if \(n\equiv2\pmod3\). These bounds are attained by disjoint unions of triangles, with one \(K_4\) or \(K_2\) for the respective remainders. All maximal stable sets can be enumerated in \(O(3^{n/3}\operatorname{poly}(n))\) time, which is worst-case output-optimal up to polynomial factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An n-vertex graph has at most about three to the n-over-three maximal stable sets, and enumeration can match this bound up to polynomial factors.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite simple graph on \(n\) vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(G)\leq g(n)=O(3^{n/3})\), with matching extremal graph families and enumeration time up to polynomial factors.

notation.meaning: number of maximal stable sets of G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sharp piecewise bound and extremal constructions are correct, but both the Moon–Moser theorem and the claimed enumeration complexity need specific citations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial solvability of unweighted maximum stable set through König’s theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}W,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph. The complement of every vertex cover is a stable set and conversely, so \(\alpha(G)=|V(G)|-	au(G)\). König’s theorem gives \(	au(G)=
u(G)\), where \(
u(G)\) is the cardinality of a maximum matching. Therefore \(\alpha(G)=|V(G)|-
u(G)\). A maximum stable set can be recovered from a maximum matching by constructing a minimum vertex cover through alternating reachability and taking its vertex complement; hence the problem is polynomial-time solvable on bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a bipartite graph, maximum stable-set size equals the vertex count minus maximum-matching size, yielding a polynomial-time construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha(G)=|V(G)|-\tau(G)=|V(G)|-\nu(G)\), and a maximum stable set is computable in polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bipartitions, Bipartite Graphs, and Complete Bipartite Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and notation for undirected bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bipartition of an undirected graph $G$ consists of disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ such that $A\cup B=V(G)$ and every edge has one endpoint in $A$ and one endpoint in $B$. The graph $G$ is bipartite if it has a bipartition. If $A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B=V(G)$, $|A|=n$, $|B|=m$, and $E(G)=\{\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$, then $G$ is the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,m}$. The notation $G=(A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B,E(G))$ declares that $A\mathbin{\dot\cup}B$ is a bipartition of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartition divides an undirected graph's vertices into two disjoint parts so that every edge joins the two parts. A graph with such a partition is bipartite. The graph containing every possible edge between parts of sizes n and m is denoted K_{n,m}; the displayed disjoint-union notation declares a bipartition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is bipartite exactly when it admits a bipartition; the fully joined bipartite graph with part sizes }n,m\text{ is }K_{n,m}.

knowledge_statements.title: Claw-Free Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial tractability of maximum-weight stable set on claw-free graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph is claw-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to \(K_{1,3}\). For every finite claw-free graph \(G=(V,E)\) and rational vertex-weight vector \(w\in\mathbb Q^V\), a stable set maximizing \(\sum_{v\in S}w_v\) can be found in time polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\) and the binary encoding length of \(w\). Thus both Maximum Independent Set and Maximum-Weight Independent Set are polynomial-time solvable on the claw-free graph class, despite being \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard on unrestricted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum-weight stable set is polynomial-time solvable on graphs containing no induced three-leaf claw.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha_w(G)\) and an attaining stable set are computable in polynomial time.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Polynomial-time solvability of maximum-weight stable set on claw-free graphs is a nontrivial theorem requiring a precise authoritative citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Splittable Vertices Relative to Similarity Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local neighborhood decomposition used in the claw-free stable-set augmentation analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\sim\) be the similarity relation on \(V\setminus S\). A vertex \(s\in S\) is splittable if \(N(s)\) can be partitioned into two classes \(X,Y\) such that, for all \(u,v\in N(s)\) with \(u\not\sim v\), \(uv\in E\) if and only if either \(u,v\in X\) or \(u,v\in Y\). When \(s\) is splittable, \(X\) and \(Y\) are called its classes. Define \(S'=\{s\in S:s\text{ is splittable}\}\) and \(S''=S\setminus S'\). Under conditions (69.1) in the claw-free setting, \(s_a,s_b\in S'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex s in S is splittable when its neighborhood can be divided into two classes such that two nonsimilar neighbors are adjacent exactly when they lie in the same class. The splittable vertices form S prime, and the remaining vertices form S double prime. Under the stated normalized claw-free conditions, s_a and s_b are splittable.

u\sim v\iff N(u)\cap S=N(v)\cap S\text{ for }u,v\in V\setminus S
a,b,s_a,s_b\text{ satisfy conditions }(69.1)\text{ for the final consequence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S'=\{s\in S:s\text{ is splittable}\},\quad S''=S\setminus S',\quad s_a,s_b\in S'\text{ under }(69.1)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating and augmenting paths relative to a stable set, as used in the claw-free stable-set setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), let \(S\subseteq V\) be stable, and let \(P=(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_k)\) be a walk. The walk \(P\) is \(S\)-alternating if precisely one of \(v_{i-1},v_i\) belongs to \(S\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\). It is an \(S\)-augmenting path if, in addition, \(P\) is a path, \(v_0,v_k\notin S\), and \((S\setminus\{v_1,v_3,\ldots,v_{k-1}\})\cup\{v_0,v_2,\ldots,v_k\}\) is stable. Consequently, if \(k\ge 2\), each of \(v_0,v_k\) has exactly one neighbor in \(S\), and each of \(v_2,v_4,\ldots,v_{k-2}\) has exactly two neighbors in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An S-alternating walk alternates between vertices inside and outside the stable set S. It is S-augmenting when it is a path with both endpoints outside S and replacing its odd-indexed vertices of S by its even-indexed vertices preserves stability. When its length is at least two, each endpoint has exactly one neighbor in S and each internal even-indexed vertex has exactly two.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq V\text{ is a stable set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }S\text{-augmenting}\iff P\text{ satisfies the stated path, endpoint, and exchanged-set stability conditions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Standing Conditions for Two Distinguished External Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A context-dependent package of standing assumptions for the subsequent claw-free stable-set analysis; it is not asserted for arbitrary choices of the graph, stable set, or vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(a,b\in V\setminus S\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The analysis fixes distinct vertices a and b outside S. Each has degree one and a different neighbor in S; every other vertex outside S has exactly two neighbors in S; every other vertex of S has at least two vertices of S at distance two; and the graph is connected.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds Auxiliary Graph for Claw-Free Stable-Set Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary graph and bone-level directed-path test in the claw-free stable-set construction; unrelated intrusive extraction text is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The auxiliary graph \(H\) has vertex set \(\{(s,X):s\in S',\ X\text{ is a class of }s\}\setminus\{(s_a,\{a\}),(s_b,\{b\})\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Edmonds graph represents vertex-class pairs and joins them either within a split vertex or when an appropriate augmenting path exists. Inside a bone, those augmenting paths are exactly the directed paths in a layered nonadjacency digraph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme stable sets and alternating augmentations in claw-free graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted alternating-path properties used in stable-set optimization on claw-free graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be claw-free, let $w:V\to\mathbb{R}_+$, and let $S$ be an extreme stable set. Every $S$-alternating chordless circuit $C$ satisfies $w(V(C)\setminus S)\leq w(V(C)\cap S)$. Moreover, if $P$ is an $S$-augmenting path maximizing $w(V(P)\setminus S)-w(V(P)\cap S)$, then $S\triangle V(P)$ is an extreme stable set of cardinality $|S|+1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nonnegatively vertex-weighted claw-free graph, an alternating chordless circuit cannot have more weight outside an extreme stable set than inside it. Toggling a maximum-gain augmenting path produces an extreme stable set with one additional vertex.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is an extreme stable set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall C\text{ an }S\text{-alternating chordless circuit},\ w(V(C)\setminus S)\leq w(V(C)\cap S);\quad P\in\arg\max_Q\{w(V(Q)\setminus S)-w(V(Q)\cap S)\}\implies S\triangle V(P)\text{ is extreme and }|S\triangle V(P)|=|S|+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cardinality-Stratified Reduction for Weighted Stable Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and reduction used in the weighted claw-free stable-set algorithm; the conditional reduction itself is stated for an arbitrary weighted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}_+\). A stable set \(S\) is extreme if \(w(S)\ge w(T)\) for every stable set \(T\) satisfying \(|T|=|S|\). If, from every extreme stable set \(S\), one can derive an extreme stable set of size \(|S|+1\) whenever one exists, then starting with \(S=\varnothing\), enumerating extreme stable sets of all attainable cardinalities, and selecting one of maximum weight yields a maximum-weight stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme stable set has maximum weight among stable sets of the same size. If an extreme set of the next attainable size can always be derived, enumerating these sets from the empty set and taking the heaviest one solves the maximum-weight stable-set problem.
assumptions_latex: \text{From each extreme stable set }S\text{, an extreme stable set of size }|S|+1\text{ can be derived whenever one exists}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The heaviest extreme stable set enumerated from }\varnothing\text{ is a maximum-weight stable set.}

children.title: Chordal Graph Stable Set
children.top_down_role: Stable-set structure and tractable optimization on chordal graphs.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A maximum-weight stable set of \(G\) can be computed in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time.

notation.meaning: Maximum weight of a stable set in G
A perfect elimination ordering of G

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear-time maximum-weight stable-set algorithms on chordal graphs via perfect elimination orderings are standard
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic tractability assumes an adjacency-list representation and a perfect elimination ordering computed or supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be chordal and let \(w:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\). A perfect elimination ordering of \(G\) can be found in \(O(|V|+|E|)\) time. Dynamic programming along the associated elimination structure computes a stable set \(S\subseteq V\) satisfying \[\sum_{v\in S}w(v)=\alpha_w(G):=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in T}w(v):T\subseteq V\text{ is stable}\right\}.\] The total running time and storage are \(O(|V|+|E|)\) in the adjacency-list model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-weight stable set in a chordal graph is computable in linear time using a perfect elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Graph Stable Set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf and the statement is mathematically plausible, but no inspectable citation supports the claimed linear-time weighted algorithm, storage bound, and representation assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Interval Graph Stable Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses an interval representation; endpoint ties follow the convention that intersecting closed intervals are adjacent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given intervals \(I_j=[\ell_j,r_j]\) with weights \(w_j\ge 0\), sort them so that \(r_1\le\cdots\le r_n\). Define \(p(j)=\max\{i<j:r_i<\ell_j\}\), with \(p(j)=0\) when the set is empty, and initialize \(F(0)=0\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\), update \[F(j)=\max\{F(j-1),w_j+F(p(j))\}.\] Backtracking through the selected alternatives returns pairwise disjoint intervals, hence a stable set, of weight \(F(n)=\alpha_w(G)\). Sorting and predecessor search give running time \(O(n\log n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort intervals by finishing time and apply weighted-interval-scheduling dynamic programming to obtain an optimal stable set in O(n log n) time.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_n\) are closed intervals representing a finite interval graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recurrence \(F(j)=\max\{F(j-1),w_j+F(p(j))\}\) returns a maximum-weight stable set.

notation.meaning: Last interval ending before I_j begins
Optimal weight among the first j sorted intervals

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weighted interval scheduling is the standard maximum-weight stable-set algorithm for interval graphs

children.title: Interval-to-Chordal Class Relation

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The graph \(G\) is chordal, while the converse fails in general.

notation.meaning: An induced cycle on k vertices

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the inclusion of interval graphs in chordal graphs and its strictness are standard graph-class facts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States strict class inclusion for finite simple graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G\) is the intersection graph of finitely many intervals on a line, then \(G\) has no induced cycle \(C_k\) with \(k\ge 4\); consequently, \(G\) is chordal. The inclusion is strict: the three-sun graph with clique \(\{c_1,c_2,c_3\}\), stable set \(\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}\), and neighborhoods \(N(s_i)=\{c_i,c_{i+1}\}\), with indices modulo \(3\), is chordal but is not an interval graph.

notation.meaning: A bag of the tree decomposition

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: subset dynamic programming over a nice tree decomposition is standard for maximum-weight stable set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bound is parameterized by treewidth and assumes a supplied decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,(B_t)_{t\in V(T)})\) be a tree decomposition of \(G\) with \(|B_t|\le k+1\). For each bag, retain one dynamic-programming value for every subset \(X\subseteq B_t\) that is stable in \(G[B_t]\), recording the best compatible weight in the processed subgraph. The introduce, forget, and join transitions of a nice decomposition preserve these boundary states. The root optimum equals \(\alpha_w(G)\), and at most \(2^{k+1}\) states are processed per bag, yielding time \(O(2^{k+1}|V|)\) and fixed-parameter tractability in \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a width-k tree decomposition, maximum-weight stable set is computable by bag-subset dynamic programming in O(2^k n) time.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Width Graphs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the bounded-width container, but the exact bound requires a source specifying nice-decomposition size, join processing, arithmetic-cost assumptions, and whether dependence on k is suppressed.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a polynomial-time stable set \(S\) with \(w(S)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\alpha_w(G)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Baker-style layer deletion gives a PTAS for weighted stable set on planar graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baker-style PTAS for nonnegative vertex weights; dependence on accuracy may be exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(0<\varepsilon<1\), choose an integer \(q\ge 1/\varepsilon\). A planar embedding can be layered so that, for each residue class modulo \(q\), deleting that class leaves components of treewidth bounded as a function of \(q\). Solve maximum-weight stable set exactly on every resulting bounded-width graph and return the best lifted solution \(S\). Averaging over the \(q\) deleted classes gives \[w(S)\ge\left(1-\frac1q\right)\alpha_w(G)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\alpha_w(G).\] The running time is \(|V|^{O(1/\varepsilon)}\), and hence polynomial for fixed \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Planar maximum-weight stable set has a PTAS obtained by deleting layers and solving the remaining bounded-treewidth instances exactly.
knowledge_statements.title: Planar Stable-Set Approximation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the approximation leaf, but an authoritative source is needed for the weighted Baker construction, the treewidth consequence of the chosen layering, and the stated runtime dependence on epsilon.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A graph on vertex set V is a threshold graph if there exists w:V\to\mathbb{R} such that, for all distinct u,v\in V, uv\in E if and only if w(u)+w(v)>0. Equivalently, neither G nor \bar G has an induced subgraph isomorphic to P_4 or C_4; equivalently, G and \bar G are trivially perfect. Every threshold graph is both a split graph and a permutation graph, but the converse fails: P_4 is split and permutation but is not threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A threshold graph admits real vertex weights for which two distinct vertices are adjacent exactly when their weight sum is positive. Equivalently, neither the graph nor its complement contains an induced four-vertex path or four-cycle, or, equivalently, both are trivially perfect. Threshold graphs are split and permutation graphs, but the four-vertex path shows that being both split and permutation is insufficient.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration, nonsingularity, intersection, and uniqueness properties of maximum cliques and stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a partitionable graph on \(n\) vertices. Then: (i) \(G\) has exactly \(n\) maximum cliques and exactly \(n\) maximum stable sets; (ii) the matrices \(N\) and \(M\) formed from the incidence vectors of the maximum cliques and maximum stable sets, respectively, are nonsingular; (iii) each maximum clique intersects all but one maximum stable set, and each maximum stable set intersects all but one maximum clique; and (iv) for any distinct vertices \(u,v\), there is a unique pair consisting of a maximum clique \(C\) and a maximum stable set \(S\) such that \(u\in C\), \(v\in S\), and \(C\cap S=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partitionable n-vertex graph has exactly n maximum cliques and n maximum stable sets. Their incidence matrices are nonsingular; each member of either family misses exactly one member of the other; and each ordered pair of distinct vertices uniquely determines a disjoint maximum clique and maximum stable set containing the respective vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\mathcal C_{\max}(G)|=|\mathcal S_{\max}(G)|=n,\quad N\text{ and }M\text{ are nonsingular, and properties (iii) and (iv) hold}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-kernel formulation equivalent to the clique-order definition of kernel-solvable graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A kernel of a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) is a set \(S\subseteq V\) that spans no arc and satisfies \(\forall v\in V\setminus S\;\exists u\in S:(v,u)\in A\). A digraph \(D=(V,A)\) is a superorientation of \(G=(V,E)\) if \(\{u,v\}\in E\) if and only if \((u,v)\in A\) or \((v,u)\in A\). Then \(G\) is kernel solvable if and only if, for every superorientation \(D\) of \(G\), the condition that \(D[C]\) has a kernel for every clique \(C\) of \(G\) implies that \(D\) has a kernel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A digraph kernel is an arc-independent vertex set to which every outside vertex has an arc. A superorientation represents every graph edge by one or both directions and has no arcs on nonedges. A graph is kernel solvable exactly when every superorientation having a kernel on each clique-induced subdigraph also has a global kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is kernel solvable}\iff\forall D\text{ superorientation of }G,\;\bigl[(\forall C\text{ clique of }G,\ D[C]\text{ has a kernel})\Rightarrow D\text{ has a kernel}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint definition of three structures used in Berge-graph decomposition theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\). A \(2\)-join is a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) such that \(|V_i|\ge 3\) and each \(V_i\) contains disjoint nonempty sets \(A_i,B_i\), with every \(v_1\in V_1\) and \(v_2\in V_2\) satisfying \(v_1v_2\in E\iff (v_1\in A_1\land v_2\in A_2)\lor(v_1\in B_1\land v_2\in B_2)\). A skew partition is a partition \(V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2\) for which \(G[V_1]\) and \(\overline G[V_2]\) are disconnected. A homogeneous pair is a pair of disjoint sets \(A,B\subseteq V\) such that \(3\le |A|+|B|\le |V|-2\) and, for all \(x,y\in A\cup B\) and \(z\in V\setminus(A\cup B)\), \(xz\in E\) and \(yz\notin E\) imply that \(x\) and \(y\) belong to distinct sets among \(A,B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A 2-join partitions the vertices into two parts of size at least three whose cross edges occur exactly between two designated pairs of nonempty disjoint attachment sets. A skew partition has one side disconnected in the graph and the other disconnected in the complement. A homogeneous pair consists of two disjoint sets of total size between 3 and |V|-2 such that an outside vertex cannot distinguish two vertices in the same set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated partition and adjacency conditions define a 2-join, a skew partition, and a homogeneous pair of }G.
