knowledge_statements.statement_title: Light sets and the family \(\mathcal S\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-set construction used in the combinatorial development of Scarf's lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) and \(N\) be disjoint finite nonempty sets, and for each \(i\in M\) let \(<_i\) be a total order on \(N\). For \(U\subseteq N\), write \(y<_iU\) if \(y<_iu\) for every \(u\in U\), and put \(K:=M\cup N\). A set \(L\subseteq K\) is light if, for every \(j\in N\), there exists \(i\in M\setminus L\) such that \(j\le_i u\) for every \(u\in L\setminus M\). With \(m:=|M|\), define \(\mathcal S:=\{M\}\cup\{L\subseteq K:L\text{ is light and }|L|=m\}\). Every subset of a light set is light, and \(M\) is not light.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is light when every element of N precedes or equals all N-elements of the set in at least one order indexed by an element of M outside the set. The family S consists of M and all light sets of size |M|. Lightness is hereditary, whereas M is not light.
assumptions_latex: \forall i\in M,\;<_i\text{ is a total order on }N.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal S=\{M\}\cup\{L\subseteq M\cup N:L\text{ is light and }|L|=|M|\},\quad (L\text{ light}\land L'\subseteq L)\Rightarrow L'\text{ light},\quad M\text{ is not light}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure and Perfectness of p-Comparability Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-circuit construction, perfectness, proper extension of comparability graphs, induced-hereditary closure, and clique-cover integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A) be a directed graph and U\subseteq V meet every directed circuit of D in exactly one vertex. Define G on V\setminus U by uv\in E(G) exactly when some directed circuit of D contains both u and v. Then G is a p-comparability graph. Every p-comparability graph is perfect and is closed under taking induced subgraphs; every comparability graph is p-comparability, but the converse fails. Moreover every clique is contained in a directed circuit of D, and the minimum fractional clique cover is attained by an integral clique cover, so \bar\chi^*(G)=\bar\chi(G).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a vertex set meets every directed circuit of a digraph exactly once, joining two remaining vertices when they lie on a common directed circuit produces a p-comparability graph. These graphs are perfect and induced-hereditary. They properly contain the comparability graphs, every clique lies on a directed circuit, and the fractional clique-cover optimum has an integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: V(G)=V\setminus U,\quad uv\in E(G)\iff\exists\text{ directed circuit }C:\ u,v\in V(C)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the induced-subgraph quantifier and distinguishes bipartite line graphs from their complements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(k\in\mathbb Z_{+}\). A graph \(H\) is \(k\)-perfect if every induced subgraph \(G=(V,E)\) of \(H\) satisfies
\[
\omega_k(G)=\min_{U\subseteq V}\left(k\chi(G-U)+|U|\right),
\]
where \(\omega_k(G)\) is the maximum cardinality of a union of \(k\) cliques. Comparability graphs, their complements, and complements of line graphs of bipartite graphs are \(k\)-perfect for every \(k\). A line graph of a bipartite graph need not be \(2\)-perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph is k-perfect when every induced subgraph satisfies the stated identity between the largest union of k cliques and the minimum of k times a residual chromatic number plus the number of deleted vertices. Comparability graphs, their complements, and complements of bipartite line graphs satisfy this for every k, whereas a bipartite line graph can fail to be 2-perfect.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ ranges over all induced subgraphs of the graph being classified}.
\omega_k(G)\text{ denotes the maximum size of a union of }k\text{ cliques}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega_k(G)=\min_{U\subseteq V}\left(k\chi(G-U)+|U|\right)\text{ for every induced }G\text{ exactly when the graph is }k\text{-perfect; the stated positive classes and }2\text{-perfection failure hold}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyomino graph min-max and perfection results
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the stated convexity hypotheses, graph constructions, and failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a union of unit squares. Form \(G_P\) on the unit squares of \(P\), joining two squares exactly when an axis-parallel rectangle contained in \(P\) contains both. If every horizontal line meets \(P\) in a convex set, then \(\alpha(G_P)=\bar\chi(G_P)\); orthogonal convexity is a sufficient special case, whereas the corresponding unrestricted and merely simply connected extensions fail. If \(P\) is orthogonally convex, the subgraph of \(G_P\) induced by boundary squares is perfect. If \(P\) is simply connected, the intersection graph of the rectangles contained in \(P\), with adjacency meaning a shared unit square, is perfect. The visibility graph of a horizontally convex polyomino is a permutation graph and hence is perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the graph whose vertices are a polyomino's unit squares and whose edges record containment together in a rectangle lying in the polyomino, horizontal convexity gives equality between the stability number and clique-cover number. Orthogonal convexity also makes the boundary-square subgraph perfect, while unrestricted or merely simple connectivity does not support the earlier min-max claim. For a simply connected polyomino, the intersection graph of its contained rectangles is perfect; the visibility graph of a horizontally convex polyomino is a permutation graph and therefore perfect.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a union of axis-aligned unit squares with integer-coordinate vertices.}
G_P\text{ has the unit squares of }P\text{ as vertices, with adjacency defined by a rectangle contained in }P.
P\text{ is orthogonally convex for perfection of the boundary-square induced subgraph.}
P\text{ is simply connected for perfection of the rectangle-intersection graph.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(G_P)=\bar\chi(G_P)\text{ under horizontal convexity; the stated boundary-square, rectangle-intersection, and visibility graphs are perfect under their respective hypotheses, with the stated weakening failures.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definition of the Schrijver Theta-Prime Parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a nonnegative semidefinite strengthening of the theta bound for the stable-set number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(\mathcal M_G\) be the set of symmetric \(V\times V\) matrices \(M\) such that \(M_{uv}=0\) for distinct adjacent vertices \(u,v\) and \(\operatorname{Tr}M=1\). Then \[\vartheta'(G):=\max\left\{\mathbf 1^{\top}M\mathbf 1\mid M\in\mathcal M_G,\ M\succeq0,\ M\ge0\right\}.\] This parameter is an upper bound on \(\alpha(G)\) and strengthens the usual theta bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a graph G, theta-prime is the maximum of 1-transpose M 1 over symmetric, entrywise nonnegative, positive-semidefinite matrices M having trace one and zero entries on pairs of distinct adjacent vertices. It upper-bounds the stable-set number and is at least as sharp as the usual theta bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \vartheta'(G)=\max\{\mathbf1^{\top}M\mathbf1:M\in\mathcal M_G,\ M\succeq0,\ M\ge0\},\qquad \alpha(G)\le\vartheta'(G)

Its stable-set inequality weights the center by half the rim length minus one and dominates the rim's odd-cycle inequality. The W system combines these inequalities with nonnegativity, clique, and odd-cycle constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an inequality-class relaxation and records the algorithmic consequence of exactness and polynomial-time membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a class \(\mathcal L\) of valid inequalities for \(\operatorname{STAB}(G)\), define \(\mathcal L\operatorname{STAB}(G):=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^V:x\text{ satisfies every inequality in }\mathcal L\}\). The graph \(G\) is \(\mathcal L\)-perfect if \(\mathcal L\operatorname{STAB}(G)=\operatorname{STAB}(G)\). If membership in \(\mathcal L\operatorname{STAB}(G)\) is decidable in polynomial time, then optimization over this relaxation is polynomial-time solvable and hence so is the stable-set problem on every \(\mathcal L\)-perfect graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any class L of valid stable-set inequalities, L-STAB(G) consists of the nonnegative vectors satisfying all inequalities in L. A graph is L-perfect when this relaxation equals its stable-set polytope. Polynomial-time membership for the relaxation yields polynomial-time optimization and therefore a polynomial-time stable-set algorithm on L-perfect graphs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural recognition criterion from the Strong Perfect Graph Theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite simple graph \(G\) is perfect if and only if neither \(G\) nor its complement contains an induced odd cycle of length at least five. Equivalently, \(G\) is perfect exactly when it contains no odd hole and no odd antihole. This characterization yields verifiable obstruction certificates for nonperfection. Moreover, perfect-graph recognition is solvable in polynomial time: a recognition algorithm either declares \(G\) perfect or returns an induced odd hole or odd antihole witnessing that it is not perfect.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite perfect graph \(G=(V,E)\) and binary-encoded rational weights \(w\in\mathbb{Q}^{V}\), let \(U:=\{v\in V:w_v\ge 0\}\). Compute a maximum-weight stable set of the perfect induced subgraph \(G[U]\) by exact polynomial-time optimization over \(\operatorname{TH}(G[U])=\operatorname{STAB}(G[U])\), reconstruct an optimal incidence vector, and return its support. Because no optimal stable set needs a negative-weight vertex, the returned set is maximum-weight for the original instance \((G,w)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-preserving transfer between clique and stable-set optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every subset \(S\subseteq V\), \(S\) is a clique of \(G\) if and only if \(S\) is a stable set of \(\overline G\). Therefore the identity map on vertex subsets preserves weights and gives \[\omega(G,w):=\max_{S\text{ clique in }G}\sum_{v\in S}w_v=\max_{S\text{ stable in }\overline G}\sum_{v\in S}w_v=\alpha(\overline G,w).\] Likewise, \(\alpha(G,w)=\omega(\overline G,w)\). Since \(G\) is perfect if and only if \(\overline G\) is perfect, polynomial-time weighted optimization transfers in both directions within the perfect-graph class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cliques of a graph are exactly stable sets of its complement, preserving weights, optimum values, and membership in the perfect-graph class.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight-Regime Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates integral multicoloring demands from rational fractional weights and invalid negative demands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite perfect graph. For every demand vector \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\), the integral weighted coloring identity is \[\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S(G)}y_S:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)},\ \sum_{S\ni v}y_S\ge w_v\ (v\in V)\right\}=\max_{K\in\mathcal K(G)}\sum_{v\in K}w_v.\] This formulation does not extend literally to nonintegral demands because its left side is integer-valued. Replacing \(y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)}\) by \(y\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)}\) defines fractional weighted coloring instead. Negative coordinates are outside the demand interpretation and make the displayed covering model inappropriate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integral clique–coloring identity uses nonnegative integer demands. Rational or real demands require fractional coloring, while negative weights are not valid coloring demands.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S(G)\) and \(\mathcal K(G)\) contain all stable sets and cliques, including the empty set.
The integral identity is asserted only for \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G,w)=\omega(G,w)\) in the integral nonnegative regime; nonintegral and negative weights require different formulations.

notation.meaning: family of stable sets of G
integral coloring demand at vertex v

review_flags: Exact weighted perfect-graph theorem locator is absent from the supplied inventory hints.
The fractional and negative-weight boundary requires source confirmation.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Coloring on Perfect Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral vertex-demand form of the weighted perfect-graph theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite perfect graph and let \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{V}\). Assign a nonnegative integer multiplicity \(y_S\) to every stable set \(S\) so that each vertex \(v\) is covered at least \(w_v\) times. Then \[\chi(G,w):=\min\left\{\sum_{S\in\mathcal S(G)}y_S:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal S(G)},\ \sum_{S\ni v}y_S\ge w_v\ (v\in V)\right\}=\max_{K\in\mathcal K(G)}\sum_{v\in K}w_v=: \omega(G,w).\] Thus a maximum-weight clique is the exact dual obstruction to an integral weighted coloring of a perfect graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integer vertex demands on a perfect graph, the minimum number of stable-set color classes equals the maximum total demand of a clique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\chi(G,w)=\omega(G,w)\).

notation.meaning: minimum number of stable-set color classes satisfying demands w
maximum total vertex demand over a clique

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the interval-coloring parameter and superperfection, and records the unit-weight and comparability-graph results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) and \(w:V\to\mathbb Z_{+}\). A \(k\)-interval coloring assigns each vertex \(v\) an open subinterval of \([0,k]\) of length \(w(v)\), such that adjacent vertices receive disjoint intervals. Let \(\chi_{\mathrm{int}}(G,w)\) be the minimum feasible value of \(k\). If \(w(v)=1\) for every \(v\), then \(\chi_{\mathrm{int}}(G,w)=\chi(G)\). The graph \(G\) is superperfect if, for every \(w:V\to\mathbb Z_{+}\),
\[
\chi_{\mathrm{int}}(G,w)=\max\left\{\sum_{v\in K}w(v):K\text{ is a clique of }G\right\}.
\]
Every comparability graph is superperfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interval coloring assigns each vertex an interval whose length is its integral weight, with adjacent vertices receiving disjoint intervals. The interval chromatic number is the smallest containing length k. Unit weights recover ordinary chromatic number. A graph is superperfect when this parameter equals the maximum total clique weight for every integral weight function; every comparability graph is superperfect.
assumptions_latex: \text{Adjacent vertices must receive disjoint open intervals in }[0,k].
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w\equiv1\implies\chi_{\mathrm{int}}(G,w)=\chi(G),\qquad G\text{ is superperfect}\iff\forall w:V\to\mathbb Z_{+},\ \chi_{\mathrm{int}}(G,w)=\max_{K\text{ clique}}\sum_{v\in K}w(v);\ \text{comparability graphs are superperfect}.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Perfect-Graph Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity criterion distinguishing strong polynomiality from bit-length-dependent perfect-graph optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of finite perfect-graph instances \((G,w)\), an exact optimization algorithm is strongly polynomial when the number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|E(G)|\), independently of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of \(w\), and every intermediate rational number has encoding length polynomially bounded by the input length. Consequently, a runtime polynomial in \(|V(G)|+|E(G)|+\langle w\rangle\), or an iteration bound depending on \(\log\|w\|_\infty\), establishes only ordinary polynomiality unless an additional magnitude-independent bound is proved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires an operation bound depending only on graph size, not weight bit length; bit-length- or magnitude-dependent bounds are merely polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite perfect graph supplied in an explicitly represented graph model.
\(w\) is rational input data with finite binary encoding length \(\langle w\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong polynomiality requires a polynomial bound in \(|V|+|E|\) independent of \(\langle w\rangle\) and \(\|w\|_\infty\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the weight vector
